1.overview:
Elkanah of Ramathaim-zophim goes up every year to sacrifice at Shiloh with his two wives. Peninnah has children; Hannah has none, and Peninnah provokes her until she weeps and will not eat. At the sanctuary Hannah prays without a sound and vows that if the LORD gives her a son, he will be the LORD’s all his life and no razor will touch his head. Eli the priest takes her for drunk, hears her out, and blesses her. She bears Samuel, nurses him until he is weaned, and brings him to Eli at Shiloh to stay.

Hannah drives the story. She makes the vow, names the child, and decides when he will go up (v. 22); Elkanah only answers, “Do what seemeth thee good” (v. 23). The priest misreads what he sees and has to be set right before he can bless.

1.hermeneutics:
A childless man praying for a son at a holy place was a known story pattern before Israel. In the Ugaritic tale of Aqhat (14th century BC), King Danel has no son. For six days he gives food and drink to the gods at a temple; on the seventh Baal pleads with El for him, and El grants him a son. Koowon Kim (2011) reads this scene, a similar one in the Kirta epic, and Hannah’s prayer as forms of one type-scene: a childless worshiper, a sanctuary, a go-between, a promise. Beside Danel, Hannah stands out. She is a woman, not a king. She refuses food instead of offering it (vv. 7–8), and her vow gives the son himself back to the LORD. No god appears to her; the go-between is a priest who first takes her for a drunkard, and the promise reaches her as his blessing (v. 17).

The oldest Hebrew copy of Samuel, 4QSam-a from Qumran (1st century BC), often agrees with the Septuagint where both differ from the Masoretic text behind the KJV, and this chapter has several cases. In v. 11 the Septuagint adds that the child will drink no wine or strong drink, and 4QSam-a calls him a Nazirite; at v. 22 the scroll has Hannah give him as “a Nazirite forever.” In v. 23 Elkanah’s “only the LORD establish his word” reads in both “what has gone out of your mouth,” tying his consent to her vow. In v. 24 “three bullocks” is “a three-year-old bull” in both, which fits the single bullock slain in v. 25.

notes: **Ask:** words from the root *sha’al* come 7 times in vv. 17–28 (twice each in vv. 17, 27 and 28, once in v. 20), and once more in 2:20. The last in v. 28, *sha’ul* (“lent”), is spelled like the name Saul, the king Israel will ask for.
**Remember:** Hannah asks the LORD to “remember” her (v. 11), and v. 19 answers with the same verb: “the LORD remembered her.”
**Before the LORD:** she prays, pours out her soul and worships “before the LORD” (vv. 12, 15, 19), and the boy is brought to “appear before the LORD” (v. 22).

The book opens the way stories near the end of Judges do, with “a certain man” of the hill country (compare Judges 13:2; 17:1). The first subsection runs from Elkanah’s household to 2:11, where he goes home and the child stays to minister before Eli, with Hannah’s song as its close.

**Echoes:** Hannah joins Sarah, Rachel and Samson’s mother among barren women whose sons turn Israel’s story (Genesis 21:1–2; 30:22; Judges 13:2–5). Her son, like Samson, is to have no razor on his head (Judges 13:5).

traditions.text: The Church’s footnote to v. 15, where Hannah has “poured out my soul before the LORD,” points to two Book of Mormon prayers in the same words. Enos pours out his whole soul to God for the Nephites, and Amulek tells the Zoramites to pour out their souls in their closets and secret places. Amulek’s counsel describes what Hannah does at Shiloh: private, earnest, and unheard by anyone but God.

Josephus makes Elkanah a Levite of middling rank, which fits the Chronicler’s genealogy placing Samuel’s family among the Kohathites (1 Chronicles 6:33–38). His Hannah tells Eli she has drunk only water. He adds that Samuel’s hair was left to grow and his drink was water, the marks of a Nazirite, and he glosses the name as one “asked of God.”

In this retelling a leaderless Israel casts lots, first by cities and then by men, and the lot leaps out on Elkanah. He refuses to rule and says he would rather die for his own sins than bear the people’s. God answers that Elkanah cannot lead them, but the son of his barren wife will be their prince and prophet, loved “even as I loved Isaac.”

Peninnah’s taunts get words: Hannah is a dry tree, and Jacob’s love did Rachel no good until she bore a child. Hannah prays silently so that, if she is not heard, Peninnah will have nothing new to mock. To Eli’s charge she answers that she is drunk with sorrow and has drunk the cup of her weeping, and Eli, who knows a prophet is to be born of her, keeps it from her.

Here the name Samuel is interpreted “Mighty,” where v. 20 ties it to asking, and Hannah nurses him for two years. When she sets the boy before Eli as the request she sought, Eli answers that it was never hers alone: the people had prayed for it too, and it was promised to the tribes beforehand. Her private vow becomes the answer to Israel’s prayer for a leader in chapter 49.

Rav Hamnuna draws rules for prayer from v. 13. She spoke in her heart, so prayer needs attention; her lips moved, so the words must be said; her voice was not heard, so the standing prayer is said quietly. Eli’s mistake yields one more rule: a drunk person may not pray.

Rabbi Elazar says no one called God “LORD of hosts” until Hannah did in her vow (v. 11); the narrator has already used the title in v. 3. Her argument, as he tells it: you made all the hosts of heaven and earth, so is one son too hard for you? He compares her to a poor man at a king’s feast who asks for a single slice of bread.

The Talmud asks why v. 25 joins the slaughter of the bull to bringing the boy to Eli. Its answer: Samuel saw the men looking for a priest and told them a layman may slaughter an offering, and Eli, though he agreed, held the boy liable for ruling in his teacher’s presence. Hannah intervened with “for this child I prayed” (v. 27) and refused Eli’s offer to pray for a better son.

The Mishnah’s tractate on Nazirites ends with Samuel. Rabbi Nehorai argues that he was one, since the razor (*morah*) of v. 11 is the word used of Samson, who is called a Nazarite (Judges 13:5). Rabbi Yose objects that *morah* could mean fear of man; Nehorai answers that Samuel did fear Saul (16:2), so the word must mean a razor.

Luke gives Mary words from Hannah’s vow in its Greek form. The Septuagint of v. 11 asks God to look on the lowliness (*tapeinosis*) of his handmaid (*doule*), and Mary sings that he “hath regarded the low estate of his handmaiden,” with the same two nouns. She has already called herself the Lord’s handmaid (Luke 1:38).

In his treatise on the Lord’s Prayer the bishop of Carthage holds up Hannah, “a type of the Church,” as the model of praying silently and modestly within the heart, as v. 13 describes, and notes that God heard her. He draws the same lesson from the same verse as the Talmud’s rule on quiet prayer.

2.overview:
Hannah’s prayer becomes a song: the LORD breaks the bows of the mighty, raises the poor from the dust, lets the barren bear seven, and will give strength to his king. Elkanah goes home, and the boy Samuel serves before Eli. Eli’s sons, Hophni and Phinehas, have their servant seize meat from the sacrifices before the fat is burned, and they lie with the women who serve at the tabernacle door. Eli rebukes them mildly and they ignore him. A man of God announces that Eli’s house will be cut off, his two sons will die on one day, and a faithful priest will take their place.

The song’s reversals become the chapter’s plot. Hannah sings that the full hire themselves out for bread (v. 5). The priests who fatten themselves on Israel’s offerings (v. 29) end the chapter with their heirs begging for a priest’s post “that I may eat a piece of bread” (v. 36).

2.hermeneutics:
Horns meant power, and in Mesopotamian art they marked the gods. On the victory stele of Naram-Sin of Akkad (c. 2250 BC, now in the Louvre), the king climbs a mountain over the fallen Lullubi wearing a horned helmet, a headdress otherwise given to gods. Israel’s poets used the same picture: to exalt someone’s horn was to give him strength and victory (Psalms 89:17, 24; 112:9). Hannah’s song opens with her own horn raised and her mouth enlarged over her enemies (v. 1), and it closes with the LORD exalting “the horn of his anointed” (v. 10). A barren woman’s vindication is sung in the language of a conquering king, and the song ends by passing that horn to a king Israel does not yet have.

The song and the scandal both survive in more than one form. The Septuagint inserts into v. 10 lines found in Jeremiah 9:23–24: let not the wise man boast in his wisdom, nor the mighty in his strength, nor the rich in his wealth, but let him who boasts boast in knowing the LORD. Its v. 9 opens with a line that fits Hannah herself, God “granting his petition to him that prays.” In v. 22 the Septuagint and 4QSam-a, the Qumran scroll of Samuel, lack the clause about the women at the tabernacle door, so the sons’ sin there is the meat alone. That clause shares its wording with Exodus 38:8, and many textual critics treat it as a later addition.

notes: **One word, two kinds of servant:** *na’ar* (“child, young man, servant”) comes 7 times in vv. 11–26. It names Samuel (vv. 11, 18, 21, 26), the priest’s servant with the flesh-hook (vv. 13, 15), and the “young men” whose sin was very great (v. 17).

**Honour and contempt:** the root *kabed* (to be heavy, to honour) comes 3 times in vv. 29–30. Eli honours his sons above the LORD, and “them that honour me I will honour.” Its opposite, “lightly esteemed” (*qalal*), returns in 3:13, where the sons make themselves vile.
**Faithful:** the oracle ends on one word used twice in v. 35: a “faithful” priest (*ne’eman*) and a “sure” house built for him.

The chapter straddles two subsections. Hannah’s song and Elkanah’s return home (2:1–11) close the birth story. From v. 12 the subject is Eli’s house, which runs to the end of chapter 3, where the LORD’s word to Samuel confirms the man of God’s oracle (3:11–14).

**Forward:** the sign of v. 34 comes true when Hophni and Phinehas die on one day (4:11). The priesthood leaves Eli’s line when Solomon thrusts out Abiathar, “that he might fulfil the word of the LORD” spoken at Shiloh (1 Kings 2:27).

traditions.text: The Church’s footnote to v. 35, the promise of a faithful priest to replace Eli’s house, points to a short revelation given at Far West. Where men holding office deny the Lord’s name, “others shall be planted in their stead and receive their bishopric.” Both texts treat priestly office as held on condition of faithfulness.

To v. 30, on God honouring those who honour him, the footnotes add Acts 10:35 and Nephi’s teaching to his brothers that the Lord “esteemeth all flesh in one” and favors the righteous. Nephi applies the rule to whole peoples; the man of God applies it to a priestly family that had been promised it would walk before the LORD for ever.

Counts Hannah among Israel’s seven prophetesses and finds the proof in v. 1. She sang that her horn was exalted, not her flask: David and Solomon, anointed from a horn, founded lasting lines, while Saul and Jehu, anointed from a flask, did not. Her song thus foretold which kings would endure.

The Aramaic translation opens with Hannah praying “in a spirit of prophecy” and turns the song into a forecast of Israel’s history. It finds in it Samuel’s victories, his grandson Heman the singer, the ark coming back on a new cart, Macedon’s fall before the Hasmoneans, the sons of Haman, the end of Rome, and Gog. Its v. 10 ends with the LORD magnifying the kingdom of his anointed, a royal reading Augustine also gives the verse (below).

Hannah calls on her breasts to nurse one whose words will enlighten the people, and the people anoint the boy at Shiloh. Eli pleads with his sons to repent, reminding them that Phinehas entrusted the priesthood to him; they answer that they will repent when they are old. The writer says repentance was then withheld from them because they had always rebelled, his reading of v. 25, “because the LORD would slay them.”

Josephus calls the sons unjust to men and impious toward God: they took some gifts as their due and others by violence, and were guilty of “impurity with the women that came to worship God at the tabernacle.” His Bible had the clause the Septuagint lacks (see Hermeneutics). Eli, he says, was angry and expected God to punish them.

Rabbi Yohanan ben Torta says the tabernacle at Shiloh was destroyed for two sins found in it: sexual immorality (v. 22) and contempt for holy offerings (v. 17). Rabbi Jonathan holds that anyone who says Eli’s sons sinned with the women is mistaken. In his reading they delayed the bird-offerings of women after childbirth, keeping them from going home, and Scripture counts it as if they had lain with them.

Rabbi Yohanan reads the end of v. 8, where the LORD has set the world on “the pillars of the earth,” as a saying about the righteous. God saw that they were few, so he planted some in every generation, and the world rests on them. The same passage says no righteous person dies before another like him is born, and its example is Eli and Samuel (see chapter 3).

Mary’s song follows Hannah’s reversals: the Lord puts down the mighty from their seats, exalts the lowly, fills the hungry and sends the rich away empty (Luke 1:52–53; compare vv. 4–8), and the Church’s footnote to v. 1 points there. Luke also describes the boy Jesus in Samuel’s terms; as v. 26 says of Samuel, he grew “in favour with God and man.”

Augustine reads the song as prophecy and says Hannah’s name means “His grace.” The barren woman who bears seven is the Church among the nations, seven marking its completeness. He asks how Hannah could sing of a king before Israel had one, and answers from v. 10 that the anointed is Christ, together with the whole body of believers joined to its head.

The man of God’s oracle, Augustine argues, was not fulfilled in Samuel, who was not of Aaron’s line, but in Christ, “the true Priest of the New Testament.” The sure house of v. 35 is the eternal Jerusalem. The survivor who crouches for a piece of silver stands for the remnant of Israel who come to believe, and the bread they ask for is the Christian sacrifice.

3.overview:
The boy Samuel lies down in the LORD’s house at Shiloh, where the ark is, before the lamp of God has gone out. A voice calls his name, and he runs to Eli, thinking the old priest called. After the third time Eli understands and tells him to answer, “Speak, LORD; for thy servant heareth.” The LORD comes, stands, calls again, and tells Samuel that the judgment already spoken against Eli’s house is about to fall, because Eli knew his sons’ sin and did not restrain them. In the morning Samuel is afraid to tell, but Eli makes him, and accepts it: “It is the LORD.” Samuel grows, and all Israel knows him as a prophet.

Watch the lights. Eli’s eyes have grown so dim he cannot see (v. 2), but the lamp of God has not yet gone out (v. 3). On the night the old priest can no longer see, the boy first hears.

3.hermeneutics:
In Mesopotamia a god could speak to a ruler in the night, and the texts admit that a message might come without its meaning. On Cylinder A of Gudea, ruler of Lagash (c. 2100 BC), Gudea sees his god Ningirsu in a night vision and confesses that he does not understand it, so he goes to the goddess Nanshe, who explains it in every detail. Later Ningirsu comes and stands at the head of the sleeping Gudea, and Gudea wakes trembling to find it was a dream. Samuel’s night has the same outline: a sleeper at a sanctuary, a call he cannot place, an elder who tells him what it is, and a God who comes and stands (v. 10). The differences carry the chapter. Samuel is a boy attendant, not a ruler seeking instructions; Eli interprets nothing and only tells him how to listen; and the message is a sentence against Eli himself.

Verse 13 is one of the places Jewish scribes are said to have softened out of reverence. The Masoretic text says Eli’s sons “made themselves vile,” literally cursed *lahem*, “to them,” an odd phrase. The Septuagint reads that they “spoke evil against God,” and the old lists of the eighteen scribal corrections (*tiqqune soferim*) include this verse, implying an original *Elohim*, “God.” Read that way, v. 13 repeats the charge of 2:17 and 2:25: the sons’ contempt was aimed at the LORD, which is why no sacrifice can purge it (v. 14).

notes: **Call:** *qara* (“call”) comes 12 times, all but the last in vv. 4–10. The LORD calls four times (vv. 4, 6, 8, 10); then Eli calls Samuel (v. 16), and Samuel answers him as he answered the LORD, “Here am I” (KJV vv. 4, 5, 6, 8, 16).

**Word:** *davar* (“word, thing”) comes 9 times, from the rare word of v. 1 to “the word of the LORD” in v. 21. Verse 7 explains the boy’s mistake: “neither was the word of the LORD yet revealed unto him.”
**Revealed:** the verb *galah* frames Samuel’s call (vv. 7, 21). In 4:21–22 the same verb will say the glory has “departed” from Israel.

Chapter 3 closes the subsection on Eli’s house (2:12–3:21). The LORD’s words to Samuel confirm the man of God’s oracle (2:27–36), and the subsection ends as it began with Samuel serving, now recognized by “all Israel” (v. 20). The next verse, 4:1, brings Samuel’s word to Israel just before the battle that fulfills the sentence.

**Echoes:** the call and answer, “Here am I,” is how Moses (Exodus 3:4) and Isaiah (Isaiah 6:8) answer God. The ear-tingling phrase of v. 11 returns in the prophets’ warnings of Jerusalem’s fall (2 Kings 21:12; Jeremiah 19:3).

traditions.text: The Church’s footnote to v. 1, “there was no open vision,” points to Joseph Smith’s account of a Methodist preacher who told him in 1820 that visions and revelations had ceased with the apostles. It also cites Mormon 1:13–14, where gifts and the Holy Ghost are withdrawn because of wickedness. The footnotes read Samuel’s call as the end of such a silence, as Latter-day Saints read Joseph’s.
traditions.cite: 1 Samuel 3:1, footnote a; Joseph Smith—History 1:21; Mormon 1:13–14

traditions.text: To v. 10, where the LORD “came, and stood, and called,” the footnotes add Joseph Smith’s First Vision, in which one of two personages standing above him called him by name, and the vision in the Kirtland Temple, where Joseph and Oliver Cowdery saw the Lord standing on the pulpit. Joseph, like Samuel, was a boy when he was first called by name.
traditions.cite: 1 Samuel 3:10, footnote a; Joseph Smith—History 1:17; D&C 110:2

traditions.text: To Eli’s failure to restrain his sons (v. 13), the footnotes join two revelations on parents. D&C 68:25 lays the sin on parents in Zion who do not teach their children, and in D&C 93 the Lord tells Frederick G. Williams of the First Presidency that he has not taught his children light and truth, and that this is the cause of his affliction.

Josephus gives Samuel’s age: he was twelve when he began to prophesy. In his version God tells the boy that the priesthood will pass to the family of Eleazar, because Eli loved his sons more than God’s worship. Eli then binds Samuel by oath to repeat the message, since the boy had no wish to grieve him. Afterward, Josephus says, Samuel’s reputation kept growing because everything he prophesied came to pass, his reading of v. 19.

Here Samuel is eight. God reasons that Moses was eighty when he first heard him and still feared the fire, so he will speak to the boy first with a human voice. Samuel hears what sounds like Eli, then his father Elkanah, and Eli, fearing an unclean spirit, makes a rule that a second call may be an evil spirit but a third is an angel, and tells Samuel that the LORD speaks to the right ear. When the word comes, Samuel grieves that his first prophecy is the ruin of the man who raised him, and Eli answers, Can the thing formed answer the one who formed it?

The Aramaic translation moves Samuel out of the holy place: he lay in the court of the Levites, and a voice was heard from the temple where the ark was. Rashi follows it, placing the boy in the Levites’ court among those who guarded the sanctuary. Both readings keep the boy out of the sanctuary proper.
traditions.cite: Targum Jonathan and Rashi on 1 Samuel 3:3

traditions.text: Rabbi Yohanan teaches that no righteous person leaves the world until another like him has arisen, citing “the sun also ariseth, and the sun goeth down” (Ecclesiastes 1:5): before Eli’s sun set, Samuel’s had already risen. David Kimhi reports a midrash that applies this to v. 3, taking the lamp of God not yet out as the lamp of prophecy still burning in Eli when it passed to Samuel.

The rabbis ask how a sentence sworn by oath (v. 14) can be lifted. Rava says Eli’s house cannot be atoned by sacrifice or offering but can be by Torah study; Abaye adds deeds of kindness. It adds that Rabbah and Abaye were both of Eli’s line: Rabbah, who gave himself to study, lived forty years, and Abaye, who also did deeds of kindness, lived sixty.

Preaching in the temple after healing a lame man, Peter dates the line of prophets from this chapter: “all the prophets from Samuel and those that follow after” foretold the days of Christ. Moses comes first in his speech as the prophet like whom another would be raised (Acts 3:22), and then Samuel, recognized in v. 20 by all Israel, heads every later prophet.

Writing for bishops, Gregory makes Eli the warning against leniency. Overcome by false affection, Eli would not punish his sons, and so he struck himself down with them before the strict Judge (4:17–18), and was told that he honoured his sons more than God (2:29). A ruler, Gregory argues, can sin more gravely by treating wrongdoers as equals than by being strict with them.

4.overview:
Israel camps at Eben-ezer and the Philistines at Aphek, and Israel loses about four thousand men. The elders send to Shiloh for the ark of the covenant so that it may save them, and Hophni and Phinehas come with it. The camp’s shout frightens the Philistines, who remember what Israel’s God did to Egypt, but they fight harder and win: thirty thousand Israelites fall, the two priests die, and the ark is taken. A Benjamite runs to Shiloh with the news. Eli, ninety-eight and blind, falls backward from his seat when he hears of the ark and breaks his neck. His daughter-in-law goes into labor, and dying, she names her son Ichabod: “The glory is departed from Israel.”

The deaths are told by the ark. Eli falls when the messenger mentions the ark (v. 18), and the mother names her son for it before her husband (vv. 21–22).

4.hermeneutics:
Losing a god’s image in war did not have to mean the god had lost. Babylon’s statue of Marduk was carried off by the Hittites, later by the Assyrians, and later by the Elamites. The so-called Marduk Prophecy, known from 7th-century BC copies at Assur and probably composed under Nebuchadnezzar I (12th century BC), who brought the statue home, retells those losses in Marduk’s own voice as journeys he chose to make. Israel’s elders assume the ark will save them (v. 3), and the Philistines assume “God is come into the camp” (v. 7). Phinehas’ dying wife reads it another way. Her word for “departed” (*galah*) is the verb for going into exile: the glory has gone, and chapter 5 shows it acting on its own in the enemy’s land.

The battlefield can be placed. Aphek is the large mound at the springs of the Yarkon, at the northern edge of Philistine country. About 3 km east, at the foot of the hills, lies Izbet Sartah, a small Iron Age village of stone-lined grain silos that its excavator, Moshe Kochavi, proposed as Eben-ezer. Its second phase lasted only a few decades before it was abandoned, perhaps under Philistine pressure from Aphek. If the identification holds, Israel camped at the edge of its own farmland, facing an enemy base across the plain.

The Greek text tells the battle a little differently. The Septuagint begins v. 1 with the Philistines gathering for war against Israel, so they are the attackers. It makes Eli ninety, not ninety-eight (v. 15), and says he judged Israel twenty years, not forty (v. 18).

notes: **Taken:** the ark of God “was taken” five times with the same passive verb (*nilqach*: vv. 11, 17, 19, 21, 22). It is the last thing the messenger tells Eli and the last word of the chapter.
**What meaneth the noise?** The Philistines ask it of the shout in Israel’s camp (v. 6), and Eli asks it of the cry in Shiloh (v. 14). Each hears the noise before he knows the news.
**Heavy and glory:** Eli dies because he is “heavy” (*kaved*, v. 18), and Ichabod means “no glory” (*kavod*, vv. 21–22), the same root. In chapter 5 the LORD’s hand is “heavy” on Ashdod (5:6, 11).

Chapter 4 opens the ark narrative (4:1–7:1). It follows the ark from Shiloh to the battlefield and into Philistine hands, and the next two chapters follow it through Philistine cities and back to Israel. The deaths of Hophni and Phinehas on one day fulfill the sign given to Eli in 2:34.

**Backward and forward:** carrying the ark out against God’s word failed once before (Numbers 14:44–45). Ichabod’s line continues: his nephew Ahiah, “the LORD’s priest in Shiloh,” wears the ephod in Saul’s camp (14:3).

traditions.text: The Church’s footnotes set two Book of Mormon passages beside the Philistines’ speech. Their memory of the plagues of Egypt (v. 8) is linked to Nephi’s rebuke of brothers who have forgotten the great things the Lord did for them, so the enemy remembers what Israel’s own sons forget. Their cry to be men (v. 9) is linked to Lehi’s charge, “arise from the dust, my sons, and be men.”

traditions.text: Josephus says the people sent for the ark without considering that the God who had condemned them was greater than the ark, and that it was honoured only for his sake. He adds that Eli sent his sons with it, warning them not to come back into his presence if they survived its capture. Phinehas, he says, was already serving as high priest because Eli had resigned on account of age.

In Josephus Eli sits on a high throne at the gate, and he is not much grieved for his sons, since he had known by revelation that they would die; the ark’s capture is what he had not expected. The child is born at seven months, and Josephus glosses Ichabod as “disgrace.” He then notes that Eli was the first high priest from Aaron’s son Ithamar, and that Eleazar’s line regained the office under Solomon.

When the ark enters the camp, the LORD thunders that this time is like the wilderness, when the ark was taken out without his command, and the ark will be lost to punish both peoples. Goliath reaches the ark, takes it with his left hand, and kills Hophni and Phinehas while Saul son of Kish holds it. The dying mother says one soul is born and four die: her father-in-law, his two sons, and herself.

Pseudo-Philo explains why Samuel is absent from the battle: three days before it, God sent him away to see Ramah, where he would live. When he hears of the defeat he asks why he should go on living now that the ark is not with him. God promises to bring the ark back and to destroy its captors before Samuel dies.

The Mishnah’s rules of war cite the messenger’s report that Israel fled and there was “a great slaughter among the people” (v. 17). Flight is the beginning of defeat, so officers post guards with iron rods at the rear of the army, and Saul’s last battle on Gilboa (31:1) is cited alongside this one.

The rabbis identify the runner from Benjamin (v. 12) as Saul. In the midrash he hears that the tablets of the covenant have been captured, snatches them back from Goliath, and runs to Shiloh the same day; the rabbis argue over whether he covered sixty, a hundred and twenty, or a hundred and eighty miles. Rashi repeats the identification, and Pseudo-Philo (above) already put Saul at the ark in the battle.

The midrash counts three women who died giving birth: Rachel, Eli’s daughter-in-law, and Michal. The pairing with Rachel, who named Ben-oni “as her soul was in departing” (Genesis 35:18), fits v. 21: Phinehas’ wife also names her son as she dies, and gives him a name of loss.

When the Romans besieged Jerusalem in AD 70, Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai sat waiting for news “as Eli had sat and waited,” and the text cites v. 13, his heart trembling for the ark of God. When word came that the Temple was burning, he and his disciples rent their clothes. The loss of Shiloh’s ark becomes the pattern for the loss of the Second Temple.

Rashi cites the Sifre to explain why vv. 7–8 sound like two different speeches. The worthy among the Philistines asked who could save them from such mighty gods. The wicked answered that this was the God who struck Egypt with every plague and had none left to use on them.

Commenting on Psalm 78 (77 in his Bible), Augustine applies its lines on Shiloh to this battle. The strength and beauty God gave into captivity is the ark, “whereby they thought themselves invincible.” The widows who were not lamented include Phinehas’ wife, who died in childbirth amid the confusion and could not be mourned with a proper funeral.

A Gallic chronicler retelling the Bible in brief. He has the Philistines, terrified at the sight of the ark as if by God’s presence, nearly flee before they rally, and he blames Eli for reproofs too gentle to serve as discipline. He gives Eli twenty years, the Septuagint’s figure (see Hermeneutics).

5.overview:
The Philistines carry the captured ark to Ashdod and set it beside the image of their god Dagon. Next morning Dagon lies on his face before the ark. They stand him up, and the following morning he is down again, his head and both hands broken off on the threshold. Then the LORD’s hand falls on Ashdod with tumors and death. The ark is moved to Gath, where tumors break out on small and great, and then to Ekron, whose people cry out as it arrives. The Philistine lords meet and agree to send it home.

The captured God fights alone. No Israelite appears in the chapter, and no prophet or priest explains anything; the Philistines name the cause themselves: “his hand is sore upon us, and upon Dagon our god” (v. 7).

5.hermeneutics:
Victors brought their enemies’ sacred objects home and set them before their own gods. Mesha, king of Moab, boasts on his stele (c. 840 BC) that he took the vessels of YHWH from Nebo and dragged them before his god Chemosh. Setting the ark “by Dagon” in Dagon’s house (v. 2) was the same act: a captured god displayed as tribute to the winner. The next two mornings turn the display around. Dagon lies face down “before the ark of the LORD,” the posture of a subject before his king, and the second time his head and hands lie broken off on the threshold.

Plague was a god’s hand. About 1350 BC the king of Alashiya (Cyprus) wrote to the pharaoh to explain a small shipment of copper: the hand of Nergal, his lord, had killed the men of his land, and not one copper-worker was left (Amarna letter EA 35). Nergal was the Mesopotamian god of plague and the dead. The Philistines use the same idiom: the hand of the LORD is heavy on them (vv. 6, 9, 11). They read their sickness the way their world did, as the act of an offended god, and their question is only which god and what he wants.

The text itself handles the disease delicately. In vv. 6, 9 and 12 the consonants written in the Hebrew spell *ofalim*, “swellings,” but the Masoretes marked them to be read aloud as *tehorim*; the Talmud lists this word among coarse terms that are read in a refined form (Megillah 25b, on Deuteronomy 28:27). The Septuagint also differs on the route: in v. 10 it sends the ark from Gath to Ascalon, not Ekron.

notes: **Dagon and the ark:** Dagon is named 11 times in vv. 2–7 and the ark 12 times in the chapter. After v. 7 Dagon is never named again; the ark goes on alone.

**Hands:** Dagon’s hands lie cut off on the threshold (v. 4), while the LORD’s hand (*yad*) acts in vv. 6, 7, 9 and 11. It is “heavy” (*kabed*) in vv. 6 and 11, the root of the glory that departed in 4:21–22.

**Rising alarm:** each city fares worse. Ashdod is destroyed and smitten (v. 6), Gath suffers “a very great destruction” (v. 9), and Ekron cries out as soon as the ark arrives (v. 10), until “the cry of the city went up to heaven” (v. 12).

Chapter 5 is the middle of the ark narrative (4:1–7:1). Chapter 4 ended with the glory gone from Israel; here it acts in exile, and 6:1 continues with seven months in Philistine country and the plan to send the ark back.

**Echoes:** the Philistines who recalled the plagues on Egypt (4:8) now suffer them. Psalm 78:66 sums up the episode: the LORD “smote his enemies in the hinder parts.” The LORD’s hand stays against the Philistines “all the days of Samuel” (7:13).

traditions.text: The Church’s footnote to v. 9, where the LORD’s hand is against Gath, gathers Restoration passages on the hand of God against peoples. Moroni introduces the Jaredites as a people destroyed by the hand of the Lord, and the revelation on war of December 1832 warns that plague, famine and earthquake will make the nations feel “the chastening hand of an Almighty God.” Mormon 5:23 asks readers whether they know they are in the hands of God.

traditions.text: Rabbi Yohanan and Resh Lakish disagree about why the Philistines set the ark beside Dagon (v. 2). Rabbi Yohanan says they meant to honour it, reasoning that one god should dwell beside another. Resh Lakish says they meant the reverse: this one conquered and that one was conquered, so let the conquered serve the conqueror. His reading is the victor’s custom seen on the Mesha stele (see Hermeneutics).

The same two rabbis argue whether a broken idol stays forbidden. Rabbi Yohanan cites vv. 4–5: Dagon was broken, yet his priests still honoured the threshold, so worshipers do not give up a broken god. Resh Lakish answers that they abandoned Dagon and began to worship the threshold instead, saying Dagon’s spirit had left the image and rested there.

Josephus says the Philistines put the ark beside Dagon “as one of their spoils,” and in the morning found Dagon paying it worship, lying prostrate in adoration. The disease at Ashdod is a sudden, fatal dysentery, and mice rise from the ground to ruin the crops. Like the Septuagint he sends the ark to Ascalon, and has it go round all five cities.

The Philistines bring the ark into Dagon’s temple to ask Dagon about their next campaign and find him fallen, his hands and feet laid before the ark. They crucify his priests, and on the second morning find the same. God had promised Samuel that the Philistines would perish by scorpions and creeping things, and at Ekron the creeping things destroy pregnant women, nursing mothers and infants.

The midrash ties this chapter to the Philistines’ boast in 4:8. Their wicked had said Israel’s God spent his plagues on Egypt and had none left, so God answers with a plague never seen before: a mouse comes up from the deep as a man sits at his needs and drags out his bowels. When they turn to seats, the mouse tells the seat it is the messenger of the One who spoke and the world came to be, and the seat splits.

On v. 5 Kimhi cites a midrash of Rabbi Jeremiah: Israel was more zealous in idolatry than the nations. Of the Philistines it is written that they would not tread on Dagon’s threshold, but of Israel the prophet says, “I will punish all those that leap on the threshold” (Zephaniah 1:9). The Philistine custom becomes a rebuke to Israel.

Kimhi reports a tradition that Dagon was shaped like a fish from the navel down and like a man above, which is why he was called Dagon (from *dag*, “fish”). On that reading “only the stump of Dagon” left in v. 4 means only the fish-part remained once the head and hands broke off. Modern scholars derive the name from a Semitic word for grain instead.

Rashi explains the *tehorim* of v. 6 as a disease of the rectum and adds that mice entered the bowels of the people of Ashdod and dragged out their entrails. On v. 9 he notes a Masoretic spelling: the verb “had emerods” is written with one letter and read as another, giving “they were struck in their hidden parts.” His mice match those of Josephus and Sulpicius Severus and the golden mice sent back with the ark (6:4–5).

In his short sacred history the Gallic writer says the image “dedicated to a demon” fell when the ark was brought in and was torn to pieces the next night when set up again. He then has mice spring up across the country and kill many thousands with venomous bites, so that the men of Ashdod move the ark to escape. Like Josephus and the Septuagint, he sends it on from Gath to Ascalon, where the chief men of the nation decide to return it to the Hebrews.

6.overview:
After seven months of plague the Philistines ask their priests and diviners how to be rid of the ark. Send it home with a trespass offering, they answer: five golden emerods and five golden mice, one for each lord. Then test it. Two milk cows that have never worn a yoke are hitched to a new cart and their calves shut up at home. If the cows head for Israel’s border, the God of Israel struck them; if not, it was chance. The cows go straight to Beth-shemesh, lowing all the way. The harvesters rejoice, burn the cart and offer the cows, but the LORD strikes men who looked into the ark.

The danger does not stay on the Philistine side of the border. Beth-shemesh asks, “Who is able to stand before this holy LORD God?” (v. 20) and sends the ark on to Kirjath-jearim, just as Ashdod, Gath and Ekron passed it from city to city in 5:8–11.

6.hermeneutics:
In the *Iliad*, when plague sweeps the Greek camp at Troy, Achilles proposes asking “some priest or prophet” why Apollo is angry. The seer Calchas names the cause, a priest’s daughter held captive, and the plague ends only when she is sent home with a great sacrifice (Iliad 1). The priest had prayed to Apollo as lord of Sminthe, and Strabo explains the title from a local word for mice; the god’s statue at Chryse stood with a mouse beneath its foot (Geography 13.1.48, 64). Philistines with Aegean roots reason the same way. They call priests and diviners (v. 2), read the plague as a god’s anger over a captured holy thing, and send it back with gifts. What chapter 6 adds is the test of v. 9, built to tell a god’s hand from chance.

The Hebrew first mentions mice in v. 4, as if the reader already knew of them. The Septuagint does tell of them: mice spring up in Ashdod’s land (5:6), and the land swarms with them (6:1). The “emerods” were swellings, and many readers have linked swellings and rodents with bubonic plague. The text names no disease.

Verse 19’s number is a known puzzle. The Hebrew reads “seventy men, fifty thousand men,” with no “and” between them, for a single town. A few medieval Hebrew manuscripts lack the fifty thousand, and Josephus counts seventy. The NIV and NRSV print seventy, while the NET keeps the longer number for lack of stronger evidence. The Septuagint opens the verse differently: “the sons of Jechonias” were displeased with the men of Beth-shemesh.

notes: **Sending:** the verb *shalach*, “send,” comes 6 times (vv. 2, 3 twice, 6, 8, 21). The Philistines want the ark sent away, and the chapter ends with Israelites sending for someone else to take it.
**Returning:** *shuv* comes 8 times, most often for “returning” the trespass offering (*asham*, 4 times: vv. 3, 4, 8, 17). The gift pays back a debt to the God whose ark was taken.
**The ark** is named 10 times. The test of v. 9 is answered in v. 12: the cows turn neither right nor left.

Chapter 6 closes the ark narrative (4:1–7:1), where Samuel drops out of sight between 4:1 and 7:3. The unit ends when the ark comes to rest in Abinadab’s house (7:1), and Samuel’s call to repentance opens the next scene.

**Forward:** the ark stays at Kirjath-jearim, also called Baalah (Joshua 15:9), until David brings it up on another new cart from Abinadab’s house, and Uzzah dies for touching it (2 Samuel 6:2–7; 1 Chronicles 13:6–7).

traditions.text: Josephus gives the Philistine debate a skeptic’s side: some argued that the ark had no such power, since God would not have let it fall into human hands, and that nature at certain times simply brings such changes on bodies, land and crops. The counsel that won called the five golden images a thank offering for their survival. He also adds a crossroads, where the cart is left where three ways meet and the cows choose the road to the Hebrews as if someone were driving them.

His account of Beth-shemesh gives the reason for the deaths: the men struck were not priests and so were not worthy to touch the ark, yet they came near it. He makes Abinadab a Levite praised for his righteous life, whose sons served as the ark’s keepers for its twenty years at Kirjath-jearim. He also says the ark had been only four months with the Philistines, where v. 1 says seven.

Here the plague is “creeping things” that kill pregnant women, nursing mothers and infants, and Dagon’s priests are put to death to no purpose. So the wise men choose nursing cows for the test: if they leave their own young behind, the ark is to blame. Like Josephus, Pseudo-Philo sets the cart at a fork of three roads near Ekron, and the cows take the right-hand road to Judea while lowing for their calves.

The ending departs from Samuel. The Philistines bring the ark back to Shiloh with timbrels, pipes and dances and offer golden seats, which James’s notes connect with the Septuagint’s word for the emerods. It numbers the dead by category, 75,000 pregnant women, 65,000 infants, 55,000 nursing mothers and 25,000 men, and says the land then had rest seven years.

The rare verb for the cows going “straight” in v. 12 (*vayisharna*) was heard as “they sang” (*shirah*). The rabbis then debate the song. Proposals include the Song of the Sea (Exodus 15), Isaiah 12:4, Psalms 98, 99 and 93, and one sage gives an unbiblical song in praise of the acacia-wood ark overlaid with gold.

The same page asks how cows, which are female, could be offered as a burnt offering (v. 14). One answer is that it was a one-time ruling made for an emergency, outside the usual law; another is that a private altar allowed it, as with Samuel’s nursing lamb in 7:9. The rabbis also argue over the cows’ age, since animals that had already calved could not be very young.

Why should looking bring death? Rabbi Abbahu and Rabbi Elazar disagree. One says the men kept reaping while they bowed, never stopping work out of reverence for the ark; the other says they also spoke slightingly of it, asking who had angered it so that it let itself be captured. They also divide the number of v. 19: seventy men each worth fifty thousand, or fifty thousand each worth the seventy of the Sanhedrin.

The Aramaic paraphrase explains the offense as rejoicing at the sight of the ark while it was uncovered. It also solves the number by splitting it between two groups: seventy of the elders of the people and fifty thousand of the congregation, a different answer from the Talmud’s on the same verse. Rashi later reports both readings side by side.

traditions.text: Rashi explains why the test uses unyoked nursing cows: such animals cannot pull a cart and will yearn for their young, so if they go, the ark itself must be drawing them. On v. 18 he takes “Abel” as the same great stone of v. 14, its name changed by one letter, and reads it as “mourning,” because Beth-shemesh mourned its dead there (v. 19).

traditions.source: Gregory the Great, Morals on Job
traditions.text: Gregory reads the cows as a picture of affection that is felt but kept under control. They moan for the calves shut up at home, yet “never alter their steps” from the path, and so those who carry the ark of God’s law may pity their kin without turning aside from righteousness. Since Beth-shemesh means house of the sun, he adds, the road leads toward eternal light. He finds the same pattern in Job, who mourned his children and still blessed God.

7.overview:
The men of Kirjath-jearim lodge the ark in Abinadab’s house, and it stays there twenty years while Israel laments after the LORD. Samuel tells them to put away Baalim and Ashtaroth and serve the LORD only. At Mizpeh they pour out water before the LORD, fast and confess. The Philistines march on the gathering; Samuel offers a nursing lamb and cries to the LORD, who thunders on the Philistines and routs them. Samuel sets up a stone, Eben-ezer, saying, “Hitherto hath the LORD helped us,” and the lost cities return. He judges Israel on a yearly circuit and lives at Ramah.

The same name marks a defeat and a victory. At the first Eben-ezer Israel carried the ark into battle and lost it (4:1–11). Here the ark stays in Abinadab’s house, Israel repents and Samuel prays, and the Philistines are the ones who flee.

7.hermeneutics:
Kirjath-jearim is Deir el-Azar, a hill above Abu Ghosh about 13 km west-northwest of Jerusalem. Its Arabic name seems to preserve “Monastery of Eleazar,” after the ark’s keeper in v. 1. Excavations begun in 2017 by Israel Finkelstein, Thomas Römer and Christophe Nicolle traced a flat summit platform of about 150 by 110 meters. Activity on the hill was light in the early Iron Age and peaked in the 8th century BC. The team reads the compound as a cult and administrative center of Jeroboam II and proposes that the ark story took shape in the northern kingdom; that is one team’s interpretation, not a consensus. The chapter itself treats the hill as a holding place, with the ark in a private house for twenty years (v. 2) and no national shrine around it.

Thunder was a god’s weapon in ancient war reports. In the annals of the Hittite king Mursili II (14th century BC), the Storm-god, “my lord,” shows his might and hurls a thunderbolt that both armies see; it strikes the land of Arzawa and Apasa, the city of King Uhhaziti. Verse 10 uses the same picture with a difference in timing. The LORD thunders while Samuel is still at the altar, before Israel has fought at all, and the men of Israel only pursue (v. 11).

The place-names of v. 12 are uncertain. The Hebrew sets the stone between Mizpeh and “Shen,” literally “the tooth.” The Greek and Syriac read Jeshanah, a town named in 2 Chronicles 13:19, and the NRSV follows them.

notes: **Two hands:** Israel is to be saved “out of the hand of the Philistines” (vv. 3, 8, 14), and in v. 13 “the hand of the LORD” is against the Philistines. *Yad*, “hand,” comes 4 times.
**Judging:** Samuel “judged” at Mizpeh (v. 6), and the verb returns three more times in the closing summary (vv. 15–17), framing the chapter as the record of a judge.
**A judge’s formula:** “the Philistines were subdued” (v. 13) uses the verb of the book of Judges’ victory notices (Judges 3:30; 4:23; 8:28; 11:33).

Verse 1 closes the ark narrative (4:1–7:1); from v. 2 Samuel returns to the story for the first time since 4:1, and 7:2–17 forms a short account of his judgeship. The closing summary (vv. 15–17) rounds off the era of the judges before the elders ask for a king (8:1–5).

**Backward and forward:** Hannah sang that the LORD would “thunder upon” his adversaries (2:10). Samuel later lists himself among the deliverers the LORD sent (12:11) and calls down thunder again at wheat harvest (12:17–18).

traditions.text: The Church’s footnote to v. 3, where Samuel says “If ye do return unto the LORD with all your hearts,” sends readers to Book of Mormon calls in the same terms. In Helaman the Lord promises to turn away his anger if the people repent and return to him. After the great destruction at the Savior’s death, his voice pleads with the spared house of Israel to return with full purpose of heart. Samuel’s condition is the same: the strange gods go first, and deliverance follows.

The footnote to v. 9, where Samuel cries to the LORD for Israel, points to Amulek’s warning to Ammonihah. If not for the prayers of the righteous in the land, he says, the people would already be destroyed, “by famine, and by pestilence, and the sword.” Both passages credit a people’s rescue to one praying person standing between them and judgment.

traditions.date: LDS edition of the King James Bible, 1979
traditions.text: The Church’s Bible Dictionary says that after Eli’s death Samuel became the great prophet and judge of Israel and restored law and order and regular worship in the land, citing this chapter (7:2–17). It adds that though he was not a priest, he performed priestly functions and offered sacrifice at various places, as he does at Mizpeh (v. 9) and at the altar he builds in Ramah (v. 17).

Josephus gives Samuel a speech before Mizpeh: liberty will not come by weapons, bodily strength or allies, but by being righteous, and he will stand surety for God’s promises. He explains that Mizpeh means “watch tower” in Hebrew. The frightened people tell Samuel they are “naked and unarmed,” since they came to pray and take oaths, not to fight.

His battle is larger than the text’s. God first shakes the ground, so that some Philistines lose their footing and others drop into opened chasms, then sends thunder and lightning that nearly burn their faces and shakes the weapons from their hands, so that they flee home naked. Samuel names the stone the Stone of Power, a boundary marking the Philistines’ flight. Josephus then adds that Samuel won back the land from the borders of Gath to Ekron.

Ben Sira’s praise of the fathers recalls this chapter: Samuel called on the Lord when enemies pressed him on every side, “when he offered the sucking lamb,” and the Lord thundered from heaven with a great noise. The Greek then says he destroyed the rulers of the Tyrians. The surviving Hebrew has the princes of the enemy; the Hebrew words for “enemy” and “Tyre” share the same consonants, which explains the Greek.

The water of v. 6 is unexplained in the Hebrew. The Targum reads it as repentance: they poured out their hearts like water before the LORD. Rashi reports the Targum and adds a plain-sense reading, a sign of humility, as if to say “we are before you like this poured-out water,” and takes Samuel’s judging as settling disputes between the people.
traditions.cite: Targum Jonathan and Rashi on 1 Samuel 7:6

traditions.text: The rabbis explain why Samuel sacrifices at Mizpeh and builds his own altar at Ramah instead of offering at one sanctuary. The Mishnah teaches that when Shiloh was destroyed and the tabernacle came to Nob and then Gibeon, private altars became permitted. The Talmud adds a tradition that Shiloh fell when Eli died, and that this is when Samuel began to lead Israel, so his whole judgeship falls in the time of local altars.

Augustine reads v. 12 as a figure of passing from the old covenant to the new. In his Latin Bible the stone stands between the old and the new Massephat (Mizpeh), a name he interprets as “desire,” and Ebenezer means the stone of the helper. That stone, he says, is the mediation of the Savior, by which believers pass from desiring carnal happiness in an earthly kingdom to desiring the truest spiritual happiness in the kingdom of heaven. Since nothing is better than that, he concludes, the Lord helps us “hitherto.”

Hebrews names Samuel with Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah and David among those who “through faith subdued kingdoms.” Of the deeds listed for that group, chapter 7 is the clearest one in Samuel’s own story: a Philistine army routed while he prays at the altar, before Israel draws a sword, and then subdued all his days (v. 13). The letter does not tell Samuel’s story, but the verb it chooses fits this one.

8.overview:
Samuel grows old and makes his sons judges at Beer-sheba, but they take bribes and pervert judgment. The elders come to him at Ramah and ask, “make us a king to judge us like all the nations.” Displeased, Samuel prays. The LORD tells him to listen: the people have rejected the LORD, not Samuel, as they have since Egypt. Samuel must warn them what a king will do. He will take their sons, daughters, fields and servants and a tenth of their harvest and flocks, and they will cry out and not be heard. The people refuse: they want a king to judge them and fight their battles. The LORD says to give them one.

Three times the LORD tells Samuel, “Hearken unto their voice” (vv. 7, 9, 22). He grants the request he calls a rejection of himself, and sends it forward with a warning attached.

8.hermeneutics:
Samuel’s “manner of the king” (vv. 11–17) describes how kingship in Canaan actually worked. In 1956 Isaac Mendelsohn compared it with Akkadian texts from Ugarit and Alalakh in Syria (14th–13th century BC). There kings kept a class of chariot warriors in their service, drafted men for royal estates and workshops, and seized land and granted it to their officials. Samuel’s list follows the same order: sons for chariots and horsemen (v. 11), plowing, harvest and weapon-making (v. 12), and the best fields handed to the king’s servants (v. 14). The warning describes the known practice of the very nations Israel wanted to resemble.

The royal tithe was real as well. A tithe is attested at Ugarit in the 14th century BC, and one text there records the king granting the tithe of a whole town to an official for loyal service. Verse 15 says the same: the king will take a tenth of seed and vineyards “and give to his officers, and to his servants.” Israel’s law had already called the tithe the LORD’s (Leviticus 27:30). Here a king claims a tenth of seed and flock for himself (vv. 15, 17).

The Hebrew of v. 16 has the king take “your goodliest young men” between the servants and the asses. The Septuagint reads “your good herds,” which pairs men and women servants with cattle and asses, and the NRSV follows it. The two readings differ by a few letters in Hebrew.

notes: **Hearken:** *shama’* comes 5 times, four of them with “the voice”: the LORD’s “hearken unto the voice” (vv. 7, 9, 22) against the people who “refused to obey the voice of Samuel” (v. 19).
**Take:** the verb *laqach* comes 4 times in the warning (vv. 11, 13, 14, 16), with “take the tenth” twice more (vv. 15, 17). It began with the sons who “took bribes” (v. 3).
**Servants:** the king’s servants get your fields and tithes (vv. 14, 15), your own servants are taken (v. 16), and the list ends, “ye shall be his servants” (v. 17).

Chapter 8 opens the second part of the book, “A king like the nations: Saul” (8:1–15:35). The judges’ order fails the way Eli’s house did, through sons unfit to succeed their father (2:12; 8:3). The chapter ends with no king named; the next scene starts with a Benjamite looking for his father’s asses (9:1–3).

**Backward and forward:** Deuteronomy 17:14 foresees Israel saying, “I will set a king over me, like as all the nations.” Gideon had refused the crown because “the LORD shall rule over you” (Judges 8:23), and Samuel returns to the request in his farewell (12:12, 19).

traditions.text: A thematic parallel. When the Jaredites ask their leaders to anoint one of their sons king, the request grieves them, and the brother of Jared warns, “Surely this thing leadeth into captivity.” Two generations later Corihor rebels against his father, King Kib, gathers an army and takes him captive, and Ether notes that this brought to pass the brother of Jared’s saying. Samuel’s warning runs the same direction, ending with the people as the king’s servants (v. 17), and both records follow the request to the loss of freedom it was warned to bring.

The Church’s footnote to v. 7, “Hearken unto the voice of the people,” points to King Mosiah’s law for the Nephites. He tells them it is not common for the voice of the people to desire what is wrong, so they should do their business by that voice. But if the time comes that the voice of the people chooses iniquity, then the judgments of God will come. Israel’s voice in 1 Samuel 8 is heard and granted, with that kind of warning attached.

The footnote to v. 18, “the LORD will not hear you in that day,” points to Limhi’s people in bondage to the Lamanites. There the Lord was slow to hear their cry because of their iniquities, yet he did hear: he softened their captors’ hearts and eased their burdens, though he did not yet free them. The Book of Mormon account shows what Samuel’s warning can look like when a people cries out under a yoke of its own making.

The midrash reads the warning of v. 18 forward into Israel’s history. When kings arose over Israel and began to oppress them, it says, God answered their complaint: did you not forsake me and ask for a king yourselves? It pairs this with the psalm’s counsel, “Put not your trust in princes” (Psalm 146:3), and praises the one who trusts in God instead.

Josephus places Samuel’s sons at Bethel and Beer-sheba, where v. 2 has both at Beer-sheba, and says they turned to luxury and costly living. He explains Samuel’s displeasure by his politics: Samuel hated kingly government and was very fond of aristocracy. The request so troubled him that he could neither eat nor sleep and lay awake all night.

In his retelling of vv. 11–17 the king uses Israel’s sons “as if they were slaves bought with money.” Daughters will do the work of women slaves who fear the whip, and the people’s land goes to the king’s eunuchs and bodyguards. The people answer that it is no absurdity to have the same government as their neighbors.

Here the people cite Moses, that they must surely appoint a prince over them (Deuteronomy 17), and Samuel grieves because they ask “a king before the time.” He fears this means no lasting kingdom yet and no house of the Lord. God answers that he will send them a king who will lay them waste and then be laid waste himself.

The rabbis read this chapter through the law of the king in Deuteronomy 17:14. Rabbi Nehorai calls the request an insult to Israel, citing v. 7, and says they wanted a king only to take up foreign worship, citing “that we also may be like all the nations” (v. 20). Rabbi Judah objects that the Torah commands a king; Israel was punished in Samuel’s day only because they took the initiative and asked too soon.

Was the manner of the king a grant of royal rights or only a warning? Shmuel and Rabbi Yosei say a king may do everything in vv. 11–17. Rav and Rabbi Yehuda say the passage was spoken only to make the people stand in awe of the king. Rabbi Nehorai holds that the whole request was a complaint, and Rabbi Eliezer splits the blame: the elders asked properly for a king “to judge us,” but the ignorant ruined it by adding “like all the nations” (vv. 19–20).

Rashi locates Samuel’s displeasure in the words “to judge us,” as the nations’ kings judge. Commentators on Rashi explain that Deuteronomy 17 permits a king, so the fault was not in asking for one but in the motive, rejecting Samuel to be like the nations. The reading agrees with Rabbi Eliezer in the Talmud.

9.overview:
Kish, a Benjamite, sends his tall son Saul with a servant to find some lost asses. After three days of searching, at Zuph the servant suggests asking the man of God in the nearby city, offering a quarter shekel of silver as a gift. The day before, the LORD had told Samuel that he would send a man of Benjamin to be anointed captain over Israel and save it from the Philistines. Samuel meets Saul at the gate, tells him the asses are found, seats him at the head of about thirty guests, serves him the portion set aside, and lodges him on the roof. At dawn he sends the servant ahead so that he can give Saul the word of God.

Saul goes looking for animals and is found by a prophet. The LORD says, “I will send thee a man” (v. 16), and every step of Saul’s errand turns out to be the way he is sent.

9.hermeneutics:
The servant’s “fourth part of a shekel of silver” (v. 8) was a weight, not a coin. Coins came to the region centuries later. In Saul’s world silver changed hands as cut pieces and scraps weighed on a balance, and a 2018 study of Iron Age silver hoards from the Phoenician coast, including Dor, describes such hacked silver weighed in every transaction. A quarter shekel was a small amount, a courtesy gift rather than a fee. Visitors to a man of God brought something with them (1 Kings 14:3; 2 Kings 4:42), and Saul’s worry that “the bread is spent” (v. 7) assumes that custom.

The cook sets before Saul “the shoulder” (v. 24), the *shoq*, the cut of the leg Leviticus reserves for the priest from peace offerings (Leviticus 7:32–33). Jonathan Greer’s study of animal bones from the sacred precinct at Tel Dan (Iron Age II) found right-side limb bones outnumbering left in a deposit from the priestly area, while the area for common worshipers had more from the left. Portions at a sacred meal were assigned by rank, and the bones bear that out. Samuel had this one held back for Saul before the guests were invited (vv. 23–24), honoring an unknown Benjamite with the best piece at the high place.

Verses 25–26 differ between the Hebrew and the Greek. The Hebrew says Samuel “communed with Saul upon the top of the house.” The Septuagint says they spread a bed for Saul on the roof and he lay down, which fits Samuel calling him from the roof at dawn; the NRSV follows the Greek.

notes: **Finding:** *matsa’*, “find,” comes 7 times: the asses are not found (v. 4), the servant “finds” silver at hand (v. 8), they find the maidens (v. 11), they will find Samuel (v. 13, twice), and the asses are found (v. 20).
**Seer:** *ro’eh* comes 5 times (vv. 9 twice, 11, 18, 19). Saul asks for the seer’s house, and Samuel answers, “I am the seer.”
**Flashback:** vv. 15–17 stop the story to tell what the LORD said a day earlier, so the reader knows before Saul does why Samuel is waiting.

Chapters 9–10 tell how Saul is anointed and then chosen (9:1–10:27). The unit opens the way the book did, with “there was a man” and a family line (1:1), and the asses frame it: lost in 9:3, found in 10:2 and 10:16.

**Backward and forward:** Saul calls Benjamin “the smallest of the tribes” (v. 21), the tribe nearly destroyed in Judges 20:46–48. The word of God promised in v. 27 is spoken in 10:1, when Samuel pours the oil.

traditions.text: On v. 9, “when a man went to inquire of God,” the Church’s footnote points to Joseph Smith’s account of the First Vision. There he says his object in going to inquire of the Lord was to learn which of the churches was right, and that he found the promise of James to be true, that one who lacks wisdom may ask of God. The same footnote lists Book of Mormon and Doctrine and Covenants passages on inquiring of the Lord. The verse’s custom of going to God for an answer becomes, in the Restoration, the opening act of Joseph Smith’s ministry.

The Topical Guide entry “Seer” lists vv. 9 and 19 with Mosiah 8, where Ammon tells King Limhi that “a seer is a revelator and a prophet also.” A seer, he says, can know things past and to come, and no greater gift can a man have. The Church’s Bible Dictionary repeats that a seer is greater than a prophet, names Joseph Smith as the great seer of the latter days, and notes that the First Presidency and the Twelve are sustained as prophets, seers and revelators.

Josephus says Kish valued his she-asses above all his other livestock, and that Saul’s understanding was better even than his looks. When the servant offers the quarter shekel, Josephus remarks that the two did not know the prophet took no such reward. He places the city near Ramah and has Samuel praying every day to learn beforehand whom God would make king, and sitting on his rooftop waiting for the hour God had named.

In Josephus’s version Saul thinks Samuel is mocking him with talk of great things for so small a tribe and family. The guests number seventy, as in the Septuagint, where the Hebrew has about thirty (v. 22), and Samuel orders the royal portion set before Saul. Saul and his servant then sleep at the prophet’s house when the other guests go home.

God tells Samuel at night that the king will come “to-morrow at the sixth hour,” a king who will waste the people and afterward be wasted himself. When Saul protests that he does not understand, since he is only a youth, Samuel answers that his words will be like those of a prophet named Jeremiah. The link is Jeremiah 1:6, where the young Jeremiah protests that he is a child and cannot speak.

The rabbis look for a scriptural source for saying a blessing before eating, and Rabbi Natan finds it in v. 13. The maidens say the people will not eat until the seer comes, “because he doth bless the sacrifice,” so the blessing comes first and the meal after it. Jewish practice of blessing before a meal is tied in part to this verse.

Why do the maidens say so much (vv. 12–13)? One answer is simply that women talk. Shmuel says they drew out the conversation to keep looking at Saul’s good looks (v. 2). Rabbi Yohanan gives a theological answer: one reign may not overlap another by even a hair’s breadth, so the delay kept Saul’s anointing from cutting short Samuel’s leadership.

The rabbis ask what “that which was upon it” means in v. 24, where the cook sets the shoulder before Saul. Rabbi Yohanan says the thigh came with the fat tail resting on it; Rabbi Elazar says with the breast, laid on the thigh for waving as in the peace offering; Rabbi Shmuel bar Nahmani says with the top of the leg. Each answer treats Saul’s portion as a priestly cut of a sacrifice.

Rashi takes v. 9 as an aside by the book’s author, explaining that the one called a prophet today was formerly called a seer. His modern editors note the puzzle this makes for the tradition that Samuel wrote the book. The Targum renders the old custom as going “to seek instruction from before the Lord.”
traditions.cite: Rashi and Targum Jonathan on 1 Samuel 9:9

traditions.text: Augustine dates a new era from Samuel. Abraham, Moses and others before him may rightly be called prophets, he says, but the age of the prophets properly begins when Samuel began to prophesy, “who at God’s command first anointed Saul to be king.” From there he traces prophecy down to the return from Babylon, which suits v. 9’s note that the old seer is now called a prophet.

10.overview:
Samuel pours a vial of oil on Saul’s head, kisses him and names three signs: two men at Rachel’s tomb with news of the asses, three men bound for Beth-el who give him bread, and a band of prophets at the hill of God, among whom he will prophesy and be turned into another man. Then he must wait seven days at Gilgal. The signs come true, and people ask, “Is Saul also among the prophets?” Saul tells his uncle only about the asses. At Mizpeh the lot falls on Benjamin, then the family of Matri, then Saul, who has hidden among the baggage. The people shout, “God save the king,” and Samuel writes the manner of the kingdom in a book.

Saul is made king twice, in secret and in public, and both times he says nothing. He keeps the kingdom from his uncle, hides from the lot, and holds his peace when scoffers despise him (v. 27).

10.hermeneutics:
Pouring oil on the head was how a great king installed a lesser one. In an Amarna letter of the 14th century BC (EA 51), Addu-nirari of Nuhasse in Syria reminds Pharaoh that when Thutmose III made his ancestor king, he “placed oil upon his head.” The letter recalls the act to claim Egypt’s protection: the overlord who anointed a vassal’s house was expected to stand behind it. Samuel’s words in v. 1 put the LORD in the overlord’s place. Saul is anointed captain over “his inheritance,” a ruler set over a people that belongs to someone else, and the title used for him is *nagid*, “captain” (9:16; 10:1), the appointee of a higher king.

The Hebrew of v. 1 is short: Samuel asks whether the LORD has not anointed Saul “captain over his inheritance.” The Septuagint is longer. Samuel says the LORD has anointed Saul ruler over his people Israel, that he will rule and save them from their enemies, and that this will be the sign that the LORD has anointed him ruler over his inheritance. The NET notes argue that a Hebrew copyist’s eye skipped from the first “the LORD hath anointed thee” to the second, dropping everything between, and the NRSV and ESV print the longer text. Read that way, the signs of vv. 2–7 are announced as proof of the anointing. Saul is not only told that he is chosen; he is given things to watch for that will prove it.

notes: **King, delayed:** the word *melekh*, “king,” does not occur from 9:1 to 10:18. Samuel and the LORD say *nagid*, “captain.” It appears first when Samuel quotes the people’s demand (v. 19), and then in their shout (v. 24).
**Prophesying:** the verb *naba’* comes 5 times (vv. 5, 6, 10, 11, 13), and the two “signs” (vv. 7, 9) point to it.
**Taken:** the lot “takes” Benjamin, Matri and Saul (vv. 20–21), the same verb and procedure that found Achan (Joshua 7:14–18).

Chapter 10 completes the unit begun at 9:1: the asses lost in 9:3 are reported found (vv. 2, 16), and the private anointing becomes a public choice. Saul has still done nothing as king, and the scoffers’ question, “How shall this man save us?” (v. 27), is answered in chapter 11 (11:12).
**Forward:** the seven days at Gilgal (v. 8) return when Saul does not wait for Samuel (13:8). The proverb of vv. 11–12 is told again, in darker form, at Naioth (19:24).

traditions.text: The Church’s footnote to v. 9, where God gives Saul another heart, is the Topical Guide entry *Man, New, Spiritually Reborn*. The entry sets the verse beside King Benjamin’s people, whose hearts were changed so that they had no more disposition to do evil, and beside Alma’s question to the church in Zarahemla, whether its members had “experienced this mighty change” in their hearts. The Topical Guide files Saul’s new heart under the same heading, and the rest of 1 Samuel shows that such a heart could be lost.

traditions.text: The Church’s Bible Dictionary entry “Anoint” lists v. 1 first among the passages where kings were anointed to their office by the prophets, followed by David (16:13) and Solomon (1 Kings 1:39). It adds that holy consecrated olive oil is used in the Church today for sacred anointings, including administering to the sick.

Josephus’s Samuel speaks plainly, “Be thou a King, by the ordination of God,” and names the Philistines as the enemy to be fought. He reverses the order of the first two signs and puts the band of prophets at Gabatha. Saul’s uncle becomes Abner, whom Saul loved above his other relatives, and Josephus explains the silence of v. 16: men envy those whom God raises up.

When the lot falls on him, Saul hides out of modesty, Josephus says, so no one would think he wanted the rule. After the people cry “God save the King,” Samuel writes down what would come to pass, reads it in the king’s hearing, and lays the book up in God’s tabernacle as a witness to later generations.

Pseudo-Philo leaves out the lot at Mizpeh altogether. As soon as Saul leaves Samuel, the people come asking for the king Samuel promised, and he tells them the king will come in three days; Saul arrives, and all the signs befall him. The writer then sends the reader to the book of the Kings for the rest, as if the details were already familiar.

The Aramaic translation turns the prophets of this chapter into scribes. Saul meets a band of scribes coming from the banquet hall with harps and drums (v. 5), and when a spirit of prophecy rests on him he sings praise among them (vv. 6, 10). The onlooker asks who their master is, and the proverb becomes “Is Saul also among the scribes?” The Targum also places the ark at Gibeah, the hill of v. 5, where the Philistine governors are.

On v. 12 Rashi reads “who is their father?” as a rebuke to the doubters: prophecy is not inherited, so why ask about Saul’s father? On v. 22 he explains that Saul hid among the baggage because he was running from high office, and he cites the Talmud’s saying that honor pursues the one who flees from it.

The midrash reads “the stuff” of v. 22 as the Urim and Thummim: Saul told the people he was unworthy and asked them to inquire by the Urim, hoping it would release him, and hid until they did. It sets him against Abimelech, who pursued rule and lost it (Judges 9), and beside Moses, who refused his calling for seven days at the bush. Whoever flees authority, it says, authority pursues.

The midrash takes Samuel’s cry in v. 24, “See ye him whom the LORD hath chosen,” as the first step in a pattern. Saul was chosen, then rejected when the LORD regretted making him king (15:11), and never brought near again (16:1). Aaron and David, by contrast, were chosen, fell under displeasure and were brought near again.

Augustine notes that every king consecrated with the sacred oil was called the Lord’s christ, beginning with Saul, “who first was anointed king” of Israel, whom David himself calls the Lord’s anointed. Yet there was one true Christ, whose figure all of them bore by their prophetic anointing. The very name Christ, he says elsewhere in the same book, comes from that anointing.

11.overview:
Nahash the Ammonite besieges Jabesh-gilead and names his price for a treaty: every man of the town loses his right eye. The town’s messengers reach Gibeah just as Saul comes in from the field behind his oxen. The Spirit of God comes on him; he cuts a yoke of oxen in pieces, sends them through Israel with a threat, and the army that gathers at Bezek crosses over and breaks the Ammonites by midday. When the people demand the deaths of the men who had scorned him, Saul refuses, and Samuel leads everyone to Gilgal to “renew the kingdom.”

Saul becomes king in stages. Samuel anointed him in private (10:1), the lot chose him in public (10:20–24), and some still asked, “How shall this man save us?” (10:27). Only here, after a victory, does all Israel make him king “before the LORD in Gilgal” (v. 15).

11.hermeneutics:
The Masoretic text opens the chapter abruptly, but the oldest surviving Hebrew copy of Samuel, 4QSam-a from Qumran (1st century BC), has an extra paragraph just before it. There Nahash, king of Ammon, has been oppressing the tribes of Gad and Reuben east of the Jordan, gouging out each man’s right eye; seven thousand men escape him to Jabesh-gilead, and about a month later he besieges the town. The NRSV prints the paragraph at the end of 10:27. Frank Moore Cross and others hold that a copyist’s eye skipped it; others read it as a later expansion. Either way it changes v. 2. Nahash is not inventing a cruelty on the spot. He has followed refugees to their shelter, and his terms are a policy his victims already know.

Jabesh-gilead lay in the hills east of the Jordan valley. Most scholars place it at Tell el-Maqlub on the Wadi Yabis, a stream that seems to keep the town’s name, and Eusebius put it six miles from Pella on the road to Gerasa. Saul musters at Bezek, west of the river, so the promise “to morrow, by that time the sun be hot” (v. 9) means a night march down into the valley, across the Jordan, and up the other side. Israel divided the night into three watches (Judges 7:19 names “the middle watch”), and Saul’s three companies strike in “the morning watch” (v. 11), the last of them, before dawn. The same town’s men would later walk all night in the other direction to recover Saul’s body (31:11–13).
