notes: **Saving:** the elders ask for anyone who will “save” them (v. 3, *moshia*); the messengers promise “help” (v. 9) and Saul announces that the LORD has wrought “salvation” (v. 13), both the noun *teshuah*. The question of 10:27, “How shall this man save us?”, gets its answer, and Saul gives the credit away.

**Two names together:** Saul summons Israel to come out “after Saul and after Samuel” (v. 7), and the chapter ends with both at Gilgal (vv. 14–15). The new king still moves under the prophet’s authority.
**Time pressure:** seven days’ respite (v. 3), “to morrow” twice (vv. 9, 10), and “this day… to day” (v. 13) keep the clock running until the rescue.

Chapters 11–12 close the story of how Saul became king. Chapter 11 settles the doubt of 10:27 and brings the people to Gilgal (vv. 14–15), where Samuel gives his farewell speech in chapter 12. Saul’s wars, and his rejection, begin in chapter 13.

**Backward and forward:** the Church’s footnote at v. 7 points to Judges 19:29, where a Levite sends the pieces of his concubine through Israel. Jabesh had refused that earlier muster and was destroyed, its surviving daughters given to Benjamin (Judges 21:8–12). Now a Benjamite king rescues it, and its men repay him at his death (31:11–13).

traditions.text: The Greek translation tells the story a little differently. It counts the muster at Bezek as 600,000 men of Israel and 70,000 of Judah, double the Hebrew’s Israel and more than double its Judah, and it names Nahash as the one the men of Jabesh answer in v. 10. At Gilgal it says Samuel “anointed Saul there to be king,” where the Hebrew has the people make him king, and it ends with Samuel and all Israel rejoicing where the Hebrew names Saul. Josephus agrees on the anointing: Samuel poured the holy oil on Saul a second time in front of the crowd, and from then on, he says, Israel’s government was a kingdom.

Josephus knows the background found in 4QSam-a. Before Jabesh, he says, Nahash had already overrun the Israelites beyond the Jordan and put out the right eye of everyone who surrendered or was captured. His reason was military: a soldier fights with his shield in his left hand, so a man without his right eye would be blind “when their left eyes were covered by their shields.” Only then does Nahash march on Jabesh, which Josephus calls the chief city of Gilead.

His Saul promises the messengers help on the third day and a victory before sunrise, so that the rising sun would find Jabesh already free. He cuts the sinews of his oxen rather than cutting them in pieces, and his numbers are larger still: 700,000 besides 70,000 of Judah. Saul marches all night, attacks before sunrise, kills Nahash himself, and then lays Ammon waste. When the crowd demands the doubters’ deaths, Saul swears that no one of “the same lineage with themselves” will die on a day God has given them, and turns the people to feasting.

Rashi tells his readers to take Nahash’s demand literally. He then reports a midrash that reads it as a figure: the “right eye” is the Torah, given from God’s right hand, and Nahash wanted it burned because it says an Ammonite may not enter the congregation of the LORD (Deuteronomy 23:3). In this reading the siege is an attack on the law that kept Ammon out, and the “reproach upon all Israel” of v. 2 is the burning of its Torah. Radak reports the same midrash in his own commentary, so it was well known to medieval readers.

On v. 14 Rashi explains why the kingdom had to be “renewed” at all. At the first choosing there had been opposition (10:27); now, after Jabesh, everyone agreed. He reads v. 12, “Shall Saul reign over us?”, as the mocking question of those earlier doubters, which the people now want punished. Saul’s refusal leaves the doubters alive and lets the whole people, the former scoffers included, confirm the king together at Gilgal.

The Aramaic translation makes the doubters’ words in v. 12 a flat judgment: they had said Saul was not fit to reign over them. In v. 7 it has dread “from before the Lord” fall on the people, its usual way of keeping God at a reverent distance, and they go out “as one man.”

Kimhi asks why Saul’s summons names Samuel at all. Not everyone had yet accepted Saul as king, he answers, so a man unwilling to follow Saul would still turn out for Samuel, and the muster would be quick. He also explains the setting of v. 14: Samuel chose Gilgal to honor the place where the ark and the tent of meeting first stood when Israel entered the land, even though the tabernacle had since moved to Nob. The renewal, in his reading, was a second acclamation won by the victory over Nahash.

In his questions on the books of Kingdoms, the Syrian bishop gives the same explanation as Josephus. A man who holds his shield toward the enemy with his left hand hides his left eye and sights the enemy with his right, so “he therefore that plucks out that eye, makes men useless in war.” John Hudson quoted the note in his edition of Josephus, and Whiston carried it into his English translation of 1737, so the Jewish historian and the Christian bishop reached English readers side by side.

12.overview:
At Gilgal, with the new king standing by, Samuel puts himself on trial before Israel: whose ox has he taken, whom has he cheated, from whom has he taken a bribe? The people clear him, and the LORD is called as witness. He then recounts the LORD’s rescues from Moses to the judges and charges that, when Nahash came, they demanded a king though the LORD was their king. As proof he calls down thunder and rain at wheat harvest. Terrified, the people beg him to pray for them. He tells them not to fear, to serve the LORD with all their heart, and promises he will not stop praying for them.

The king stays, on terms. One condition binds people and king together: if they fear and obey the LORD, both will continue; if they do wickedly, “ye shall be consumed, both ye and your king” (v. 25). Israel has its king, and the covenant still governs both.

12.hermeneutics:
In the land of Israel the rain comes in winter. Most of the year’s rainfall arrives between November and March, and June through September are usually dry. The wheat harvest came at the start of that dry season, around the feast of weeks, which Exodus 34:22 ties to “the firstfruits of wheat harvest.” A storm then was no blessing; it could only beat down standing grain or soak what lay cut in the fields, and Proverbs 26:1 uses “rain in harvest” as a picture of something out of place. Samuel chooses a sign no one could mistake for ordinary weather, and the people’s terror (vv. 18–19) is the right response. The sign is itself a small judgment on the crop.

Samuel’s list of deliverers (v. 11) is one place where the Hebrew and the early translations part ways. The Hebrew names Jerubbaal (Gideon), Bedan, Jephthah and Samuel. No judge called Bedan appears in Judges, and the Septuagint and Syriac read Barak, a similar-looking name that also fits the mention of Sisera in v. 9. Some Greek manuscripts of the Lucianic family, with the Syriac, also read Samson for Samuel, which would spare Samuel from naming himself; Hebrews 11:32 lists Gideon, Barak, Samson and Jephthah side by side. Most modern translations print Barak and keep Samuel. Either way the list does the same work in the speech: every time Israel cried out, the LORD had already sent someone, so the demand for a king when Nahash came (v. 12) was a vote against a deliverer they had never lacked.

notes: **Voice:** the Hebrew *qol* comes 5 times. Samuel heeded the people’s voice (v. 1); they must obey the LORD’s voice (vv. 14, 15); and the LORD answers with “thunder,” literally “voices” (vv. 17, 18).
**Fear:** the verb comes 4 times, turning terror into reverence: “if ye will fear the LORD” (v. 14), “the people greatly feared” (v. 18), “Fear not” (v. 20), “only fear the LORD” (v. 24).
**If, but if:** the paired conditions of vv. 14–15 return at the close (vv. 24–25), so the speech ends where its terms began, with “king” named 12 times along the way.

Chapter 12 closes the account of Israel’s request for a king that began in chapter 8. Samuel hands public leadership to Saul with a covenant speech, much as Joshua’s farewell closes the conquest (Joshua 23–24). From chapter 13 the story follows the king, and Samuel appears as the prophet who confronts him.

**Echoes:** Samuel’s promise not to cease praying (v. 23) fits how later scripture remembers him beside Moses as an intercessor (Psalm 99:6; Jeremiah 15:1). Paul’s sermon at Antioch summarizes the same turn: judges “until Samuel the prophet,” and then Israel “desired a king” (Acts 13:20–21).

traditions.text: The Church’s footnote at v. 2 points to King Benjamin’s farewell address. Like Samuel, Benjamin reviews his own conduct before the people: he has not sought gold or silver from them, has worked with his own hands so they would not be taxed, and says, “ye yourselves are witnesses this day.” The footnote at v. 24, where Samuel tells Israel to consider the great things the LORD has done for them, points to the same speech, where Benjamin says that even serving God with the whole soul leaves us unprofitable servants.

At v. 22, where Samuel says the LORD will not forsake his people “for his great name’s sake,” the footnote points to Nephi’s copy of Isaiah 48 from the brass plates. There the Lord says that for his name’s sake he will defer his anger and not cut his people off. Both passages ground God’s faithfulness in his own name rather than in the people’s record, which in Samuel’s speech has just been shown to be poor.

The footnote at v. 15, where the LORD’s hand will be against a disobedient people, points to King Limhi’s speech to his people in bondage to the Lamanites. Limhi quotes the Lord: “I will not succor my people in the day of their transgression.” Both passages tie a people’s safety to its obedience, whoever its ruler is.

Josephus has Samuel name the deliverers as Jephtha and Gideon and accuse the people of “great impiety” in asking for a king. He promises them something none of them had ever seen there, a winter storm in the middle of harvest, and God sends thunder, lightning and hail. The people confess that they sinned through ignorance and beg Samuel, as a tender father, to win God’s forgiveness. Whiston’s note adds that thunder in Palestine comes almost only in winter.

This retelling makes Samuel quote Moses directly: at Korah’s rebellion Moses said he had taken nothing from anyone, and the earth swallowed those who lied. Samuel then asks whether they wanted a king because he had wronged them. The people answer that they were unworthy to be judged by a prophet, and king and people weep together, crying, “Let Samuel the prophet live.”

The rules for fasts in a drought say that public prayers for rain stop when the month of Nisan ends. Rain after that is a sign of a curse, and the proof text is Samuel’s question in v. 17, “Is it not wheat harvest to day?” Samuel’s sign became the rabbis’ rule for when rain stops being a blessing.

Verse 5 ends with a singular verb: “And he said, He is witness,” where the people should have answered in the plural. The rabbis conclude that a voice from heaven spoke, God himself testifying for Samuel. Samuel’s court is one of three places, they say, where the holy spirit appeared in an earthly court.

Rava compares Samuel with Moses. Moses said, “I have not taken one ass from them” (Numbers 16:15), meaning he took nothing against an owner’s will. The people tell Samuel he took nothing from any man’s hand, which Rava reads as not even with the owner’s consent, not even hired. Another passage draws a rule from v. 23: anyone who can pray for others and does not is called a sinner.

The Aramaic translation solves the puzzle of Bedan in v. 11 by naming Gideon, Samson, Jephthah and Samuel. Rashi gives the reasoning: Bedan is Samson, the son (*ben*) of Dan, since Samson came from that tribe (Judges 13:2). This is the rabbinic answer to a riddle the Greek translators solved another way (see Hermeneutics).
traditions.cite: Targum Jonathan on 1 Samuel 12:11; Rashi on 12:11

traditions.text: Rashi reads the sign as an argument about prayer. If Samuel’s prayer could change the seasons, it could also have protected them in war, so they had no need of a king while he lived. Since rain at harvest is a curse and God is slow to punish, Samuel had to ask for it on purpose.

Preaching on Paul’s farewell to the Ephesian elders, Chrysostom notes how reluctant Paul is to praise himself, and compares him to Samuel handing the government to Saul. Samuel too asked the people whether he had taken anything from their hands and called them and God as witnesses. In Acts Paul says he has coveted no one’s silver or gold and has worked with his own hands, the same defense Samuel and Benjamin give.

13.overview:
Saul keeps three thousand men under arms, and Jonathan strikes the Philistine garrison at Geba. The Philistines answer with chariots, horsemen and a vast army camped at Michmash; Israel’s men hide in caves and pits or flee across the Jordan. At Gilgal Saul waits the seven days Samuel set, but Samuel does not come and the troops slip away, so Saul offers the burnt offering himself. Samuel arrives as he finishes and tells him his kingdom will not continue: the LORD has sought “a man after his own heart.” The chapter ends with Philistine raiders loose in the land and no smith in Israel.

Saul’s fault is a broken instruction. At his anointing Samuel had told him to go down to Gilgal and wait seven days “till I come to thee” (10:8). Saul waits the days but not for the prophet, and his excuse (vv. 11–12) is the pressure of the moment.

13.hermeneutics:
Verse 1 uses the formula Samuel and Kings use to open a reign: the king’s age when he began to rule and the length of his rule, as when David is said to be thirty at his accession and to reign forty years (2 Samuel 5:4). Here both numbers are broken. Word for word, the Hebrew says Saul was “a son of a year in his reigning,” and “two years he reigned” over Israel. The KJV smoothed this into “Saul reigned one year,” but a king aged one is impossible, and Saul already has a son commanding a thousand men (v. 2). Most Septuagint manuscripts leave the verse out, and a few late Greek copies supply “thirty years.” Modern translations leave blanks, borrow the Greek thirty, or take forty years from Acts 13:21.

The Hebrew of v. 21 baffled translators for centuries, and the KJV guessed “a file.” In the early 20th century excavators at Gezer and elsewhere turned up small domed stone weights inscribed *pym*, about 7.6 grams, roughly two-thirds of a shekel. The obscure word *pim* is a price. Most modern translations read the verse as a bill: a pim to sharpen plowshares and mattocks, a third of a shekel for axes and goads. Israel paid its overlords to keep even its farm tools sharp, and the ban on smiths (v. 19) left Saul’s army without swords (v. 22).

Kings across the region offered sacrifice as a matter of course; from the 14th century BC Assyrian kings called themselves the *šangû*, the priest, of their god Ashur. Israel’s later kings also offer burnt offerings unrebuked (2 Samuel 6:17; 1 Kings 8:62–64). What Samuel condemns is Saul’s breach of the specific order he was given.

notes: **Commanded:** Samuel’s verdict turns on one word. Saul has not kept “the commandment of the LORD,” “which he commanded thee” (v. 13), and the LORD has “commanded” another man to be captain “because thou hast not kept that which the LORD commanded thee” (v. 14): the verb three times and its noun once.

**Found:** the Hebrew verb *matsa* comes 5 times. The army dwindles to the men “found” with Saul (vv. 15, 16), no smith is “found” in Israel (v. 19), and in v. 22 no sword or spear is “found” except with Saul and Jonathan.
**Hebrews:** three times the narrator or the Philistines use the outsiders’ name for Israelites (vv. 3, 7, 19), a reminder of who rules the land.

Chapters 13–15 tell Saul’s wars and his rejection in two steps. Here Samuel says Saul’s kingdom will not continue (vv. 13–14); in chapter 15 Saul himself is rejected. Verse 23 leads straight into 14:1, where Jonathan crosses to the garrison at the pass.

**Backward and forward:** the seven days go back to Samuel’s instruction at the anointing (10:8). The “man after his own heart” of v. 14 points ahead to David, chosen because the LORD “looketh on the heart” (16:7).

traditions.text: The footnotes to Saul’s offering point to the Topical Guide entries “Priesthood, Authority” and “Unrighteous Dominion” at v. 9, and to “Priesthood, Qualifying for” at v. 12, where Saul says he “forced” himself. They read the scene as a king taking a priestly act on himself without the authority to perform it, and v. 14 is tied to the entry “Called of God.”

traditions.text: The entry on Saul lists his offering of sacrifice (13:9) among the main events of his reign and gives a one-line verdict on his life: his downfall shows the consequences of “uncontrolled self-will and disobedience to counsel.” Chapter 13 is where that pattern first appears: Saul has counsel from Samuel and sets it aside under pressure, and chapter 15 repeats the pattern.

The Aramaic translation turns the broken v. 1 into a tribute: Saul was like a year-old child with no sins when he became king, and he reigned two years over Israel. The impossible age becomes a statement about his innocence, and the “two years” are kept as written. The same reading turns up in the Talmud, next.

Rav Huna gives the same reading as the Targum: Saul began his reign like a one-year-old who had never tasted sin. Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak objected that a one-year-old is also covered in filth, and that night he had a frightening dream. He apologized to “the bones of Saul, son of Kish,” but the dreams stopped only when he added “king of Israel.”

Rashi gives a plainer second reading of v. 1: Saul had reigned one year when he chose his three thousand men, and two years in all. On the offering he notes that a non-priest was allowed to sacrifice at a high place in that period, so the sin was not the act itself. Samuel’s complaint is that he had said he would offer it: “I will offer it up, and not you.”

Josephus says the Philistines had disarmed the Hebrews and forbidden them any iron at all, which is why farmers went to Philistine smiths. In his account Saul did wait but not to the end, and Samuel tells him he acted more hastily than the moment required, taking over the prayers and sacrifices Samuel should have offered for the people. Had he waited, Samuel says, he and his descendants would have reigned a long time.

Josephus skips the age-and-reign formula of v. 1 entirely and opens the war with Saul choosing his three thousand men; Whiston noted the gap in 1737. At Saul’s death he gives his own total instead: eighteen years while Samuel lived and two after, which some copies read as twenty-two, giving forty in all.

In his sermon at Antioch of Pisidia, Paul says God gave Israel “Saul the son of Cis… by the space of forty years.” He then joins the words of v. 14 to Psalm 89:20 to describe David as a man after God’s own heart, who would fulfil all his will. Paul reads Samuel’s rebuke as the hinge between Saul and David, the point where the promise passes to another house.

This church order uses Saul to argue that lay people must do nothing without the bishop. As Saul, “when he had offered without Samuel,” was told it would not avail him, so a lay person who acts without the priest labors in vain; King Uzziah’s leprosy is the second example. A later book says Saul drew on himself a sin and a curse without remedy by offering without the prophet and high priest Samuel.

Marcion’s followers said the God of the Old Testament was fickle or short-sighted, choosing Saul and then rejecting him. Tertullian answers that a good judge chooses and rejects on the merits of the moment. When Saul was chosen (ch. 9) he was not yet “the despiser of the prophet Samuel” (ch. 13), and God does not condemn a man in advance for sins he has not yet committed.

Augustine takes up v. 13, where the LORD would have established Saul’s kingdom “for ever.” God did not change his plan or fail to foresee Saul’s sin, he argues; Saul’s kingdom was set up as a figure of an eternal kingdom. The “man after his own heart” of v. 14 means David, or the Mediator whom David’s anointing foreshadowed.

14.overview:
Without telling his father, Jonathan and his armourbearer cross the gorge to the Philistine garrison at Michmash, set themselves a sign, climb up on hands and feet, and kill about twenty men. Panic and an earthquake shake the Philistine camp, and Saul’s army, joined by deserters and men from hiding, routs them. But Saul has bound the troops by oath to eat nothing until evening, and Jonathan, who never heard it, tastes honey. When God gives no answer that night, the lot falls on Jonathan and Saul swears he will die; the people refuse and rescue him. A summary of Saul’s wars closes the chapter.

Two kinds of leadership run side by side. Jonathan acts on the conviction that nothing restrains the LORD from saving “by many or by few” (v. 6). Saul binds his men with oaths, calls for the priest and then cuts him off (v. 19), and in the end his own army overrules him (v. 45).

14.hermeneutics:
Michmash is the modern village of Mukhmas, on the north side of a steep gorge known today as the Wadi es-Suweinit, with Geba facing it from the south. The chapter’s geography is exact: one rocky crag fronts Michmash on the north, the other fronts Geba on the south (vv. 4–5), and the climb takes hands as well as feet (v. 13). Isaiah 10:28–29 traces an invader’s march down the same route, leaving his baggage at Michmash and crossing “the passage” to Geba. First hearers knew the pass as a natural barrier. Two men could cross where an army could not, and a garrison on the far side had no reason to expect visitors from below.

Two verses read differently in the Septuagint, and both bear on how Saul consults God. In v. 18 the Hebrew has Saul call for “the ark of God,” though the ark had been at Kirjath-jearim for years (7:1–2). The Greek reads “the ephod,” which Ahiah is wearing in v. 3 and which held the lots used to ask God’s will. Some translators keep the Hebrew as the harder reading; others follow the Greek. In v. 41 the Hebrew is short, “Give a perfect lot.” The Greek has a full prayer, which most modern translations follow: if the guilt is in Saul or Jonathan, give Urim; if it is in the people, give Thummim (compare Exodus 28:30). That longer text shows the procedure. The lot answers yes or no, so the guilty party is found by halving: Saul and Jonathan against the people, then Saul against Jonathan (v. 42).

rows.text: Saul’s oath and the hungry army

notes: **Saving:** the verb and its noun come 4 times. Jonathan trusts the LORD to save by many or few (v. 6); “the LORD saved Israel that day” (v. 23); Saul swears by the LORD “which saveth Israel” (v. 39); and the people credit Jonathan with “this great salvation” (v. 45).
**That day:** “day” comes 12 times. Saul’s oath runs “until evening” (v. 24), so the whole story of the honey, the slaughter and the lot plays out against the clock of one day.
**Honey and eating:** “honey” comes 5 times (vv. 25, 26, 27, 29, 43) and “eat” 8 times in vv. 24–34. The food Saul forbade is what Jonathan tasted and what the starving army fell on.

Chapter 14 is the center of chapters 13–15, Saul’s wars and rejection. It picks up from 13:23, where the Philistine garrison moves to the pass, and its closing summary (vv. 47–52) reads like the end-notice of a reign, set before the second confrontation with Samuel in chapter 15.

**Backward and forward:** the Church’s footnote at v. 20 points to Judges 7:22, where the LORD likewise set every man’s sword against his fellow in Midian’s camp. God’s silence in v. 37 returns at the end of Saul’s life, when the LORD answers him “neither by dreams, nor by Urim, nor by prophets” (28:6).

traditions.text: The Church’s footnote at v. 12, where Jonathan takes the Philistines’ taunt to come up as the LORD’s sign, points to a Nephite commander who reasoned the other way. When his people asked to go up into the mountains against the Gadianton robbers, Gidgiddoni answered that if they went up “the Lord would deliver us into their hands,” and he waited for the enemy to come down. The two passages set the same question side by side: when to attack and when to wait, and how to know which the Lord wants.

traditions.date: LDS edition of the King James Bible, 1979
traditions.text: The footnote at v. 45, where the people refuse to let Saul kill Jonathan, points to the Topical Guide entry on common consent. That entry lists the verse with the instruction to the Church that “all things shall be done by common consent” (D&C 26:2). The people’s voice overrules a king’s oath here, and the footnote reads that as an early example of the principle.

In Josephus, Saul has the high priest put on his vestments and prophesy, and is promised victory. Josephus then calls Saul’s curse an act “liable to be very much blamed,” made either in ignorance or in the giddiness of an unexpected victory. His curse forbids anyone to stop the slaughter to eat before night, and Jonathan, on hearing of it, says his father had not done well, since fed men would have killed more.

When the lot falls on Jonathan, Josephus gives him a speech of his own. He asks his father not to spare him: death will be welcome coming from his father’s piety after so great a victory, and it is consolation enough to leave the Hebrews victorious. The people are grieved and swear they will not see the author of their victory die, and so they snatch him from his father. Josephus turns Jonathan into a model of filial piety ready to die for an oath he never heard.

The Aramaic translation adds a reason to the people’s defense of Jonathan in v. 45: “it is revealed before the Lord” that he acted in error that day. He had not heard the oath, so in the Targum’s eyes he never broke it knowingly. In v. 41 it turns Saul’s terse plea into a request that God bring the matter out in truth. Both changes protect Jonathan’s name: the lot finds him, but the Targum makes clear that heaven knew he meant no wrong.

The rabbis use v. 24 in a legal question: does the word “cursed” carry the force of an oath? The verse says Saul adjured the people with a curse on any man who ate, and v. 27 calls the same words an oath, so a curse can bind like one. Elsewhere they treat Jonathan’s honey as medicine: someone seized with faintness from hunger should be fed honey and sweets, which restore the eyes, and the hint is Jonathan’s “mine eyes have been enlightened” (v. 29).

The great stone Saul has rolled up (v. 33) becomes, in the rabbis’ reading, a private altar for slaughter, and they note that the people slaughtered there by day and then at night (v. 34), which helps them decide what could be done at such altars. Rav Hisda takes Saul’s “slay them here” to mean that Saul checked the knife himself, the source for inspecting a slaughtering knife.

Rashi reads the honey in the wood as sugar cane, which he says grew in the land of Israel, flowing from the canes, and he cites Rabbi Nathan that sugar is called *sukkar* in Arabic. For “ark of God” in v. 18 he explains that Saul meant the Urim and Thummim, so the priest could ask God. On v. 32 he offers his own view that the people killed a mother and its young on the same day, against Leviticus 22:28, and reports the rabbis’ view that they had made the animals peace offerings and ate before the blood was sprinkled.

Against Marcion’s claim that the Creator is harsh, Tertullian lists his acts of mercy, among them the mercy that spared Saul’s son, about to die, at the people’s plea. In a later book he says Jonathan “blotted out by his deprecation” the guilt of breaking the fast. Tertullian treats Jonathan as guilty and forgiven, where the Targum treats him as innocent through ignorance.

15.overview:
Samuel sends Saul to carry out the LORD’s old sentence on Amalek: destroy all of it, people and animals. Saul warns the Kenites away and wins from Havilah to Shur, but he spares King Agag and the best of the flocks and herds. The LORD tells Samuel he repents of making Saul king, and Samuel cries to him all night. Next day Saul claims obedience while sheep bleat behind him. Samuel answers that “to obey is better than sacrifice” and that the LORD has rejected Saul as king. As Samuel turns to go, the robe tears, and he says the kingdom has been torn from Saul. Samuel kills Agag himself, and the two never meet again.

Saul never admits a plain refusal. Twice he says he has done what the LORD commanded (vv. 13, 20), and the spared animals are, in his telling, for the LORD (vv. 15, 21). Samuel’s answer in v. 22 is aimed at that defense.

15.hermeneutics:
Samuel’s rule that obeying is better than sacrifice had an Egyptian counterpart far older than Saul. The Teaching for King Merikare, set around 2100 BC as an old king’s advice to his son and successor, tells the new ruler that the character of one upright of heart is more acceptable to God than the sacrificial ox of a wrongdoer. A few lines later the same text urges him to make offerings that enrich the altars. Neither text abolishes sacrifice; both rank it below the life of the one who brings it. In Egypt this was counsel for a king, and Samuel turns it on a king whose offering grows out of disobedience. Israel’s later prophets repeat the point, and the Church’s footnotes at v. 22 gather them (Psalm 40:6; Proverbs 21:3; Micah 6:7).

The Hebrew of v. 27 does not say who seized whose robe. It reads only that as Samuel turned away “he laid hold upon the skirt of his mantle, and it rent.” English readers usually assume Saul grabbed Samuel’s robe in a plea to stay, and the Septuagint names Saul; but the Hebrew leaves room for the tear to be Samuel’s act. Samuel at once makes the torn cloth a sign that the LORD has torn the kingdom away (v. 28). A torn garment carried that meaning for Israel’s storytellers. Later the prophet Ahijah tears a new garment into twelve pieces and gives Jeroboam ten of them, saying the LORD will tear the kingdom from Solomon’s hand (1 Kings 11:29–31).

structure.summary: No strong pattern; the chapter moves in sequence, framed by the LORD’s repenting in vv. 11 and 35.
notes: **Voice:** the Hebrew *qol* comes 7 times. Saul must hearken to “the voice of the words of the LORD” (v. 1); the bleating and lowing of v. 14 are literally the voice of sheep and oxen; the LORD’s voice returns in vv. 19, 20, 22; and Saul confesses he “obeyed their voice” (v. 24).
**Repent:** the verb comes 4 times, at the edges and the center. The LORD repents of Saul (vv. 11, 35), and in between Samuel says the Strength of Israel will not repent (v. 29, twice).
**Utterly destroy:** the verb of the ban comes 7 times (vv. 3, 8, 9 twice, 15, 18, 20), and “reject” 4 times in two matching pairs (vv. 23, 26): Saul rejected the word, so the LORD rejected him.

Chapter 15 closes chapters 13–15 and the larger section that began when Israel asked for “a king… like all the nations” (8:5). The rejection of 13:14 fell on Saul’s house; here it falls on Saul himself (vv. 23, 26), and Samuel’s parting in v. 35 clears the way for David’s anointing in 16:1–13.

**Backward and forward:** the order of v. 2 carries out the sentence of Exodus 17:14 and Deuteronomy 25:17–19. The Church’s footnote at v. 8 points to Haman “the Agagite” (Esther 3:1), and an Amalekite later claims to have killed Saul (2 Samuel 1:8–10).

traditions.text: The Church’s footnote at v. 11 gives the JST wording, which drops the LORD’s “It repenteth me.” Instead the LORD says he has set up Saul “to be a king, and he repenteth not that he hath sinned.” The repenting moves from God to Saul, and the fault named is Saul’s refusal to repent. A second footnote on the KJV word explains that the Hebrew root means “to sigh,” and so “to feel sorrow.”

At v. 35, where the KJV ends the chapter with the LORD repenting that he had made Saul king, the JST footnote reads instead that “the Lord rent the kingdom from Saul,” whom he had made king over Israel. The JST closes the chapter with the image of v. 28, the torn kingdom, and leaves v. 29 standing: God does not repent as a man does.

Josephus says Saul spared Agag because he admired the beauty and tallness of his body, a misplaced pity where God had commanded none. He writes that Saul killed the women and children believing it neither barbarous nor inhuman, since they were enemies and God had commanded it. The people share the blame, he adds, for taking the flocks, herds and other wealth.

In Josephus, Samuel pleads all night for Saul’s forgiveness and God refuses, since injuries grow great through the easy tempers of those who forgive them. Samuel tells Saul that God “is not delighted with sacrifices; but with good and with righteous men.” When the cloak tears, Samuel says that changing what has been decided belongs to human passion, not to divine power.

Here Saul spares Agag because Agag promises to show him hidden treasures, and God tells Samuel the king has been corrupted with money. God lets Agag and his wife come together that night before Agag dies, so that the child born of her will be a stumbling block to Saul. The prophecy comes true at Saul’s death, when the man who finishes him off on Gilboa names himself Edab, son of Agag.

Rabbi Mani reads the fight “in the valley” (v. 5) as Saul arguing with God about a valley. If the Torah requires a heifer’s neck broken in a valley for one unsolved killing (Deuteronomy 21), how much more should he spare so many lives; and if the men sinned, what had the animals and children done? A heavenly voice answered, “Be not righteous over much” (Ecclesiastes 7:16). Rashi repeats the argument in his note on the verse, so it became the standard Jewish reading of “in the valley.”

The Aramaic translation also avoids saying God repents. In vv. 11 and 35 the LORD has “turned back in his Memra,” his word, from making Saul king. In v. 29 it lets Saul speak: if he says he will repent and be forgiven so his sons may reign, the decree is already sealed, for God does not go back on what he has said. Targum and JST reach the same problem from different directions.

Rabbi Yohanan says old age came on Samuel suddenly at v. 11. Samuel pleaded that God had ranked him with Moses and Aaron (Psalm 99:6), whose work was not undone in their lifetimes, so his anointing of Saul should not be undone in his. Another passage draws a lesson from v. 6: if Jethro’s descendants were spared for kindness to Moses, how much more will a host who feeds a scholar be rewarded.

This chapter is read in synagogue as the prophetic reading for the Sabbath of Remembrance, Shabbat Zakhor, before Purim, beside Deuteronomy’s command to remember Amalek. The pairing rests on Esther 3:1, which calls Haman “the Agagite”: the king Saul spared becomes the ancestor of the man who later tried to destroy the Jews.

On v. 27 Rashi gives the plain sense: Saul grabbed Samuel’s robe to keep him until he could bow before the LORD at Gilgal. He then reports that the rabbis of the midrash disagreed, some saying Saul tore Samuel’s robe and others that Samuel tore Saul’s as a sign that the kingdom would pass from him.

Marcion’s followers cited v. 11 as proof that the Creator is fickle and short-sighted. Tertullian answers that God’s repentance here does not confess an error; it reproaches Saul. He points to v. 29 in the same chapter, which says God does not repent as a man does, so the two verses must be read together.

Augustine’s Bible, following the Greek, has Samuel add in v. 28 that God “will divide Israel in two.” He reads Saul as a figure for the Israel that would lose the kingdom, and the neighbor “good above you” as Christ, of Israel by descent. When scripture says God repents, he explains, it describes a change in circumstances that God foreknew; when it says he does not repent, it means he does not change.

16.overview:
The LORD sends Samuel, still mourning Saul, to Bethlehem with a horn of oil and a heifer to explain his visit. Jesse's sons pass before him one by one, beginning with tall Eliab, and each is refused, for the LORD looks on the heart. The youngest, David, is fetched from the sheep and anointed among his brothers, and the Spirit of the LORD comes on him. Then the Spirit departs from Saul, an evil spirit troubles him, and his servants go looking for a harpist. They find David, who enters Saul's service as musician and armourbearer.

The hinge is vv. 13–14. The Spirit that comes on David “from that day forward” leaves Saul in the very next verse. Saul does not know whom Samuel has anointed, yet he brings his replacement into his own house, loves him, and is calmed by him.

16.hermeneutics:
Younger sons who became kings explained their rule by divine choice. Esarhaddon of Assyria (681–669 BC) says in his Nineveh prism that he was the youngest of his older brothers, yet his father gathered the brothers and asked the sun god Shamash whether this son was his heir, and the god confirmed it. The brothers then turned against him. Verses 6–12 have the same parts: brothers assembled, a question put to God, the youngest named. Samuel's first guess, the eldest who looks like a king, is the natural one the scene is built to overturn.

A king who took the throne from another line also needed a defense. Hattusili III of the Hittites (13th century BC), the youngest of four children, deposed his nephew and left a long account of why: the goddess Ishtar had chosen and protected him, and he acted only when wronged. Kyle McCarter (1980) argued that the story of David's rise, which begins at v. 14, reads like an Israelite royal apology of this kind. The second half of the chapter fits that reading closely. David asks for nothing. Saul's own servant recommends him, Saul sends for him twice, and Saul comes to love him (vv. 17–22).

Kings kept musicians close. An engraved ivory from Megiddo, about 1180 BC, shows a ruler on a cherub throne at a victory banquet with a lyre player in attendance, probably his court singer. David's two posts, player and armourbearer (vv. 21, 23), put a young man from Bethlehem at the king's side day and night.

rows.text: The sons pass by; David anointed

notes: **Spirit:** *ruach* comes 7 times. It rests on David (v. 13) and leaves Saul (v. 14); the other five are the troubling spirit (vv. 14, 15, 16, 23 twice).
**Seeing:** *ra'ah*, “see,” also comes 7 times: the LORD has “provided” (literally seen) a king (v. 1), three times in v. 7, and Saul's servants “provide” and “have seen” David (vv. 17–18).
**Looks:** v. 7 sets aside “the height of his stature,” Saul's mark (9:2), yet David is “goodly to look to” (v. 12). Appearance is not what decides.

Chapter 16 opens the book's last section, David's rise and Saul's fall (16–31). Its first words answer 15:35, where Samuel mourned for Saul, and the anointing makes good 15:28: the kingdom goes to “a neighbour of thine, that is better than thou.” From v. 14 David moves toward the throne as Saul declines.
**Forward:** this private anointing is the first of three. The men of Judah anoint David at Hebron (2 Samuel 2:4), and later all Israel's elders do the same (2 Samuel 5:3).

traditions.text: The Church's footnotes show the JST changing every evil spirit “from the LORD” or “from God” in vv. 14–23. In v. 14 the troubling spirit becomes one “which was not of the Lord,” and vv. 15–16 and 23 make the same change to “from God.” The revision separates the spirit that torments Saul from the God who, in the Hebrew, sends it. Augustine, below, worked at the same problem without changing the text.

A thematic link, not a footnote. In Joseph Smith's vision of the celestial kingdom the Lord says he will judge all men by their works, “according to the desire of their hearts.” It carries the principle of v. 7, that the LORD looks on the heart, from the choosing of a king to the judgment of every person.

Josephus enlarges God's answer in v. 7: the kingdom is a reward not for beauty of body but for “the virtue of souls,” and he lists the virtues as piety, righteousness, fortitude and obedience. He also has Samuel seat David beside him at the sacrificial meal, anoint him, and whisper in his ear that God had chosen him king. The whisper explains how the anointing could stay secret from Saul.

Here the divine power leaves Saul and passes to David, who begins to prophesy. Saul suffers “demoniacal disorders” that nearly choke him, and physicians, not servants, prescribe a man who can play the harp and sing hymns over him. Josephus calls David the king's only physician against the demons.

When Samuel admires Eliab, God rebukes him: was it not Samuel who told Saul, “I am he that seeth”? After his anointing David sings a psalm. He compares himself to Abel the shepherd, whose brother envied him, and says his own brothers envied him too, his parents made him of no account, and no one called him when the prophet came.

The same book gives the song David played to Saul, addressed to the evil spirit itself. Darkness and silence came before the world, and only after heaven and earth “was the tribe of your spirits made.” Because the spirit is a later creation, David warns it to do no harm and says one born of his line will subdue such spirits. As he sings, the spirit spares Saul.

The Greek Psalter ends with an extra psalm in David's voice. He was small among his brothers and kept his father's sheep, his hands made an instrument, and God sent his angel and anointed him. His brothers were handsome and tall, but “the Lord did not take pleasure in them.” A longer Hebrew form was found among the Dead Sea Scrolls (11QPsalms-a).

The rabbis held that a person on the way to do a commandment is protected from harm, then tested the rule against v. 2. Samuel, sent by God himself, still fears Saul will kill him, and God gives him a heifer for cover. Their conclusion: where danger is known and common, one does not rely on a miracle.

Rav assigns the praise of v. 18 to Doeg the Edomite, the chief of Saul's servants (21:7), and says he spoke it to make Saul jealous. Each phrase is read as Torah skill, and “the LORD is with him” means the law follows David's rulings. Saul could bear the rest, since Jonathan was David's equal, but not that.

Rashi gives a reason Eliab was refused: he was quick-tempered, as his anger at David in 17:28 shows. He also hears a rebuke in v. 7. Samuel had called himself the seer (9:19), and now he is told that he does not see. Pseudo-Philo's rebuke above makes the same point about a thousand years earlier.

traditions.source: Clement of Alexandria, Exhortation to the Heathen
traditions.text: Clement sets David against Orpheus and the pagan singers who, he says, lured people to idols. David's music did the opposite and drove demons away; when Saul was plagued with a demon, “he cured him by merely playing.” Clement goes on to call the human being God's own instrument, tuned by the Spirit.

Bishop Simplician of Milan asked how a spirit could be both evil and the Lord's. Augustine answers that the spirit tormenting Saul was evil by its own will, and in that sense not God's; it is called the Lord's because it served his hidden judgment and could harm only as far as he allowed. The JST reaches a similar separation by changing the wording itself.

17.overview:
The Philistines camp at Ephes-dammim, and Israel faces them across the valley of Elah. Morning and evening for forty days Goliath of Gath, armed in bronze, dares Israel to send one man to fight him, and no one goes. David, sent by Jesse with food for his brothers, hears the challenge, shrugs off Eliab's rebuke, and tells Saul that the LORD who saved him from the lion and the bear will save him from this Philistine. He refuses Saul's armour, takes five stones and his sling, and brings Goliath down with one stone. Israel routs the Philistines, and Saul asks Abner whose son the young man is.

Watch the swords. David says the LORD saves “not with sword and spear” (v. 47), and the narrator stresses that “there was no sword in the hand of David” (v. 50). Then David draws the giant's own sword and cuts off his head with it.

17.hermeneutics:
This chapter survives in two forms. The Masoretic Hebrew makes Goliath “six cubits and a span” tall (v. 4), about 9 feet 9 inches; the Dead Sea Scroll 4QSam-a, the main Septuagint manuscripts and Josephus give four cubits and a span, about 6 feet 9 inches. J. Daniel Hays (2005) argued the smaller figure is original; Clyde Billington (2007) answered that the two may use different cubits and both describe a man near eight feet. Codex Vaticanus is also much shorter, lacking vv. 12–31, 41, 48b, 50 and 55–58. Emanuel Tov sees there an older, separate telling; others think the translator cut passages that seemed to repeat or clash. Either way, v. 12 introduces David as if ch. 16 had not, and in vv. 55–58 Saul asks about a youth already in his service.

The valley itself has been dug. Khirbet Qeiyafa, a walled town of about 2.3 hectares with two gates on a ridge above the Elah, was excavated from 2007 by Yosef Garfinkel and Saar Ganor and dated by radiocarbon to about 1020–980 BC. Garfinkel identifies it with Shaaraim, “two gates” (v. 52), and calls it Judahite; Nadav Na'aman and others think it Canaanite, and Israel Finkelstein links it to a northern Israelite power. Down the valley lay Tell es-Safi, Gath, a large Philistine city. A sherd found there in 2005 bears two names, *'lwt* and *wlt*, of the same type as Goliath's but not his.

Duels between champions were an old way to settle a fight. In the Egyptian *Story of Sinuhe* (c. 1900 BC) a strong man of Retenu challenges the exile Sinuhe, takes an arrow in the neck, falls on his face, and is killed with his own axe while Sinuhe stands on his back. Verses 49–51 follow the same moves.

notes: **Defy:** the verb comes 5 times (vv. 10, 25, 26, 36, 45). Twice David calls Goliath “uncircumcised” (vv. 26, 36), and he turns the dare into an insult against “the living God.”
**Sword:** *ḥerev* also comes 5 times: Saul's (v. 39), Goliath's (v. 45), not the LORD's way to save (v. 47), absent from David's hand (v. 50), and Goliath's own, used on him (v. 51).
**Deliver:** *natsal* comes 3 times in vv. 35–37, tying the lion and the bear to the Philistine.

The battle in the valley of Elah is a unit of its own, but vv. 55–58 run straight on into 18:1–5: Jonathan's love for David begins “when he had made an end of speaking unto Saul.” The court stories that follow all grow out of this victory.

**Forward:** Goliath's sword turns up behind the ephod at Nob (21:9), and the Philistines quote the victory song it earned (21:11). 2 Samuel 21:15–22 lists four more champions of Gath killed by David's men.

traditions.text: The Church's footnote on David's offer in v. 32 points to Nephi's answer to his father: “I will go and do the things which the Lord hath commanded.” Both young men volunteer for a task their elders think impossible, and both rest the outcome on the Lord. Another footnote, on v. 47, points to D&C 105:14, where the Lord promises to fight Zion's battles himself.

The footnote on v. 33, where Saul objects that David is “but a youth,” points to Joseph Smith's account of the opposition after his first vision. He describes himself as an obscure boy of fourteen or fifteen, of no consequence in the world, yet opposed by men of high standing. The cross-reference sets one youth's courage beside another's.

traditions.date: LDS edition of the King James Bible, 1979
traditions.text: The Church's Bible Dictionary takes up 2 Samuel 21:19, where Elhanan kills Goliath of Gath. It says the reference is probably to a different man of the same name, or that some error may have crept into the text, and leaves the question there.

Josephus gives Goliath four cubits and a span, the shorter reading also found at Qumran. When Goliath asks if he is taken for a dog, Josephus's David answers that he is worse than a dog, and he goes out with “an invisible assistant,” God himself. There is no scene of Saul asking whose son David is, and afterward David dedicates Goliath's sword to God.

David writes on seven stones the names of Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Moses, Aaron, himself and the Most Mighty, and an angel is sent to strengthen him. He tells Goliath they are kin, since Goliath descends from Orpah and David from Ruth, and Orpah chose the Philistines' gods. Dying, Goliath sees the angel. The angel then changes David's face so that no one knows him, which answers Saul's question in v. 55.

The Aramaic translation enlarges Goliath's speech in v. 8. He is the man who killed Eli's sons Hophni and Phinehas and carried the ark of the LORD to the house of Dagon (chs. 4–5), and he has led every Philistine battle without being made a captain of a thousand. Pseudo-Philo also has Goliath boast of taking the ark and killing the priests.
traditions.cite: Targum Jonathan on 1 Samuel 17:8; cf. Biblical Antiquities 61.2

traditions.text: Rabbi Yohanan says Goliath came out morning and evening (v. 16) to keep Israel from reciting the Shema at its set times, and that his forty days matched the forty days in which the Torah was given. Rabbi Meir counts three times his own words foretold his fall: he asked for a man to “come down” to him, put Israel's victory before his own in v. 9, and asked “Am I a dog?”

The rabbis ask how Saul could not know David (v. 55) when David was already his armourbearer (16:21). Their answer is that Saul's armour fit David (v. 38), which made Saul fear the boy was the future king, so he asked about his line, Perez or Zerah. The question “whose son” was about the throne, not about a name.

Rashi reports a rabbinic reading of v. 18, where David is to “take their pledge”: he was to bring back writs of divorce from his brothers for their wives, so that no wife would be left bound if a soldier went missing. On v. 49 he asks why a man struck in the forehead fell forward. His answers are that it spared David the walk to cut off his head, and that the mouth that had blasphemed was made to lick the dust.

The extra psalm at the end of the Greek Psalter is headed as composed when David “fought in single combat with Goliath.” In its last verses David goes out to meet the Philistine, who curses him by his idols, and David draws the giant's own sword, beheads him, and removes the reproach from Israel. The psalm says nothing of the sling; it remembers the sword.

Augustine's Psalter titles Psalm 144 (143 in the Greek count) “against Goliath,” and he reads the duel as Christ's. David chose five stones but threw one: the five books of the Law, conquering through unity. He cut off Goliath's head with Goliath's own sword, as Christ overthrew the devil with the devil's weapons.

traditions.source: Ambrose, On the Duties of the Clergy
traditions.text: Ambrose makes David a model of courage joined to prudence. He fought only when driven to it, and against Goliath he laid aside the armour he had been loaded with, trusting his own arm more than another man's weapons. After that, Ambrose adds, David never went to war without seeking counsel of the Lord.
traditions.cite: On the Duties of the Clergy 1.35.177

18.overview:
Jonathan's soul is knit with David's; he makes a covenant with him and gives him his robe, sword, bow and girdle. David succeeds wherever Saul sends him, until the women greet the army singing that “Saul hath slain his thousands, and David his ten thousands.” With the evil spirit on him, Saul hurls a javelin at David. He makes him captain over a thousand, promises him his elder daughter Merab and gives her to another man, then offers Michal, who loves David, for a bride-price of a hundred Philistine foreskins, hoping the Philistines will kill him. David brings two hundred and marries her.

Every snare Saul sets lifts David higher. The command meant to put him in danger makes him known to all the people (vv. 13, 16), and the marriage meant to trap him makes him the king's son-in-law. By the end Saul is “David's enemy continually,” and David's name is prized above all Saul's servants.

18.hermeneutics:
Kings paid for proof of kills, and the proof was counted. Ahmose son of Ebana, an Egyptian soldier at the siege of Avaris about 1550 BC, records in his tomb at Elkab that he brought back a hand from the enemy, it was reported to the royal herald, and he was given the “gold of valor.” Excavators at the Hyksos palace at Avaris (Tell el-Dab'a) reported in 2012 pits of severed right hands buried in the court before the throne room. Saul asks for the same kind of tally, and his choice of trophy can come only from an uncircumcised enemy. David's two hundred are handed over “in full tale to the king” (v. 27), counted before the man who hoped never to receive them.

The Greek text of this chapter is much shorter. Codex Vaticanus, the chief Septuagint manuscript, lacks vv. 1–5, so Jonathan's covenant and gift are missing; it lacks Saul's words about the kingdom and the first javelin (vv. 8b–11), the offer of Merab (vv. 17–19), and the closing lines from v. 29b. It has David bring a hundred foreskins, not two hundred, and has “all Israel” love him where the Hebrew names Michal (v. 28). In the short form Saul's fear grows in a straight line from the women's song. The longer Hebrew adds an attempt on David's life and a broken promise before the marriage, so the reader already knows what Saul intends when he offers Michal.

notes: **Love:** *ahav* comes 5 times as a verb (vv. 1, 16, 20, 22, 28): Jonathan, all Israel and Judah, Michal, Saul's servants as Saul tells them to say, and Michal again. David is never its subject.
**Wisely and with:** David “behaved himself wisely” 4 times (vv. 5, 14, 15, 30), and the LORD is with him in vv. 12, 14 and 28. Saul's fear follows each time (vv. 12, 15, 29).
**Hand:** Saul wants David to fall not by his own hand but by “the hand of the Philistines” (vv. 17, 21, 25), while David's hand plays the harp (v. 10).

Chapter 18 opens the court stories (18–20), which run from David's arrival at Saul's table to his flight from it. Verses 1–5 still belong to the Goliath story, and Jonathan's covenant here is the first of three (20:16, 42; 23:18).
**Forward:** Michal will save David's life (19:11–17), be given to another man (25:44), be taken back (2 Samuel 3:13–16), and despise David for dancing before the ark (2 Samuel 6:16).

traditions.text: The Church's footnote on v. 10 shows the JST changing the evil spirit “from God” to a spirit “which was not of God,” the same change made in 16:14–23 and 19:9. Here the spirit comes the day after the women's song, so in the JST Saul's attack follows his jealousy with no suggestion that God prompted it.

traditions.date: LDS edition of the King James Bible, 1979
traditions.text: The footnote on “knit” in v. 1 points to Alma's people, whose hearts were to be “knit together in unity and in love one towards another,” and to D&C 88:123, the command to love one another. The footnote on v. 12, where the LORD had departed from Saul, points to D&C 121:37: when men cover sins or exercise unrighteous dominion, the Spirit of the Lord is grieved and withdraws. Together they set Jonathan's love beside Saul's loss.

traditions.date: LDS edition of the King James Bible, 1979
traditions.text: Under Michal, Saul's second daughter and David's wife, the Bible Dictionary notes that 2 Samuel 21:8 uses the name Michal by mistake for Merab, the wife of Adriel. That ties the later verse back to v. 19, where Merab was given to Adriel the Meholathite instead of David.

Josephus has the wives sing that Saul slew his many thousands and the virgins answer that David slew his ten thousands. He leaves out Merab. Saul's price for Michal becomes six hundred Philistine heads, since asking money, Saul says, would be “to set my daughter to sale,” and David duly brings six hundred heads. Josephus also reads the captaincy of v. 13 as a demotion in disguise: an armourbearer stood too near the king for Saul's comfort, and a field command put David where Saul hoped he would be killed.

The sayings of the fathers distinguish two kinds of love. Love that depends on something ends when the thing ends, like Amnon's for Tamar; love that depends on nothing never ends, and the example is the love of David and Jonathan. The Mishnah chose the friendship that begins in v. 1 as its model of love without motive.

The rabbis ask how David could marry two sisters. One answer is that the betrothal to Merab never took effect, because it rested on the riches Saul owed David for Goliath (17:25), and a woman cannot be betrothed by cancelling a debt. Saul then argued the same over Michal, saying the foreskins had no value; David held they were worth at least a small coin as food for dogs and cats.

Rashi reads Saul's words in v. 17 as spoken to himself: he will not lay his own hand on David lest he be punished for it, so he sends him to fight the LORD's battles instead. On v. 27 he notes that David handed over all two hundred foreskins, though Saul had asked for only one hundred.

Where v. 10 says Saul “prophesied in the midst of the house,” the Aramaic Targum says he raved. Rashi explains the choice: a prophet and a madman both speak in obscure hints, so the same Hebrew verb can describe either. The JST changes the source of the spirit in this verse but leaves the verb alone.
traditions.cite: Targum Jonathan and Rashi on 1 Samuel 18:10

traditions.text: Writing to quarrelling Corinthians, Clement of Rome lists what envy and jealousy have done from Cain onward. After Joseph, Moses and Dathan and Abiram he comes to this chapter: through envy David was hated by foreigners and “was also persecuted by Saul king of Israel.” The women's song is the turning point he has in mind.

Cyprian, bishop of Carthage, gives the same list as Clement and is more specific. Saul sought again and again to kill David, innocent and patient as he was, for no cause but jealousy: when Goliath fell and the people praised David, Saul conceived the rage that drove his persecutions.

traditions.source: Basil of Caesarea, Homily on Envy
traditions.text: Basil makes Saul his chief example of how envy turns a benefactor into an enemy. The dancing women gave David the greater honour in their song, and Saul, freed from his melancholy by David's harp, tried to pierce the man who had just helped him. Basil goes on through the later pursuits in the wilderness to show that kindness only fed the envy.

traditions.source: Ambrose, On the Duties of the Clergy
traditions.text: Ambrose says good will makes friends alike in character: Jonathan, the king's son, imitated David's gentleness because he loved him. He contrasts Esau and Jacob, who grew up in one house with no good will between them and so stayed unlike.
traditions.cite: On the Duties of the Clergy 1.33.171

19.overview:
Saul now orders Jonathan and his servants to kill David. Jonathan pleads for him, and Saul swears he will not be slain, but after another war Saul again throws his javelin while David plays. That night Michal warns David, lets him down through a window, and lays the household image in his bed with goats' hair at its head. David flees to Samuel at Ramah. Saul sends three companies of messengers to take him at Naioth, and each falls to prophesying; then Saul goes himself, prophesies, strips off his clothes, and lies naked before Samuel a day and a night.

Three people stand between David and Saul in turn: Jonathan with words, Michal with a trick, and Samuel with the Spirit of God. The Spirit that once came on Saul after his anointing (10:10) now stops him in his tracks, and the old proverb is said again, of a king lying on the ground.

19.hermeneutics:
Michal's “image” is the *teraphim* (v. 13), the same kind of household object Rachel hid under her camel's saddle (Genesis 31:34). Here it is large enough, with goats' hair at its head, to pass in the dark for a sleeping man. Karel van der Toorn (1990), comparing cuneiform texts that pair the household gods with the spirits of dead kin, argued that teraphim were figures of ancestors, kept in the home and consulted for guidance. On that reading Michal uses the family's own sacred figure as a decoy for her husband. The narrator records that such a thing stood in David's house and passes no comment.

Prophets in Israel's world could act out their message in public, sometimes shockingly. A letter to King Zimri-Lim of Mari (18th century BC) reports that a prophet of the god Dagan asked for a lamb, devoured it raw before the city gate, gathered the elders there, and announced that a devouring was coming on the land. He asked to be clothed in a garment, and the official clothed him. The act carried the oracle. Saul's prophesying at Naioth has the same public, bodily character: he strips, falls, and lies naked a day and a night before Samuel (v. 24). Nothing he says is recorded. What the onlookers remember is the sight of their king on the ground, and they make a proverb of it.

notes: **Kill:** the verb *mut* (kill, slay) comes 8 times (vv. 1, 2, 5, 6, 11 twice, 15, 17), from Saul's order to Michal's invented threat.
**Escape:** *malat* comes 5 times (vv. 10, 11, 12, 17, 18) as David slips away from javelin, house and city.
**Prophesy:** the verb comes 6 times in vv. 20–24: the prophets, three companies of messengers, then Saul twice. Saul sends three times before going himself, and the third failure brings him.

Chapter 19 is the middle of the court stories (18–20). Saul's jealousy becomes open orders to kill, and the Bible Dictionary's outline of David's life ends his court years at v. 18, when he reaches Samuel. Jonathan's last attempt to reconcile them follows in ch. 20.

**Echoes:** the proverb of v. 24 first arose after Saul's anointing (10:10–12). Michal's teraphim recall Rachel's (Genesis 31:19, 34), and letting David down through a window recalls Rahab and the spies (Joshua 2:15).

traditions.text: The Church's footnote on v. 9 shows the JST changing the evil spirit “from the LORD” into one “which was not of the Lord,” the last of the changes it makes in 16:14–23, 18:10 and here. In this verse the spirit comes on Saul just after he has sworn by the LORD that David will not die (v. 6), so the JST keeps the LORD's name apart from the broken oath that follows.

traditions.date: LDS edition of the King James Bible, 1979
traditions.text: The Bible Dictionary describes teraphim as images of the size and form of a man, citing vv. 13 and 16, used from the patriarchs onward in worship and for magic in Israel and in Babylon. It judges that using them was probably not worship of strange gods but worship of the true God in a corrupt manner. That is the Church's published reading of what Michal kept in David's house.

Josephus gives Jonathan's plea (vv. 4–5) as a full speech: David ended forty days of Goliath's taunts, brought the heads he was asked for, married Jonathan's sister, and cast out the evil spirit and demons that seized Saul. Saul swears to do David no harm, and Josephus comments that “a righteous discourse proved too hard for the King's anger and fear.”

In Josephus Michal lowers David by a cord and puts a goat's liver under the bedclothes, so that its quivering makes the bed move as if he were breathing hard. The Septuagint also reads “liver” in v. 13, where the Hebrew has a pillow of goats' hair; the Greek translator seems to have read a similar Hebrew word. When Saul accuses her, Michal says David threatened to kill her and she helped him out of fear, and Saul forgives her.

At Naioth, Josephus says, Samuel made Saul prophesy before he even reached him. Saul arrived disordered in mind and under the vehement agitation of a spirit, put off his garments, and lay on the ground all that day and night in the presence of Samuel and David.

Here the spirit makes Saul prophesy against himself. He asks why he persecutes in vain, declares that the time of his kingdom is fulfilled, and foretells that he and his son will die together and David will reign. Then the spirit leaves him, and he does not know what he has prophesied. The prophecy comes true on Gilboa, where Saul and his sons fall on the same day (31:2–6).

The Aramaic Targum never names Naioth. Each time the Hebrew has it, the Targum says “the house of study” in Ramah (vv. 18, 19, 22, 23), and in v. 20 Samuel stands over the company teaching them. David's refuge becomes Samuel's school, and Rashi glosses the name the same way. The Talmud's reading of Naioth, below, also puts teacher and student at work there.
traditions.cite: Targum Jonathan on 1 Samuel 19:18–23; Rashi on 19:19

traditions.text: Rava asks what Naioth has to do with Ramah and hears in the name a word for beauty: David and Samuel sat in Ramah discussing the beauty of the world, the site of the Temple. Reasoning that the Temple must stand higher than all the land, they searched Joshua's tribal boundaries and found that only Benjamin's border is said to go up and never down. So, the rabbis say, the fugitive and the prophet fixed the Temple's place in Benjamin's territory.

Rashi pictures the teraphim as a figure made in human likeness, with the goatskin laid at its head because the figure had no hair. In v. 24 he says Saul took off his royal garments to put on the garments of the disciples. He also reports that the Targum's word for naked was heard from an Arabic speaker to mean insane.

Augustine asks how Saul, after an evil spirit had seized him, could again prophesy by the Spirit of God (v. 23). He answers that the change lay in Saul's mutable soul, not in God's unchangeable Spirit. God gives the good spirit by grace and lets an evil one serve his judgment, and the two cannot be the same, since 16:14 says one departed and the other took hold.

traditions.source: Ambrose, On the Duties of the Clergy
traditions.text: Ambrose uses v. 24 to show that what is fitting depends on the person. Saul, surrounded by the company of prophets, prophesied too, yet of him alone, as though he were unworthy, the people asked whether Saul was among the prophets. The same act honoured the others and exposed him.
traditions.cite: On the Duties of the Clergy 1.43.223

20.overview:
David flees from Naioth to Jonathan and asks what his sin is, that Saul seeks his life. They agree on a test: David will stay away from the king's new moon feast, and Jonathan will learn his father's mind and signal the answer with arrows. Out in the field they swear a covenant that reaches to their descendants. Saul says nothing the first day, but on the second he curses Jonathan for choosing the son of Jesse and hurls his javelin at his own son. Next morning Jonathan shoots beyond the boy, and the two friends weep together and part in peace.

The covenant runs the other way from what a reader expects. The king's heir asks David to spare his house when the LORD has cut off David's enemies (vv. 14–16), as if David already reigned. Saul says the same in anger: while the son of Jesse lives, Jonathan's kingdom will not be established (v. 31).

20.hermeneutics:
Hittite royal politics offers a close parallel to this friendship. On a bronze tablet found at Hattusa in 1986, King Tudhaliya IV (13th century BC) recalls that before he became king the gods made him and his cousin Kurunta friends, and the two swore to protect each other. Kurunta was the son of an earlier king, Muwatalli II, whose line had lost the throne to Tudhaliya's father, and he swore to stay loyal to Tudhaliya even if Tudhaliya's father did not make him king. Once on the throne, Tudhaliya confirmed Kurunta's own kingdom by treaty. Jonathan stands where Kurunta stood, the son of the line that will lose. He binds the future king by oath before the outcome is known: loyalty now, and kindness to his house afterward (vv. 14–16, 42).

The Greek text clears up two puzzles. Where the Hebrew has David wait by “the stone Ezel” (v. 19) and rise “out of a place toward the south” (v. 41), the Septuagint has him hide beside a mound and rise from beside it, so that both verses name the same hiding place. Modern translations such as the RSV, NRSV and ESV follow the Greek in v. 41: David rose “from beside the stone heap.” The Greek also spells out Saul's reasoning on the first day of the feast: David is not clean because he has not purified himself (v. 26). A meal at the new moon was a sacred meal, and the unclean could not eat of it (Leviticus 7:20).

notes: **Missed:** *paqad*, “miss” or “be empty,” comes 6 times (vv. 6 twice, 18 twice, 25, 27). The whole plan turns on an empty seat.

**Between:** “the LORD be between thee and me for ever” (v. 23) returns at the parting with the descendants added (v. 42). David's first plea used the same word: “there is but a step between me and death” (v. 3).
**Cut:** *karat* comes 3 times in vv. 15–16: David must not cut off his kindness when the LORD cuts off his enemies, and Jonathan cuts, that is makes, a covenant.

Chapter 20 closes the court stories (18–20). The new moon feast is the last time David's place is set at Saul's table, and the chapter's last words, which the Hebrew Bible numbers 21:1, send David away and Jonathan back to the city. From ch. 21 David is a fugitive.

**Forward:** the friends renew their covenant in the wood of Ziph (23:16–18), their last meeting. David keeps it when he seeks out Jonathan's son to show him kindness (2 Samuel 9:1) and spares him “because of the LORD's oath” (2 Samuel 21:7).

traditions.date: LDS edition of the King James Bible, 1979
traditions.text: The Bible Dictionary calls Jonathan's friendship for David, whom he might naturally have regarded as a rival, one of the most unselfish incidents in Old Testament history. It adds that Jonathan left one son, Merib-baal, later called Mephibosheth, the son David would protect for Jonathan's sake. It also counts David's lament over Saul and Jonathan (2 Samuel 1) among the most beautiful poems in the Bible.

traditions.date: LDS edition of the King James Bible, 1979
traditions.text: The footnote on Jonathan's promise in v. 4, “Whatsoever thy soul desireth, I will even do it for thee,” points back to 18:1 and to D&C 88:123, the command to love one another and to impart to one another. The footnotes on vv. 8 and 14 send the reader forward to 2 Samuel 21:7 and 9:1, where David keeps the covenant with Jonathan's son.

traditions.date: LDS edition of the King James Bible, 1979
traditions.text: The entry on the new moon cites vv. 5–6 and 29 among its examples. It explains that the law appointed special sacrifices at the new moon and that, since every feast was reckoned by the moon, the exact time of its appearance mattered greatly, with watchers posted on the hills around Jerusalem.

Jonathan takes David “into the open field, into the pure air” to swear, and calls on God, who is everywhere and knows his intention before he speaks, as witness of the covenant. If he dies, he asks David to preserve his children alive and repay the kindness to them. His signal is three darts shot at a mark in the plain where he used to exercise.

At the feast Saul, having purified himself as the custom was, supposes David has not purified himself since being with his wife. When Saul leaps at Jonathan with his spear, Josephus adds that friends held him back. Jonathan weeps all night, and at the parting the two lament the friendship that envy will take from them.

Pseudo-Philo gives the parting two long speeches. Jonathan is sure that even if death parts them their souls will know one another, and he proposes that they weep together, gather their tears in one vessel, and bury it as a witness. He tells David that the kingdom is his in this world and will come in its time. He asks David to remember not Saul's ingratitude but “the table whereat we have eaten together.”

Rashi takes Saul's thought in v. 26 as ritual impurity from an emission, which kept a man from a sacred meal until evening, the same explanation Josephus gives. On v. 5 he notes that the new moon was a festive day on which no one who ate at the king's table stayed away, so David's absence was bound to be noticed. In v. 41 he reads “until David exceeded” as David weeping more than Jonathan.

On Saul's insult, “son of the perverse rebellious woman” (v. 30), Rashi records a midrash. Saul's wife was one of the daughters of Shiloh whom the men of Benjamin seized as they danced in the vineyards (Judges 21:20–23). Saul was too bashful to seize anyone, so she came and pursued him, and the insult recalls it.

The rabbis notice what Jonathan did not give at the parting. Rav taught that had Jonathan lent David two loaves of bread for the road, David would not have asked the priests of Nob for food (21:3–6). Then Nob would not have been destroyed, Doeg would not have lost his place in the world to come, and Saul and his three sons would not have died for that massacre.

On Paul's words that love “doth not behave itself unseemly,” Chrysostom turns to v. 30. Saul's insult was full of reproach, yet Jonathan was not ashamed of his friend: a king's son held to a fugitive and a wanderer, and after it all fell on David's neck as if he had been crowned. Love, Chrysostom says, does not know what shame is.

traditions.source: Ambrose, On the Duties of the Clergy
traditions.text: Ambrose reads Saul's spear in v. 33 as jealousy of a friendship. Saul tried to strike Jonathan because he thought David's friendship held a higher place in his son's heart than filial duty or a father's authority. Ambrose sets it in a chapter on how love is won, with David as the man whom parents put even before their own children.
traditions.cite: On the Duties of the Clergy 2.7.36

21.overview:
David comes alone to Nob, the town of the priests, and tells Ahimelech a story: the king has sent him on secret business. Hungry and unarmed, he asks for bread and a weapon. The only bread is the holy shewbread, and the priest gives it once David assures him the young men have kept themselves from women. The only weapon is Goliath's sword, wrapped in a cloth behind the ephod. Then David flees to Achish, king of Gath, is recognized as the hero of the women's song, and saves himself by acting mad.

One man watches the scene at Nob: Doeg the Edomite, Saul's chief herdsman, “detained before the LORD” (v. 7). The narrator sets him down between the bread and the sword and says nothing more about him. The next chapter shows what his presence costs.

historicalContext.label: Author
historicalContext.text: Not named in the text. The Talmud credits Samuel, with Gad and Nathan completing it (1 Chronicles 29:29); many scholars see it as part of a larger history compiled in the 7th–6th century BC from older sources.
