historicalContext.label: Date of events
historicalContext.text: Late in Saul's reign, before David became king at thirty (2 Samuel 5:4). Traditional chronology places David's reign about 1010–970 BC.

historicalContext.label: Setting (events)
historicalContext.text: Nob, a priestly town near Jerusalem (Isaiah 10:32); Gath, the Philistine city usually identified with Tell es-Safi, about 23 miles to the southwest.

historicalContext.label: Parallel accounts
historicalContext.text: Jesus retells vv. 1–6 (Matthew 12:3–4; Mark 2:25–26; Luke 6:3–4). The headings of Psalms 34 and 56 tie those psalms to David's time at Gath.

21.hermeneutics:
Samuel comes down in more than one form, and the Greek Bible (the Septuagint) reads this chapter differently at three points. It calls the priest Abimelech instead of Ahimelech. It makes Doeg “the Syrian,” an Aramean, instead of the Edomite: the two words differ by one letter, and the Hebrew *d* and *r* look much alike in every period of the script. Josephus also calls Doeg a Syrian, so his Bible probably read the same way. And where the Hebrew says David “scrabbled on the doors of the gate” (v. 13), the Greek has him drum on them, from a verb one letter different; some scholars read it as “spat.” The story does not change, but the details came to ancient readers in different forms.

Achish is not a Semitic name. Scholars place it among names of Aegean and western Anatolian type, the world the Philistines came from: an Egyptian school writing board of the 18th Dynasty lists it among names of Keftiu, Crete, and it is often compared with Anchises, the Trojan father of Aeneas in Homer. More than three centuries after David, a temple dedication found at Ekron in 1996 names that city's ruler Achish son of Padi, and Assyrian records call the same king Ikausu. The name stayed in use among Philistine kings. The king David meets is a foreigner with a foreign name, and his servants quote Israel's own victory song back at David (v. 11) while David carries the sword of Gath's dead champion.

breakdown.label: At Nob: Ahimelech trembles; David claims secret orders
The hallowed bread, given on condition of purity
Doeg the Edomite, detained before the LORD
Goliath's sword taken from behind the ephod
At Gath: Achish's servants recognize David
David feigns madness and is turned away

structure.summary: No strong pattern; the chapter moves in sequence, from the priest's town to the Philistine king's gate.

rows.text: Nob: bread and sword from the priest

notes: **Two deceptions:** at Nob David invents a mission from his king (v. 2); at Gath he plays a madman before another king (v. 13). Both escapes depend on what a king is thought to want.
**Hand:** the Hebrew word comes 6 times (vv. 3, 3, 4, 8, 8, 13). David asks what is “under thine hand,” the priest has no common bread “under mine hand,” and at Gath David raves “in their hands.”
**Bread** comes 6 times in vv. 3–6 and **holy** 3 times (vv. 4–6). Doeg's verse (v. 7) stands between the bread and the sword.

The fugitive section (21:1–23:29) begins the moment David leaves Jonathan. The Hebrew Bible counts the last line of 20:42 (“And he arose and departed”) as 21:1, so its 21:2–16 are the KJV's vv. 1–15. Nob and Gath show David alone; by 22:2 he leads four hundred men.

**Echoes:** Goliath's sword is the one David drew to behead him (17:51). David will return to Achish twice, as a vassal given Ziklag (27:2–6) and as a soldier the Philistine lords refuse to trust (29:3).

traditions.text: The Church's footnote on the “hallowed” bread in v. 4 points to the Book of Mormon prayer over the sacrament bread, which asks God to “bless and sanctify this bread” for those who eat it. The cross-reference sets the priest's question, whether David's men are fit to eat holy bread, beside bread that the Restoration sets apart by prayer before it is eaten. It links the two passages without commenting on David's act.

traditions.date: LDS edition of the King James Bible, 1979
traditions.text: The Church's Bible Dictionary lists Mark 2:26, where Jesus places David's visit “in the days of Abiathar the high priest,” under Abiathar, the son of Ahimelech who escaped from Nob (22:20). The same entry says the names Ahimelech and Abiathar are probably interchanged in 2 Samuel 8:17 and 1 Chronicles 18:16 and 24:3, 31. The Joseph Smith Translation reworks the Sabbath saying that follows in Mark (2:27–28) and leaves v. 26 as it stands.
traditions.cite: Bible Dictionary, “Abiathar”; Mark 2:26–28 with JST Mark 2:26–27

traditions.text: Josephus retells the visit without the holy bread: Ahimelech simply supplies David with food, and the high priest reminds him that he had dedicated Goliath's sword to God after the victory. Like the Greek Bible, he calls Doeg a Syrian, the keeper of Saul's mules. At Gath his David lets his spittle run and acts out the madness until the king, angry with his servants, has him thrown out of the city.

The rabbis use vv. 4–6 in a debate over when the shewbread was baked, with two teachers reading David's words as a rebuke to the priests. The discussion settles on another reading: David asked for even the loaves set out that same day, because he and his men were dangerously famished, and danger to life sets aside the rule that only priests may eat. Rashi adopts this reading. It is close to the use Jesus makes of the story, need overriding a sacred rule (Mark 2:25–26).

traditions.date: compiled over centuries; final form medieval
traditions.text: A midrash on Psalm 34 has David ask God what good madness is, a man tearing his clothes in the market while children chase him, and God answers that he will need it one day. At Gath, it says, Goliath's brother was Achish's bodyguard, and David wrote on the doors that Achish owed him a hundred myriads and his wife fifty. Achish's own wife and daughter were mad, raving indoors while David raved outside, so the king complained that he had madmen enough (v. 15). The psalm calls Achish Abimelech, the midrash explains, because he was as just as Abimelech of Gerar (Genesis 20).

Jesus defends his disciples' plucking grain on the Sabbath with this chapter: David ate the shewbread “in the days of Abiathar the high priest.” First Samuel names the priest Ahimelech; Abiathar is his son, who escapes the massacre in the next chapter (22:20), and Matthew and Luke tell the saying without the priest's name (Matthew 12:3–4; Luke 6:3–4). Readers have answered in several ways: Mark or his source slipped, the two names were already confused (2 Samuel 8:17 makes Ahimelech the son of Abiathar), or Mark's Greek means in the passage about Abiathar, as he writes “in the bush” for the passage about the bush (Mark 12:26).

Defending his translations against critics who demanded word-for-word accuracy, Jerome listed places where the Gospels quote Scripture loosely. One is Mark 2:26: turn to the books of Samuel, he writes, and the high priest's name is not Abiathar but Ahimelech, the same man Doeg later killed at Saul's command. He says he raises such cases not to accuse the evangelists of falsehood but to show that the apostles cared for the sense more than the words.

Augustine's Latin, following the Greek, says David drummed on the doors and “was carried in his own hands” (v. 13). He reads it of Christ, who at the Last Supper carried his own body in his hands when he said, This is my body, and he takes the drum, skin stretched on wood, as a figure of the cross. In the same sermons Achish stands for error and ignorance.

Ambrose uses the scene in a lesson on what suits each person, time and circumstance. David's changed behavior before Achish, he says, would not have escaped the charge of levity had he done it without fear of being recognized; danger made it fitting. He sets it beside David dancing before the ark, which was not blamed in David though Samuel did not dance.
traditions.cite: On the Duties of the Clergy 1.43.222–223

22.overview:
David hides in the cave of Adullam, and his family joins him there with about four hundred men who are in distress, in debt or discontented. He leaves his parents with the king of Moab, and the prophet Gad sends him back into Judah. At Gibeah, Saul sits with his spear under a tree and accuses his own Benjamite servants of siding with “the son of Jesse.” Doeg reports what he saw at Nob. Saul summons Ahimelech and all the priests, rejects the priest's defense, and orders them killed. His footmen refuse. Doeg kills eighty-five priests and puts the whole town of Nob to the sword. Only Abiathar escapes, to David.

Notice who acts and who refuses. Saul's own guard will not lift a hand against “the priests of the LORD” (v. 17); the foreigner does it. And David, hearing the news, blames himself first: “I have occasioned the death” of the priest's whole house (v. 22).

historicalContext.text: Not named in the text. The Talmud credits Samuel, with Gad and Nathan completing it (1 Chronicles 29:29); many scholars see it as part of a larger history compiled in the 7th–6th century BC from older sources.

historicalContext.text: Unknown. Tradition places it soon after the events (11th–10th century BC); many scholars date its final form to the 7th–6th century BC, drawing on older court and prophetic sources.

historicalContext.label: Date of events
historicalContext.text: Late in Saul's reign, before David became king at thirty (2 Samuel 5:4). Traditional chronology places David's reign about 1010–970 BC.

historicalContext.label: Setting (events)
historicalContext.text: The cave of Adullam in the Judean lowland; Mizpeh of Moab, east of the Dead Sea; the forest of Hareth in Judah; Saul's court at Gibeah; the priestly town of Nob.

historicalContext.label: Parallel accounts
historicalContext.text: No parallel narrative. The heading of Psalm 52 ties it to Doeg's report, and 1 Chronicles 12:16–18 tells of men of Benjamin and Judah who came to David “to the hold.”

22.hermeneutics:
A prince driven from home who gathers outcasts and waits for his throne was a known story in the region. Idrimi, king of Alalakh in northern Syria in the 15th century BC, tells his on his statue. After trouble in his father's house at Aleppo, his family fled to his mother's relatives at Emar. He went on alone to Ammiya in Canaan, where refugees from his homeland recognized him as their lord's son and gathered around him, and he lived seven years among the Habiru, landless men outside any city's law. Then he sailed with a force, won over Alalakh and became king. David's chapter has the same pieces: a man the court has cast out, parents lodged with a foreign king (his great-grandmother Ruth was a Moabite, Ruth 4:17), and a band of the distressed, the indebted and the embittered (v. 2) who follow him in the hills until the throne comes.

The witnesses to the text do not agree on the number of the slain. The Hebrew has eighty-five priests (v. 18). The Greek Bible has three hundred and five, and Josephus and the 1st-century *Biblical Antiquities* both give three hundred and eighty-five, so the larger numbers were already in circulation in the 1st century AD. Most textual critics take the smaller number as original. All the witnesses agree that Doeg then struck the whole town, people and animals alike.

Parents left with Moab's king; Gad sends David to Judah
Saul, spear in hand, accuses his Benjamite servants
Doeg reports Ahimelech's help at Nob
Ahimelech's defense and Saul's sentence of death
The guard refuses; Doeg kills the priests and strikes Nob
Abiathar escapes to David and stays with him

structure.summary: No strong pattern; the chapter moves in sequence, cutting from David's camp to Saul's court and back.

rows.text: Saul's court and the slaughter at Nob

notes: **Two camps:** David gains followers, family and finally a priest; Saul, surrounded by his own tribe, suspects all of them of conspiracy (vv. 7–8).
**“Son of Jesse”:** the phrase comes 4 times (vv. 7, 8, 9, 13), from Saul and from Doeg, who takes up his master's word. Only Ahimelech calls him David (v. 14).
**Priests:** the word comes 8 times in vv. 11–21. The order to kill “the priests of the LORD” (v. 17) returns in Abiathar's report that Saul “had slain the LORD's priests” (v. 21).

Chapter 22 is the center of the fugitive section (21:1–23:29). It pays off the threads left in ch. 21, Doeg's presence at Nob and the priest's help, and it hands David the priest and ephod he consults in ch. 23.

**Echoes:** a man of God had told Eli that his house would be cut off and only one man of his line kept at the altar (2:31–33). Abiathar, Eli's descendant, is that survivor, and Solomon later expels him “that he might fulfil the word of the LORD” spoken against Eli's house (1 Kings 2:26–27).

traditions.text: Josephus describes the men who came to Adullam as those in want or in fear of Saul, four hundred in all. He has Saul's guards hold back because they feared disobeying God more than disobeying the king, and he puts the number Doeg and his helpers killed at 385, Ahimelech and his kindred. Saul then sends to Nob, kills everyone there without sparing women, children or the old, and burns the town. Abiathar alone escapes, and Josephus reads the slaughter as the fulfilment of God's warning to Eli about his sons' sins.

Josephus stops the story for a reflection on power. Men who are moderate in private life, he says, believe God sees their very thoughts, but once they gain authority they drop that belief, and like actors on a stage they put off the parts they were playing. He names Saul, the first king after the judges, as the proof, for slaying the priests and overthrowing the city chosen for them.

This retelling gives God's reason first: the priests of Nob were polluting the holy things as Eli's sons had done, so God would wipe them out. It counts 385 dead, the same figure as Josephus, and blames the people, who had rescued Jonathan from his father's sentence (14:45) but kept silent when the priests were slain; for that they and their king would fall. Doeg's sentence is a worm on his tongue and a dwelling “in the fire that is not quenched.”

The Talmud sets Nob beside Amalek. When Saul spared Agag and the flocks, a heavenly voice told him not to be “righteous over much”; when he had the men, women, children and animals of Nob killed, it told him not to be over much wicked (Ecclesiastes 7:16–17). Rav Huna asks why Saul lost his throne for one sin while David kept his after two, and answers that the decree against Saul came after Agag, before Nob.

A tradition holds David to his own words in v. 22. God tells him that through him the city of priests was destroyed, Doeg lost the world to come, and Saul and his sons died, and he offers David a choice of punishment. David chooses to fall into an enemy's hand rather than lose his descendants, and the enemy is the giant Ishbi-benob (2 Samuel 21:16), whose name the rabbis read as the man who came over the matter of Nob.

The rabbis make Doeg a great scholar gone wrong. The “mighty man” of Psalm 52 is mighty in Torah, they say, but his learning was on his lips and not in his heart, and he died young after forgetting all he had learned. They explain the two Hebrew spellings of his name in vv. 9 and 18 as God's worry that he would turn to evil, then God's lament when he did.

traditions.date: compiled over centuries; final form medieval
traditions.text: The midrash on Psalm 52 makes Doeg the classic case of evil speech. A murderer kills one person, it says, but slander kills three: the one who tells it, the one who accepts it and the one it is about. Doeg told it, and was driven from the world to come; Saul accepted it, and died for his transgression (1 Chronicles 10:13); Ahimelech was its subject, and heard “Thou shalt surely die” (v. 16). Another of its readings has Doeg struck with leprosy for his report.

Rashi, following a midrash, finds the end of v. 4 in a later war. David's harsh treatment of Moab after he became king (2 Samuel 8:2) was vengeance, he says, because the king of Moab killed David's father, mother and brothers: the text brings them before the king and never reports that they left. The Bible itself gives no reason for the war with Moab.

Augustine preached Psalm 52 as Doeg's psalm and made Doeg a figure of the earthly city. The psalm's mighty man glories in a strength that a scorpion or a fever shares, he says: building a house or raising a child takes years, and anyone can destroy either in a moment. He notes that his copies of the psalm's title name the priest Abimelech, not Achimelech, and takes the variation as a sign to look for a hidden meaning.

23.overview:
Philistines raid the threshing floors of Keilah, a walled town in Judah's lowland. David asks the LORD whether to go, asks again when his men are afraid, and rescues the town. When Saul plans to trap him inside its gates, David has Abiathar bring the ephod and learns that Saul will come and that the townsmen will hand him over, so he leaves with about six hundred men. In the wilderness of Ziph, Jonathan comes to him and promises that he will be king. The Ziphites offer to deliver David to Saul, and Saul closes in around a mountain in Maon until a messenger reports a Philistine raid and he turns back.

Notice how David decides. Before every move in vv. 1–13 he asks the LORD, and the answers come through the priest and ephod that escaped Nob. Saul works from reports, blesses his informers (v. 21), and is called away at the last moment.

historicalContext.text: Not named in the text. The Talmud credits Samuel, with Gad and Nathan completing it (1 Chronicles 29:29); many scholars see it as part of a larger history compiled in the 7th–6th century BC from older sources.

historicalContext.text: Unknown. Tradition places it soon after the events (11th–10th century BC); many scholars date its final form to the 7th–6th century BC, drawing on older court and prophetic sources.

historicalContext.label: Date of events
historicalContext.text: Late in Saul's reign, before David became king at thirty (2 Samuel 5:4). Traditional chronology places David's reign about 1010–970 BC.

historicalContext.label: Setting (events)
historicalContext.text: Keilah, a town of Judah's lowland (Joshua 15:44), at Khirbet Qila about 8 miles northwest of Hebron; the wildernesses of Ziph and Maon in the hills southeast of Hebron (Joshua 15:55).

historicalContext.label: Parallel accounts
historicalContext.text: No parallel narrative. The heading of Psalm 54 ties that psalm to the Ziphites' report (v. 19).

23.hermeneutics:
Keilah was a contested town long before David. In the Amarna letters of the 14th century BC, written to Pharaoh by Canaanite rulers, it appears as Qiltu. Shuwardata, probably the ruler of Gath, wrote that he had retaken Keilah with the king's permission and complained that Abdi-Heba of Jerusalem had then urged its men to follow him instead (EA 280). A walled town on the edge between the hills and the Philistine plain changed sides as power shifted. That is the situation David's question assumes: the men he has just saved will still hand him over if Saul comes (v. 12).

Kings across the region put pointed questions to their gods before acting. Hundreds of queries to the sun god Shamash survive from the reigns of Esarhaddon and Ashurbanipal of Assyria (7th century BC). One asks whether the king of Phrygia or a ruler named Mugallu will attack a fortress of Melid, and the answer was read as yes or no in the liver of a sacrificed ram. David's questions to the ephod have the same shape, a named enemy and a single event: will Saul come down? will the men of Keilah deliver me up? The answers are just as short.

Verses 11–12 also show the text of Samuel at work. In the Masoretic text David asks whether the men of Keilah will deliver him, then whether Saul will come, and is answered only about Saul, so he asks the first question again. A Dead Sea Scroll of Samuel (4QSam-b) lacks the first question in v. 11, and textual critics take it as a copying slip carried over from v. 12. In that text David asks one thing at a time.

breakdown.label: Keilah rescued after two inquiries of the LORD
Abiathar's ephod arrives; Saul plans a siege
The ephod answers; David leaves Keilah
Jonathan strengthens David in the wood of Ziph
The Ziphites offer to deliver David to Saul
Saul surrounds David at Maon; the Philistines call him away
David goes up to the strongholds of En-gedi

structure.summary: No strong pattern; the chapter moves in sequence through two near-betrayals with Jonathan's visit between them.

rows.text: Ziph and Maon: betrayal and pursuit

notes: **Deliver up:** the Hebrew verb, literally “shut in,” comes 5 times: Saul's “he is shut in” (v. 7), David's question and the LORD's answer (vv. 11–12), and the Ziphites' promise (v. 20). The town David saves and the people he hides among both offer him to Saul.
**Keilah** is named 14 times in vv. 1–13 and never again.

**Seek:** Saul seeks David four times (vv. 10, 14, 15, 25), and once the narrator adds that “God delivered him not into his hand” (v. 14). Between the hunts Jonathan comes to strengthen “his hand in God” (v. 16).

Chapter 23 closes the fugitive section (21:1–23:29). Its last verse moves David to En-gedi; the Hebrew Bible counts that verse as 24:1, joining it to the next story. The ephod Abiathar carried from Nob now guides David's moves.
**Echoes:** this is Jonathan's last meeting with David, renewing the covenant of 18:3 and 20:42 (v. 18). The Ziphites betray David a second time in nearly the same words in 26:1 (compare v. 19).

traditions.text: The Church's footnote on “inquired” in v. 2 points to Nephi's counsel that one must not “perform any thing unto the Lord” without first praying to the Father in the name of Christ. David asks before he moves and asks again when his men are afraid (vv. 2, 4). As a thematic link, the Bible Dictionary describes the Urim and Thummim, the oracle tied to the high priest's breastplate, as an instrument God prepared to help in receiving revelation.
traditions.cite: 1 Samuel 23:2 (footnote 2a); 2 Nephi 32:9; Bible Dictionary, “Urim and Thummim”

traditions.text: A teaching uses vv. 1–2 for a law of war. Keilah was a border town, the rabbis say, and the Philistines came only for straw and stubble from the threshing floors, yet the LORD told David to go and save it. From this they rule that a border town may be defended even on the Sabbath and even when only property is at stake, since the border must be guarded so that enemies gain no foothold.

The Talmud teaches that the Urim and Thummim are asked one question at a time, and that a person who asks two is answered only on the first. It finds a problem in v. 11, where David asks two questions and is answered on the second. Its answer: David asked out of order and was answered in the proper order, and once he realized it he put his first question again (v. 12). Textual critics explain the same oddity as a copying slip (see Hermeneutics).

traditions.date: compiled over centuries; final form medieval
traditions.text: The midrash on Psalm 54 opens with Proverbs 29:12: when a ruler listens to lies, all his servants are wicked, and because Saul lent his ear to slander, informers kept coming to him, first Doeg and then the Ziphites. David pleads the law that an escaped slave must not be handed back to his master (Deuteronomy 23:15), which uses the same verb as “deliver up” here: if even a slave is protected, how much more a prince descended from princes for five generations, as the genealogy of Ruth 4 shows. The same opening also counts Nabal's sneer “Who is David?” (25:10) among the fruits of a king who listens to slander.

Josephus gives David four hundred men at Keilah, as the Greek Bible does, where the Hebrew has about six hundred (v. 13). He adds that David stayed until the townspeople had safely gathered their grain and fruit, and he has a prophet, not an ephod, give God's answers. Saul, he says, was glad to hear David had entered a town with walls, gates and bars, and ordered Keilah taken and David killed; when David slipped away, the king dropped the expedition.

Josephus sets Jonathan's visit at “the New Place” of Ziph, as the Greek Bible does, reading the Hebrew for “in the wood” with one letter changed. His Jonathan tells David that such good fortune usually comes only with great labor, and the two swear lifelong goodwill. Josephus then condemns the Ziphites at length: they ran no risk by keeping quiet, yet out of flattery and hope of gain they offered to hand over a man beloved of God. When the Philistines invade, Josephus has Saul turn back on purpose, judging it more necessary to fight the nation's natural enemies than to wear himself out chasing a private one.

The Aramaic translation explains the name Sela-hammahlekoth, which the Church's footnote renders “The rock of divisions.” It was the place where the king's heart was divided, pulled one way toward David and the other toward the Philistines. Rashi repeats the explanation, and on v. 26, where Saul's men compass David round about, he pictures them encircling him the way a crown encircles the head.
traditions.cite: Targum Jonathan on 1 Samuel 23:28; Rashi on 1 Samuel 23:26, 28

traditions.text: Augustine reads the heading of Psalm 54 through this chapter. The Ziphites' betrayal, he says, did them no good and David no harm, since Saul could not catch him, and soon after David spared Saul in a cave. Taking their name to mean “flourishing,” he makes them the prosperous of this world, who bloom while the righteous hide, until the grass withers and the word of the Lord abides (Isaiah 40:6–8). To believers who envy the wicked for prospering while they themselves toil, he puts the question, “Would you also wish to be a Ziphite?”

24.overview:
Saul takes three thousand men to En-gedi to hunt David. He goes alone into a cave to relieve himself, the very cave where David and his men are hiding far inside. David's men say the LORD has delivered his enemy to him. David creeps up and cuts off the skirt of Saul's robe, then his heart strikes him, and he holds his men back. Outside, he calls after the king, bows to the ground, shows the piece of cloth as proof, and asks the LORD to judge between them. Saul weeps, calls David more righteous than himself, says he knows David will be king, and makes him swear not to cut off his descendants.

Notice that cutting the cloth troubles David at all. He has not harmed Saul's body, yet he reproaches himself for touching even the robe of “the LORD's anointed” (v. 6). That restraint is what Saul reads as proof that the kingdom will be David's (v. 20).

24.hermeneutics:
Letters from a lesser man to his lord had a stock way of bowing low on the page. In the Amarna letters of the 14th century BC, Canaanite rulers call themselves the king's dogs, and one asks who he is but a single dog. Seven centuries later, officers writing on potsherds at Lachish still opened reports to their commander by asking who their servant is but a dog, that the lord should remember him (Lachish letters 2, 5 and 6). David speaks the same courtly language: the king of Israel is chasing “a dead dog” and “a flea” (v. 14). From the man who has just held the king's life in his hand, the formula is both courtesy and argument. A vassal this small is no threat, and a king who hunts him wastes his strength.

En-gedi is a spring below steep limestone cliffs on the western shore of the Dead Sea, and the cliffs are full of caves. Nubian ibex, the “wild goats” of v. 2, still live there. Shepherds walled the mouths of caves to make folds, which the Church's footnote to v. 3 suggests the “sheepcotes” were, and a deep cave could hide men in the dark of its inner recesses while someone stood in the light at its mouth. The desert caves sheltered fugitives long after David: in the Nahal Hever canyon a few miles south, excavators in 1960–61 found letters of Bar Kokhba, leader of the revolt against Rome (AD 132–135), with the papers and bones of refugees who had hidden there.

notes: **Hand:** the Hebrew word comes 11 times. Saul is given “into thine hand” (v. 4); David will not “stretch forth mine hand” (v. 6); “mine hand shall not be upon thee” comes twice (vv. 12, 13); Saul admits he was delivered “into thine hand” (v. 18), and the kingdom will be established “in thine hand” (v. 20).
**The LORD's anointed** appears 3 times (v. 6 twice, v. 10), and the skirt (*kanaph*) of Saul's robe 4 times (vv. 4, 5, 11, 11).
**Judge and family:** “judge” comes 3 times as David hands his case to the LORD (vv. 12, 15, 15). David calls Saul “my father” (v. 11), and Saul answers “my son David” (v. 16).

Chapter 24 opens the section 24:1–26:25. The Hebrew counts KJV 23:29 as 24:1, so the move to En-gedi begins this story, and its 24:2–23 are the KJV's vv. 1–22. Chapters 24 and 26 tell two sparings of Saul in the same key words, and between them stands Nabal, the man David nearly kills (ch. 25).

**Echoes:** David refuses again to touch the LORD's anointed in 26:9–11. Saul's plea for his descendants (v. 21) is remembered when David asks whether any of Saul's house is left, that he may show kindness for Jonathan's sake (2 Samuel 9:1).

traditions.text: The Church's footnote to v. 4 explains the “skirt” as the hem or corner of the robe, the portion that symbolized Saul's authority, which gives David's remorse in v. 5 its point. At v. 12, where David asks the LORD to judge between him and Saul, the footnote points to D&C 64:11, where the Lord tells the Saints to say in their hearts, “let God judge between me and thee.” The same words that end David's quarrel with Saul become a rule for forgiving in Restoration scripture.

A thematic link, not a footnote: in a revelation given to Joseph Smith in Liberty Jail, the Lord curses “all those that shall lift up the heel against mine anointed,” who cry that they have sinned when they have not sinned before him. David's refusal to stretch out his hand against the LORD's anointed (v. 6) rests on the same idea, that the one God has anointed answers to God.

Josephus says plainly that Saul went into the cave to ease nature, and he lengthens David's speech into an argument: words can be true or false, but deeds lay a man's intentions bare, and the man who could cut a garment could have cut off a head. His Saul praises David for having the righteousness of the ancients, who held that a man should spare an enemy he catches in a lonely place. David then swears and goes up to the straits of Mastheroth.

The rabbis read v. 3 as a lesson in modesty: Saul went into a cave within a cave and covered himself even there. Rabbi Elazar takes David's odd wording in v. 10, that someone “bade me kill thee,” to mean that the law would have let David kill a pursuer, but Saul's modesty spared him. Another rabbi says David was punished for treating a garment with contempt: in old age clothes could not warm him (1 Kings 1:1).

Resh Lakish takes “the proverb of the ancients” in v. 13 as the key to the law of accidental killing, where God lets a man fall into another's hand (Exodus 21:13). Wickedness comes from the wicked, he says: an unwitnessed murderer and an unwitnessed accidental killer are brought to the same inn, where one falls from a ladder onto the other before witnesses, and each receives his due. Rashi adds that the ancient proverb is the Torah itself, the proverb of the Ancient One of the world.

traditions.date: compiled over centuries; final form medieval
traditions.text: The midrash on Psalm 57 ties the cut skirt to the robe that tore when Samuel rejected Saul over Amalek (15:27–28). When Saul asked who would receive the kingdom, it says, Samuel would only hint: the one who tears your robe will take your kingdom. So when Saul saw the corner of his robe in David's hand, he understood, and said, “I know well that thou shalt surely be king” (v. 20), which the midrash reads as king in this world and in the world to come.

The Aramaic translation drops the images of v. 14. Instead of a dead dog and a flea, David asks whom the king of Israel has come out after, and answers that he is chasing one weak man, one commoner. The Targum often turns biblical figures of speech into plain statements, and here it keeps David's point while losing the courtly self-abasement.

In his book on pastoral care, Gregory reads the cave as a lesson for those under bad rulers. Saul stands for bad rulers and David for good subjects, who will not strike their superiors with the sword of the tongue even when they rightly judge them worthy of blame. When weakness makes them speak even humbly of a ruler's faults, they have cut his robe, and like David their heart should smite them (v. 5).

Augustine preached Psalm 57, whose heading places David in the cave, as a psalm of Christ's passion. David, he says, endured his persecutor so mildly that he would not hurt him when he had him in his hands. He reads the cave as earth: as David hid in a cave, Christ hid himself in the flesh he took from the earth, so that those who crucified him would not know him as God (1 Corinthians 2:8).

25.overview:
Samuel dies, and all Israel mourns him at Ramah. In the hill country south of Hebron, David's men have guarded the flocks of Nabal, a rich and surly Calebite, and at shearing time David sends ten young men to ask for a share of the feast. Nabal sneers, “Who is David?” David arms four hundred men and swears to leave no male of Nabal's house alive by morning. A servant warns Nabal's wife Abigail, who loads donkeys with food, meets David on the road, and talks him out of shedding blood. When she tells Nabal the next morning, his heart fails, and ten days later the LORD strikes him dead. David marries Abigail.

Notice who keeps David from bloodguilt this time. In ch. 24 he restrains himself; here he sets out to kill, and a woman's speech stops him. He blesses her for keeping him “from avenging myself with mine own hand” (v. 33).

25.hermeneutics:
Here the text of Samuel shows a scribe protecting David. In v. 22 the Hebrew has David swear, “So and more also do God unto the enemies of David,” an odd oath, since the curse then falls on his foes. The Greek Bible reads “So God do to David,” the normal form of a self-curse, and textual critics generally take it as original: because David did not carry out his oath, a copyist turned the curse away from him. The Greek also sends David to the wilderness of Maon in v. 1, where the Hebrew has Paran, a desert far to the south, and Maon fits the story that follows.

Nabal is “of the house of Caleb” (v. 3). The Calebites were a clan once counted apart from Israel (Numbers 32:12 calls Caleb a Kenezite) and later absorbed into Judah, and their land centered on Hebron (Joshua 14:13–14). Maon and Carmel lie a few miles south of it. By marrying Abigail, the widow of a rich Calebite landowner, and Ahinoam of Jezreel, a town of the same district (Joshua 15:56), David gains standing in the clan country of southern Judah just as he loses Michal, Saul's daughter (v. 44). Some scholars think Nabal led the Calebites and David claimed that place by the marriage. The next step comes after Saul's death, when the men of Judah anoint David king at Hebron (2 Samuel 2:1–4).

notes: **Nabal** is named 18 times, and Abigail spells out what it means: “as his name is, so is he” (v. 25), and his name means fool.

**Evil for good:** David complains that Nabal “hath requited me evil for good” (v. 21), turning Saul's confession in 24:17 against another man. In Hebrew “good” comes 6 times in the chapter and “evil” 7.

**Haste and peace:** Abigail “made haste” or “hasted” (vv. 18, 23, 42), and David admits that only her haste saved Nabal's house (v. 34). David's greeting wishes Nabal peace three times in one verse (v. 6); he sends Abigail home “in peace” (v. 35).

Chapter 25 is the middle panel of 24:1–26:25, set between the two times David spares Saul. Here the man in David's power is not the LORD's anointed but a fool, and David nearly takes vengeance. Samuel's death opens the chapter and is recalled before Saul seeks the woman at Endor (28:3).

**Echoes:** Abigail foresees that the LORD will make David “a sure house” (v. 28), the promise Nathan brings in 2 Samuel 7:16. Abigail and Ahinoam go with David to Hebron (2 Samuel 2:2), and Michal is taken back from Phaltiel (2 Samuel 3:14–15).

traditions.text: The Church's footnote on David's “wives” (v. 43) points to Jacob 1:15, which says the Nephites under their second king began to desire many wives and concubines like David of old, and to D&C 132:37–39. That revelation says David's wives were given him by the Lord through Nathan and other prophets who held the keys of this power, and that he sinned in none of them “save in the case of Uriah and his wife.” In Jacob 2:24 the Lord calls David's and Solomon's many wives and concubines abominable before him.

The footnote on “the LORD smote Nabal” (v. 38) points to Abraham 1:20, where the Lord breaks down the altar of Elkenah and smites the idolatrous priest “that he died,” and to 2 Chronicles 13:20 on Jeroboam. The cross-references group Nabal with others whose deaths scripture assigns directly to the LORD, as David himself does in v. 39.

Josephus pauses at v. 1 to praise Samuel as a righteous man, gentle by nature and dear to God, whom the people mourned for many days, each grieving as if for someone of his own household. He counts Samuel's rule as twelve years alone after Eli's death and eighteen more together with Saul, then closes, “And thus we have finished the History of Samuel.”

In Josephus, David had ordered his men not to touch Nabal's flocks, valuing freedom from injustice above their own want. Nabal is “like a Cynick,” the Greek word for the dog-like philosophers, which the Greek Bible also uses in v. 3 where the Hebrew calls him a Calebite. When Nabal dies, Josephus has David conclude that God overlooks no one, giving the good their due and punishing the wicked, and he adds that Abigail became David's wife for her wise and righteous life, and partly for her beauty.

traditions.date: compiled c. 10th–11th century from older material
traditions.text: This midrash reads v. 1 and v. 2 together: while all Israel mourned the righteous Samuel, the wicked Nabal sat feasting. It also explains why Nabal died “about ten days” later (v. 38). God held back his death through the seven days of mourning for Samuel, so that the two mournings would not mix, then added three more. In another reading the ten days are those from the New Year to the Day of Atonement, given to Nabal in case he would repent, and he did not.

The Talmud counts Abigail among Israel's seven prophetesses and turns her meeting with David into a court hearing. When David says certain cases are not judged at night, she answers that neither are capital cases, and when he calls Nabal a rebel against the throne, she reminds him that Saul still reigns and David's coin is not yet current. Her plea that this be no offence of heart to him (v. 31) is read as foreseeing Bathsheba, and Rav Nahman notes that while pleading for her husband she also asked David to remember her, as a woman spins while she talks.

A teaching reads Abigail's words in v. 29 as a statement about the soul after death. Rabbi Eliezer says the souls of the righteous are stored beneath the Throne of Glory, “bound in the bundle of life,” while the souls of the wicked are tied up and slung back and forth by two angels standing at the two ends of the world. The bodies of the righteous, meanwhile, rest in peace on their beds (Isaiah 57:2), like royal garments laid carefully away.

The Aramaic translation already gives v. 29 a sense beyond this life. The soul of David will be stored away in the treasury of everlasting life before the LORD, while the souls of his enemies are flung away like a stone from a sling. The Talmud's reading in Shabbat 152b builds on the same image.

Gregory uses Abigail as a model for correcting an angry or drunken man. She rightly kept silent about Nabal's fault while he was drunk, he writes, and rightly told him once he had digested his wine (v. 37), because a mind drunk with fury hears every right word as wrong. Such people are better corrected when they come back to themselves and blush at having been borne with calmly.

26.overview:
The Ziphites again tell Saul where David is hiding, and Saul goes down into the wilderness with three thousand men. By night David and Abishai slip into the camp, where Saul lies asleep with his spear stuck in the ground at his head and the whole army asleep around him. Abishai asks leave to pin him to the earth with one blow. David refuses to stretch out his hand against the LORD’s anointed, takes the spear and the cruse of water, and calls from a distant hilltop, mocking Abner for failing to guard the king. Saul confesses that he has played the fool and blesses David, and they part for the last time.

The chapter retells much of ch. 24, and the differences carry the weight. This time David walks into Saul’s camp himself, and his oath hands Saul’s end to the LORD: struck down, dying in his time, or falling in battle (v. 10).

26.hermeneutics:
Saul lies “in the trench” (v. 5), with his army camped around him. The Church’s footnote renders the word “barricade,” and the Hebrew comes from a root meaning round. Assyrian palace reliefs of the 9th–7th centuries BC, from Ashurnasirpal II’s at Nimrud to Sennacherib’s siege of Lachish, draw field camps as circles or ovals inside a wall, with tents set in rows inside. A king slept in the middle of his army, with his guard and his commander nearest him; here Abner lies beside Saul and “the people round about him” (v. 7). To reach the king’s head, David and Abishai had to cross the whole sleeping camp. The text gives the reason they could: “a deep sleep from the LORD” had fallen on everyone (v. 12).

David’s last image for himself is a hunted bird. The king of Israel, he says, has come out to seek a flea, “as when one doth hunt a partridge in the mountains” (v. 20). The partridges of the Judean hills, as the naturalist H. B. Tristram noted in his *Natural History of the Bible*, save themselves by running rather than flying, darting up rocky slopes and hiding among stones. Hunters there chased a bird until it tired and then brought it down with thrown sticks. The bird’s Hebrew name, *qore*, means “caller,” and David has just stood on a hilltop calling across the valley (v. 14). Saul, with three thousand chosen men, is running one small creature to exhaustion on the hillsides of Ziph.

notes: **The LORD’s anointed** comes 4 times (vv. 9, 11, 16, 23): to Abishai, to Abner, and finally to Saul himself. Three of them pair it with the refusal to “stretch forth” the hand (vv. 9, 11, 23).
**Spear and cruse:** the spear is named in 6 verses (vv. 7, 8, 11, 12, 16, 22) and the cruse of water in 3 (vv. 11, 12, 16). The weapon Abishai wanted to use becomes the proof David hands back.
**My son David:** Saul calls him “my son” three times (vv. 17, 21, 25), and his last word to David is a blessing.

Chapter 26 closes the section 24:1–26:25, in which David twice has Saul at his mercy. Between the two refusals stands Abigail, who thanks God for keeping David from avenging himself with his own hand (25:26, 33). After this night Saul and David never meet again, and 27:1 opens with David deciding to leave for Philistia.

**Forward:** David’s oath that Saul would “descend into battle, and perish” (v. 10) is fulfilled on Gilboa, and the Church’s footnote to 31:5 points back to it. In 2 Samuel 1:14–16 David executes the man who claims to have killed “the LORD’s anointed.”

traditions.text: The Church’s footnote to v. 12 links the “deep sleep from the LORD” to two escapes in the Book of Mormon. In Mosiah 24:19 the Lord causes a deep sleep to come on the Lamanite guards so that Alma’s people can leave captivity. In Alma 55:15–16 Moroni arms the Nephite prisoners in the city of Gid while the Lamanite guards lie drunk and asleep. In each case, as at Hachilah, sleep falls on the stronger side and the weaker walk away unharmed.

Josephus names David’s companions as Abishai and Abimelech the Hittite and has David give his reason plainly: it would be a horrid crime to kill one God had made king, even a wicked man, since the God who gave him the rule would punish him in time. Saul answers that he now saw David loved him more than he loved himself. Josephus closes by noting that Saul had twice escaped David’s hands, and that this is why he gave up the chase once David fled to Gath.

Discussing slander, the Jerusalem Talmud asks why Abner was killed, and the rabbis answer from this chapter. At the cave Abner had brushed off Saul’s torn skirt (24:11) as caught on a thorn. When David now calls out to him (v. 14), the rabbis hear him ask whether the spear and the jug were also torn off by a thorn. Abner, they conclude, could have made peace between Saul and David and would not, and he paid for it with his life (2 Samuel 3:27).

Rabbi Yosei names three men whose evil impulse rose against them and who mastered it with an oath: Joseph, Boaz, and David here, swearing “As the LORD liveth” (v. 10). The rabbis disagree about whom David was swearing to. Rabbi Elazar says it was his own impulse to kill Saul; Rabbi Shmuel bar Nahman says it was Abishai, whom David warned that if he touched Saul his blood would be mixed with the king’s.

The Talmud hears a fault in David’s words “If the LORD have stirred thee up against me” (v. 19). Rabbi Elazar says God answered: you call me an inciter? Then I will make you stumble over something schoolchildren know. The census that brings a plague on Israel, where David is stirred up to number the people (1 Chronicles 21:1), is read as the result.

Who ever told David to go and serve other gods (v. 19)? The Talmud answers that the verse teaches a principle: whoever lives outside the land of Israel is counted as though he worshiped idols. David’s complaint about being driven from “the inheritance of the LORD” becomes a proof text in the rabbis’ debate over living in the land, set beside Rav Yehuda’s opposite rule that leaving Babylonia for the land breaks a commandment.

In v. 11 David tells Abishai to take the spear and the cruse, but in v. 12 David takes them himself. Kimhi explains the change: David thought better of sending Abishai to Saul’s head, fearing he could not master his urge and would strike the king after all. On v. 5 Kimhi also explains why the camp is called a ma'gal, a circle: the people camped around it in a ring.

Kimhi reads David’s oath in v. 10 as spoken to calm Abishai: Saul’s time is short. Either the LORD will strike him with sickness before his day, as he struck Nabal (25:38), or his appointed day is near, or he will fall in battle, and since God has rejected Saul and had David anointed, his end cannot be far off. Kimhi also gives the midrash’s sharper reading of the double “LORD”: as the LORD lives, you shall not kill him, and if you do, as the LORD lives, I will kill you.

traditions.source: Ambrose, On the Duties of the Clergy
traditions.text: Ambrose sets this chapter against the philosophers’ tale of a ring that made its wearer invisible, the ring of Gyges in Plato’s Republic, told to ask whether a wise man would sin if no one could see. Why imagine a ring, he asks, when Scripture shows a man who could have killed the king unseen and taken the kingdom, and chose innocence over safety? He retells the spear and the cruse and notes that David still had to flee, for he never put his own safety before innocence.

27.overview:
Sure that Saul will catch him one day, David takes his six hundred men and their households over to Achish, king of Gath, and Saul stops hunting him. David asks for a town of his own away from the royal city, and Achish gives him Ziklag. From there David raids the Geshurites, Gezrites and Amalekites in the desert toward Egypt, kills every man and woman so that no one can report him, and brings the flocks and goods back to Achish. Asked where he has raided, he names the south of Judah and its allied clans. Achish believes him and expects to keep him as a servant for ever.

The chapter turns on a lie, and the narrator tells it without comment. David fights Israel’s old enemies while letting his Philistine lord think he is fighting Israel. The deception works so well that it traps him: in 28:1 Achish orders him to march against Saul.

27.hermeneutics:
David calls Gath “the royal city” (v. 5), and it was a large one. Tell es-Safi, the site most scholars identify as Gath, has been excavated since 1996 by a team under Aren Maeir. By the 10th–9th centuries BC the city had spread into a lower town and covered some 40–50 hectares, among the largest in the land, until Hazael of Damascus took it about 830 BC (2 Kings 12:17). Six hundred armed men and their families inside such a capital would live under the king’s eye every day. David’s request for “a town in the country” (v. 5) is a request for distance, and the raids of vv. 8–11 depend on it.

Where Ziklag lay is still disputed. About a dozen sites have been proposed, among them Tel Sera' and Tel Halif in the northern Negev. In 2019 Yosef Garfinkel and his colleagues argued for Khirbet al-Ra'i near Lachish, where a settlement with Philistine-style remains of the 12th–11th centuries BC is followed by a rural village of the early 10th century that ended in a heavy fire. Other scholars reject the identification and propose another ancient name for the site. The question matters for the story, because v. 6 treats Ziklag as a border town that passed from Philistine hands to Judah’s kings.

The length of the stay differs between texts. The Hebrew of v. 7 reads literally “days and four months,” and the KJV takes “days” in its sense of a full year. The Septuagint has only “four months,” and Josephus gives four months and twenty days.

notes: **Achish** is named 7 times (vv. 2, 3, 5, 6, 9, 10, 12), and every scene runs through him: the welcome, the gift of Ziklag, the question, the misplaced trust.
**Dwell:** the verb *yashav* comes 6 times (vv. 3, 5 twice, 7, 8, 11), for David’s households, for the town he asks for, and for the peoples who had dwelt in the south since of old.
**No witness:** twice David leaves neither man nor woman alive (vv. 9, 11), and v. 11 gives the reason in David’s own words, lest they tell on him.

Chapter 27 is the outline’s whole section on David among the Philistines, but its story keeps going. Verses 28:1–2 continue the talk with Achish, and ch. 29 takes it up again after the scene at Endor. Ziklag, given here, is the base David returns to in 30:1, and it is where he hears of Saul’s death (2 Samuel 1:1).
**Back:** David’s first visit to Gath ended with him feigning madness to escape (21:10–15); this time he comes with six hundred men and is welcomed.

traditions.text: Josephus has David ask for a village because living in the city made him a burden to his host. He adds that Ziklag became a place David and his sons loved when he was king and counted as their own inheritance. In his telling David also sent part of the plunder to Achish as a free gift, and Achish hoped David had fought his own nation and would stay as his servant for life.

Why should David fear Saul more now, just after Saul blessed him and promised to do him no harm (26:21, 25)? Abarbanel answers that Saul’s jealousy grew whenever he saw the LORD with David, and David knew it would flare again. He adds that David believed God’s promises of the kingdom, yet would not rely on a miracle to keep him alive in Saul’s reach, and so took the ordinary means of escape.

When Esau plots in his heart (Genesis 27:41), the midrash sorts people into two kinds. The wicked are in the power of their hearts; the righteous hold their hearts in their power. Its examples of the second kind are Hannah, Daniel, and David here, who “said in his heart” (v. 1), and it compares them to God, who spoke in his heart after the Flood (Genesis 8:21). David’s decision to leave the land is read as a judgment he controlled, not a panic.

Kimhi asks how David could go back to Achish after barely escaping him in ch. 21. The first time, he answers, David came alone and in disguise and panicked when recognized. Now he came with six hundred men and sent word ahead that he had become hateful to Saul and his people and would help Achish fight Israel, and so Achish received him in peace.

On “Ziklag pertaineth unto the kings of Judah unto this day” (v. 6), Kimhi notes that Joshua had already listed Ziklag in Judah (Joshua 15:31). Either that list named it by its later owner, he suggests, or the Philistines had taken it and David’s holding made it crown property. That, he says, is why the verse speaks of Judah’s kings and not of the tribe.

Kimhi explains how the raids stayed secret. The Geshurites, Gezrites and Amalekites had lived in that country from of old, toward Shur and Egypt, at peace with everyone, so they kept no guard. David struck them, took great spoil, and because he left no one alive, no one knew who had done them this harm.

Kimhi explains the places David named to Achish (v. 10). The Jerahmeelites were a clan of Judah, descended from Jerahmeel son of Hezron, and the Kenites were the family of Jethro, who had joined Israel and lived among the people of Judah, as Judges 1:16 records. Their towns lay near one another, he notes, which is why the same names return among the places that receive David’s gifts after the Amalekite raid (30:29).

Rashi will not read the “days” of v. 7 as a year. Following the chronology of Seder Olam, he holds that Saul reigned only four months after Samuel’s death, and David went to Achish only after Samuel died (25:1), so the stay was four months and a few days. He checks the figure by adding up Eli’s forty years, the ark’s twenty at Kirjath-jearim, Samuel’s lifetime, and David’s years at Hebron.

Isaac Abarbanel rejects that short chronology. He reads “days” as years, as in Pharaoh’s “two full years” (Genesis 41:1), and accepts the Aramaic Targum’s reading, a year and four months, as the true text; Achish himself later speaks of David being with him “these days, or these years” (29:3). He also takes “unto this day” (v. 6) as a note by the compiler of Samuel, whom he identifies as Jeremiah.

Abarbanel refuses the reading that David was raiding Achish’s own subjects, which would repay kindness with treachery and could not have stayed hidden for long. He argues that the Geshurites, Gezrites and Amalekites were Achish’s enemies, far off toward Shur, so David betrayed no one by striking them. David killed his captives only so that no witness could contradict his account, and Abarbanel says plainly that he argues at length to clear David of betrayal.

28.overview:
Achish tells David he must march with the Philistines, who camp at Shunem while Saul gathers Israel on Gilboa. Saul is terrified, and the LORD does not answer him by dreams, by Urim, or by prophets. Though he had banished mediums, he goes by night in disguise to a woman with a familiar spirit at Endor and asks her to bring up Samuel. She sees Samuel, cries out, and realizes her visitor is Saul. Samuel’s words are hard: the kingdom is torn from Saul for his disobedience over Amalek, and tomorrow Saul and his sons will be with him. Saul collapses, and the woman kills her calf to feed him.

The narrator says what happened without saying how. The text says the woman “saw Samuel” (v. 12) and that “Samuel said to Saul” (v. 15), yet Saul must ask what she sees and knows Samuel only from her description of an old man in a mantle (vv. 13–14).

historicalContext.text: Not named in the text. The Talmud credits Samuel; asking how the book could then record his death, it quotes v. 3 and answers that Gad the seer and Nathan the prophet completed it (Bava Batra 15a).

28.hermeneutics:
Calling up the dead to question them was an old practice in Israel’s world. In the twelfth tablet of the Babylonian Gilgamesh epic, an Akkadian version of an older Sumerian poem, the god Nergal opens a hole in the earth at Ea’s word, and the spirit of Enkidu comes up out of the ground “like a wind.” The friends embrace, and Gilgamesh asks what he has seen of the laws of the underworld. Israel’s law forbade the practice (Leviticus 20:27; Deuteronomy 18:11), but the chapter speaks its language: the woman is asked to “bring up” the dead (vv. 8, 11), the figure comes “out of the earth” (v. 13), and Isaiah 29:4 pictures a familiar spirit’s voice whispering out of the dust.

The woman’s first words are “I saw gods ascending out of the earth” (v. 13). The word is *elohim*, and the verb is plural. Family religion in Syria joined household gods and the dead: wills from Emar on the Euphrates (13th century BC) charge an heir to honor the testator’s “gods and dead,” and a will from Nuzi makes a similar pairing. Calling a ghost elohim, a being more than human, fits that background, and it explains Saul’s sharp question, “What form is he of?” (v. 14).

Greek-speaking readers met the woman under another name. The Septuagint calls her an *engastrimythos*, one who speaks from the belly, a word Greeks used for ventriloquists and for oracle-givers possessed by a spirit; the Latin Vulgate calls her a *pythonissa*. These words framed the early Christian debate. If she was a belly-speaker, the voice might be a spirit’s or her own rather than Samuel’s.

rows.text: Two armies and a silent God

notes: **Hearken to the voice:** the verb *shama'* comes 5 times (vv. 18, 21 twice, 22, 23). Saul “obeyedst not the voice of the LORD” (v. 18); the woman has obeyed Saul’s voice (v. 21) and asks him to hearken to hers (v. 22), and he does (v. 23).
**Bring up:** the verb *alah* comes 6 times (vv. 8, 11 twice, 13, 14, 15), ending in Samuel’s complaint, “Why hast thou disquieted me, to bring me up?”
**No answer:** the LORD “answered him not” (v. 6), and Saul repeats it to Samuel (v. 15), naming dreams and prophets but leaving out the Urim.

Chapter 28 stands alone in the outline, but it interrupts another story. Verses 1–2 carry on David’s service to Achish from ch. 27, and ch. 29 steps back to the Philistine muster at Aphek before the armies reach Jezreel (29:1, 11). Saul hears his sentence in the same days that David is sent home from the battle that will kill Saul.

**Back:** v. 3 repeats Samuel’s death and burial at Ramah (25:1), and vv. 17–18 repeat his sentence after the war with Amalek (15:28). **Forward:** “to morrow” (v. 19) comes true on Gilboa, where Saul and his three sons die “that same day together” (31:6).

traditions.date: LDS edition of the King James Bible, 1979
traditions.text: The Church’s footnote to v. 14 states a position: “This cannot be a bona fide vision from God,” brought about as it was by a spiritualist medium. It points to v. 15 and adds that the effect of the experience was to destroy all hope, citing v. 20 and 31:1–4. The footnote to v. 3 explains that Saul had banished such practitioners as Leviticus 20:27 and Deuteronomy 18:9–11 required.

traditions.date: LDS edition of the King James Bible, 1979
traditions.text: The footnotes explain the LORD’s silence (v. 6) with Restoration scripture: the Lord will be slow to hear those who would not hearken (Mosiah 11:24), and slow to answer the prayers of those slow to hear him (D&C 101:7). At v. 15 they cite D&C 1:33, that the Spirit will not always strive with man, and at v. 18 the Lord’s words “I command and men obey not” (D&C 58:32).

A thematic link; the Church’s footnotes to this chapter cite the Topical Guide instead. Nephi copies Isaiah’s warning against those who urge people to seek mediums and wizards that “peep and mutter,” and asks whether a people should not seek unto their God. His wording of the question, “for the living to hear from the dead,” differs from the shorter, harder line in the KJV of Isaiah 8:19.

Ben Sira’s praise of famous men ends Samuel’s entry with this night: after his death “he prophesied, and shewed the king his end,” lifting up his voice from the earth to blot out the people’s wickedness. For this Jewish sage the speaker was Samuel and the prophecy was his. Augustine, below, answers doubters with this verse.

Josephus tells a true raising: the woman, not knowing who Samuel was, called him out of Hades, and Samuel told her who her visitor was. Then he stops to praise her. Though Saul had outlawed her trade, she pitied a stranger, killed the one calf she had raised by hand, and sought no reward, knowing he was about to die, and Josephus urges his readers to imitate her.

Here the woman is Sedecla, daughter of a Midianite, who says she has raised the dead for the Philistines for forty years and never seen such a sight: Samuel in a white robe with a mantle over it, led by two angels. Samuel tells them not to boast, for neither king nor woman brought him up; a command God gave him in life sent him to speak. Saul answers that he will go to die with his sons, hoping his death may atone for his sins.

The midrash gives rules for the practice: the one who raises a ghost sees it but cannot hear it, the one who asks hears but cannot see, and anyone else neither sees nor hears. So the woman saw Samuel, Saul heard him, and Abner and Amasa, the two men with him, perceived nothing. She knew her visitor was the king because a ghost rises face down for a commoner and face up for a king, and Samuel’s mantle is the little coat his mother made him (2:19).

Rabbi Elazar wept at v. 15: if Samuel, raised by a medium, feared he was being summoned to judgment, how much more should we. The Talmud reads the woman’s plural “gods ascending” (v. 13) as two figures, Samuel and Moses, whom the frightened Samuel brought up with him. Elsewhere Rabbi Yohanan takes “with me” (v. 19) to mean that Saul would share Samuel’s place, his sins forgiven.

Kimhi reports a dispute among the Geonim, all of whom held necromancy to be empty. Samuel ben Hophni said Samuel never rose: the woman knew Saul at once, used a hidden voice speaking low, and drew her message from what everyone knew of Amalek, David and Nob, guessing the rest. Saadia and Hai said she could do no such thing, but God himself raised Samuel to tell Saul his fate, which is why she screamed. Kimhi raises objections against both.

Gersonides offers a third explanation: nothing came up and nothing was spoken outside the mind. The woman’s rites stirred her imagination so that she saw a figure, and Saul, who still had some prophetic power (10:11), heard words in his own stirred imagination, joining what Samuel had told him in life to a true foresight of the defeat.

Justin offers the scene as proof that souls survive death: the soul of Samuel “was called up by the witch,” as Saul demanded. He draws a further lesson. If the souls of righteous men and prophets could fall under such powers, Christians should pray at death, as Jesus did on the cross, that their souls not fall into the hands of any evil power.

Tertullian denies that a demon can drag the soul of any saint, much less a prophet, out of its rest. What Saul met was the “Pythonic” spirit, permitted to represent Samuel, for Satan can transform himself into an angel of light (2 Corinthians 11:14). He compares the magicians’ serpents before Pharaoh, solid to the eye but a lying deceit.

Origen insists it really was Samuel. The narrator of Scripture is the Holy Spirit, he argues, and it is the narrator who says “the woman saw Samuel” (v. 12). No petty demon could prophesy that the kingdom would pass to David. Samuel’s being among the dead is no scandal, for Christ also went down there, as a physician goes where the sick are.

traditions.source: Eustathius of Antioch, On the Belly-Myther
traditions.text: Eustathius wrote a whole treatise against Origen’s sermon. The apparition, he argues, was the devil in Samuel’s shape: Saul himself saw nothing, the false Samuel only repeated what the real Samuel had said in life, and its one new prediction was a guess. Scripture reports what its characters said without vouching for it, as it reports the prophets of Baal.

traditions.source: Augustine, On the Care of the Dead
traditions.text: Augustine leaves the question open. Samuel appeared and foretold what would befall Saul, he writes, though some think a spirit fit for such evil works took his likeness. Against them he cites Sirach’s praise that Samuel prophesied after death, and if that book is questioned, he points to Moses, who died and yet appeared with Elijah to the living.
traditions.cite: On the Care to Be Had for the Dead 15.18

29.overview:
The Philistine armies muster at Aphek, and David and his men march at the rear with Achish. The Philistine commanders see “these Hebrews” and object. Achish vouches for David, but they will not take into battle the man the women sang about, who might win back Saul’s favor with their heads. Achish tells David, as kindly as he can, to go home. David protests that he has done nothing wrong, then leaves at first light for the land of the Philistines, while the Philistines go up to Jezreel.

The chapter gets David out of an impossible battle without any choice of his own. He never says whether he would have fought Saul, and his protest that he wants to fight “the enemies of my lord the king” (v. 8) does not say which king he means. The Philistines’ suspicion settles the question for him.

historicalContext.text: Aphek, at the springs of the Yarkon near the coast, where the Philistines muster; Israel camps by a spring in Jezreel; David turns back south toward Ziklag.

29.hermeneutics:
Aphek stood at the springs of the Yarkon river, east of modern Tel Aviv, where the coastal road squeezed between the marshes and the hills. It was the natural place for a Philistine army to gather before marching north and then inland to the Jezreel valley, and it is where the Philistines camped before the battle in which the ark was taken (4:1). Chapter 28 already has the armies facing each other at Shunem and Gilboa (28:4), so ch. 29 steps back in time to the muster. The Philistines do not go up to Jezreel until its last verse (v. 11).

Foreign fighters often served kings in this age, sometimes close to the king’s person. Egyptian reliefs of Ramesses II’s battle at Kadesh (about 1274 BC) show Sherden warriors, a sea people with horned helmets and round shields, among his guard, though Egyptian texts had earlier described the Sherden as raiders from the sea. Achish had offered David that kind of post, “keeper of mine head for ever” (28:2). His commanders see the risk: a foreign band at the rear could turn in battle, and David had a master to make peace with (v. 4).

The Greek text differs in two places. In v. 1 the Septuagint has Israel camped “in Endor which is in Jezreel,” where the Hebrew has “by a fountain,” linking the camp to the town of Saul’s night visit. In v. 10 it gives Achish a longer speech, sending David back to the place he had appointed him and telling him to harbor no evil thought, for he is good in Achish’s sight.

structure.summary: No strong pattern; the chapter moves in sequence, a dispute in the camp framed by two marches (vv. 1–2, 11).
notes: **Found no fault:** “found” comes 3 times (vv. 3, 6, 8). Achish twice says he has found nothing against David, and David throws the word back at him: “what hast thou found in thy servant?”
**Good in my sight:** “good” comes 3 times (vv. 6 twice, 9) and “in the eyes of” 4 times (vv. 6 twice, 7, 9), always Achish’s view of David against the lords’ view.
**Adversary:** the commanders fear David will be to them a *satan*, an adversary, in the battle (v. 4).
**Commanders and lords:** the princes (vv. 3, 4, 9) make the objection, and the five lords (vv. 2, 6, 7) carry it, so Achish yields to both.

Chapter 29 opens the outline’s last section, which moves between two fronts: David sent away from the Philistine army and rescuing his own people at Ziklag (chs. 29–30), and Saul dying on Gilboa (ch. 31). It picks up from 28:1–2, where Achish first ordered David to the war.

**Back:** the commanders quote the women’s song of 18:7, as Achish’s servants did at David’s first visit to Gath (21:11). **Forward:** sent home, David reaches Ziklag on the third day and finds it burned (30:1).

traditions.text: Pseudo-Philo gives the Philistines a reason for choosing this moment to attack. They say to one another that Samuel the prophet is dead and there is no one left to pray for Israel, and that David, who used to fight for Israel, has become Saul’s adversary and is no longer with him. So they gather to avenge the blood of their fathers. When Saul sees that Samuel is dead and David gone, his hands go slack.

The Aramaic translation has the commanders ask “What are these Judeans?” where the Hebrew says Hebrews (v. 3), naming David’s men by the tribe and kingdom they came from. In v. 9 Achish compares David to an angel of the LORD, with the divine name where the Hebrew has God. Both small changes make the scene speak in the terms of later Jewish readers.

Josephus makes Achish’s offer at the start of the campaign a reward to come: he would make David keeper of his body after the victory, if the battle went well. Josephus says the promise was made on purpose to sharpen David’s zeal, and David readily agrees, saying the time had come to repay his host’s kindness and hospitality.

In Josephus the commanders ask at whose invitation these Hebrews had come and urge Achish to send David away before he could do their friends harm. Achish then gives David a face-saving errand: go back within a day to the place I gave you and guard my country against raiders. That errand leads straight into the Amalekite raid that follows, and Josephus tells the two stories as one continuous section.

Achish says David has been with him for days or years (v. 3). Kimhi, who holds that David stayed only about four months, reads this as warmth: I know him for good as if he had been with me for years. On “the heads of these men” (v. 4) he explains that the commanders meant their own heads, speaking of themselves at a polite distance, as people do when the subject is their own death.

Kimhi notices that a Philistine king swears “as the LORD liveth” (v. 6). Everyone grants that Israel’s God is the first cause, he says, and Achish, swearing an oath to David, swore by the name David believed in. A pagan king’s oath by the LORD becomes a courtesy to his guest.

Gersonides faces the hard question directly: how could David agree to march against Israel? He answers that David was compelled, living under Achish and having led him to believe that he raided Israel. David’s real intention, he says, was to be an adversary to the Philistines in the battle and frustrate their plans, which their trust in him would make easy. In that reading the commanders’ fear in v. 4 was justified.

Abarbanel rejects Gersonides’ answer. A man like David, he says, would not repay Achish’s kindness with treachery, even to a Philistine king. In his view David meant only to stand beside Achish as the bodyguard he had been named (28:2), neither fighting Israel nor helping the Philistines, and his vague reply, “thou shalt know what thy servant can do” (28:2), was chosen to allow that. He connects Psalm 139, on the God who searches the heart, to David’s hidden purpose.

Abarbanel sets out the commanders’ two reasons: David might win back Saul with Philistine heads, and he had always hated the Philistines and killed them by tens of thousands. He gives their worry the form of an old proverb: how can the mouse be left in the keeping of the cat? The song the commanders quote (v. 5) proves the point, since it praises David for killing Philistines by the ten thousand, and such a man could hardly turn into their helper.

Why did David protest at first and then agree? Abarbanel notes that the commanders objected to David alone, not to his men. Singled out, David asked what fault Achish had found in him; when Achish included “thy master’s servants” (v. 10) and sent them all home, the dismissal no longer marked David personally, and he accepted. The early start, Abarbanel adds, spared them the shame of being seen leaving a battle.

30.overview:
David and his men reach Ziklag on the third day and find it burned. Amalekite raiders have carried off the women and children, David’s two wives among them, though they killed no one. The men weep until they can weep no more and talk of stoning David, but he “encouraged himself in the LORD his God” (v. 6) and asks through Abiathar’s ephod whether to pursue. Two hundred men, too exhausted to go on, stop at the brook Besor. An abandoned Egyptian slave, revived with food, leads the rest to the raiders’ camp, where David falls on the feasting Amalekites and recovers everyone and everything. He shares the spoil with the two hundred and sends gifts to the elders of Judah.

The chapter is built on the word “recover.” The LORD promises that David will “without fail recover all” (v. 8), and the text reports that he did, “neither small nor great” missing (v. 19).

historicalContext.text: Not named in the text. The Talmud credits Samuel, with Gad and Nathan completing it (1 Chronicles 29:29); many scholars see it as part of a larger history compiled in the 7th–6th century BC from older sources.

historicalContext.text: Unknown. Tradition places it soon after the events (11th–10th century BC); many scholars date its final form to the 7th–6th century BC, drawing on older court and prophetic sources.

historicalContext.label: Date of events
historicalContext.text: The same days as Saul’s last battle (ch. 31), traditionally about 1010 BC; David reaches Ziklag on the third day after leaving Aphek (v. 1).

historicalContext.label: Setting (events)
historicalContext.text: Ziklag in the western Negev; the pursuit crosses the brook Besor into the desert. The towns that receive David’s gifts (vv. 27–31) lie in the Negev and hill country of Judah, as far north as Hebron.

30.hermeneutics:
The Egyptian names the districts his band raided: the south of the Cherethites, the land belonging to Judah, and the south of Caleb (v. 14). The Negev was a patchwork, each stretch of grazing land and wells held by a people or a clan; 27:10 adds the south of the Jerahmeelites and of the Kenites. The Cherethites were probably a people of Aegean origin settled beside the Philistines. Zephaniah 2:5 calls the Philistine coast “the nation of the Cherethites,” the Septuagint there translates the name as “Cretans,” and Amos 9:7 brings the Philistines from Caphtor, usually taken to be Crete. The Amalekites had struck Philistine and Judahite land alike (v. 16), and David’s later royal guard would be “the Cherethites and the Pelethites” (2 Samuel 8:18).

The brook Besor is the Nahal Besor, the Wadi Ghazzeh of Arabic, the largest stream bed in the northern Negev. It rises in the central Negev highlands and runs northwest to the sea at Gaza, a dry channel most of the year that floods after heavy rain. To cross it was to leave the farmed fringe for open desert. The men who stopped there (vv. 9–10) had marched from Aphek to Ziklag in three days (v. 1) and then set out again at once, after weeping until they had no strength left (v. 4). The two hundred who stayed with the baggage are the cause of the quarrel over the spoil in vv. 21–25.
