structure.summary: No strong pattern; the chapter moves in sequence, from loss (vv. 1–6) to recovery (vv. 16–20) to the sharing of what was recovered.
notes: **Recover:** the verb *natsal* comes 5 times (v. 8 twice, v. 18 twice, v. 22), from the promise to the report; v. 19 sums it up with a different verb, “David recovered all.”
**All:** “all” comes 9 times (vv. 6, 16 twice, 18, 19 twice, 20, 22, 31), stressing that nothing was lost.
**Spoil:** *shalal* comes 6 times (vv. 16, 19, 20, 22, 26 twice), moving from the raiders’ feast to “David’s spoil” (v. 20) to “a present for you” (v. 26).
**Three days:** David arrives on the third day (v. 1), the Egyptian had gone three days without food (v. 12), and his master had left him three days before (v. 13).

Chapter 30 runs alongside the battle on Gilboa. It begins as David reaches home from Aphek and ends with gifts to the elders of Judah’s towns, Hebron last of all (v. 31). In 2 Samuel 2:1–4 those men of Judah anoint David king at Hebron. Chapter 31 then tells the other front.

**Back:** Amalek is the people Saul failed to destroy (ch. 15), the failure Samuel named at Endor (28:18). **Forward:** 2 Samuel 1:1 opens with David two days back in Ziklag after “the slaughter of the Amalekites.”

traditions.text: Josephus has David, after tears had failed him, raise his mind to God and ask Abiathar the high priest to put on his priestly garments and inquire. He paints the Amalekite camp as a drunken feast: men cut down at table, others as they drank to one another, others asleep from their full bellies. In his account the slaughter lasted from the first hour of the day to evening, and four hundred escaped on dromedaries and camels.

Abarbanel asks why the Amalekites burned Ziklag and no other town. His answer: they meant to leave David no base, since from Ziklag he had been raiding their land (27:8). He also notes that “smitten Ziklag” (v. 1) cannot mean they killed its people, since v. 2 says they slew no one; they razed the town and took the people away.

Why did the people want to stone David (v. 6)? Abarbanel first allows that they blamed him for taking every fighting man to Achish’s war and leaving Ziklag open. He prefers another reading: David grieved so much for his own two wives that he was slow to act, and the men, who had lost sons and daughters, asked why his grief should outweigh theirs. Seeing this, David put the grief away and strengthened himself in the LORD.

Kimhi explains what it meant that David “encouraged himself in the LORD his God” (v. 6). He set his hope in God, held himself back from collapsing under the disaster, and turned grief into a decision to pursue, which is why the very next words are his call to Abiathar for the ephod. On v. 26 he notes that the Hebrew has a singular, “his friend,” used for the whole group, so the gifts went to all of David’s friends among Judah’s elders.

The Talmud uses v. 8 for a rule of the Urim. Questions are normally asked one at a time, and if two are asked together only the first is answered; but when the matter is urgent both may be asked, and both are answered. David asked whether to pursue and whether he would overtake, and he was told both. The passage adds that a prophet’s dire word may be withdrawn, but a decree of the Urim cannot.

Reading Psalm 27 as David’s, the midrash finds this chapter in it: the evildoers who came to eat his flesh are the Amalekites who raided Ziklag. The battle lasted until the evening of the next day (v. 17), and an unusual plural form in the Hebrew leads Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi to count two nights and a day. God lit the night fighting with shooting stars and lightning, hence the psalm’s “thou wilt light my candle” (Psalm 18:28).

The Talmud uses v. 17 to settle what *neshef*, the KJV’s “twilight,” means. If David fought from evening to evening, the verse would have used one word twice; since it says from neshef to evening, neshef here must be the dawn. Rava concludes that the word covers both twilights, when night passes into day and when day passes into night.

The Talmud takes medical advice from vv. 11–12. A man faint with hunger should be given honey and sweet things to restore his sight, but Abaye says only after other food, since before a meal sweets merely whet the appetite. The Egyptian was given bread and water first, then the cake of figs and the raisins, and only then “his spirit came again to him.”

The Mishnah allows a king to break through fences to make his road, and no one may protest. The Jerusalem Talmud finds the proof in v. 20, where David’s men drive the flocks ahead and say “This is David’s spoil.” Kimhi, citing the rabbis, explains the scene: when field owners objected to broken fences, the drivers answered that the spoil was the king’s.

traditions.text: Gersonides reads the two hundred at the Besor less kindly than the text’s “so faint” (v. 10). In his view all agreed to march as far as the brook, and there the two hundred refused to go further, making themselves look exhausted, perhaps from fear of the raiders or from real weariness. David, seeing it, left them to guard the baggage.

Abarbanel notices how David answers the “men of Belial” (v. 22). Though he was their leader, he does not rebuke them as a ruler would but pleads with them as a brother, calling them “my brethren.” His argument is that the victory did not come from their own strength: the LORD kept them safe and gave the raiders into their hand, so the spoil was a gift to the whole company.

31.overview:
The Philistines rout Israel on Mount Gilboa. Jonathan, Abinadab and Malchi-shua are killed, and Saul, badly wounded by archers, asks his armourbearer to run him through before the uncircumcised can abuse him. When the armourbearer will not, Saul falls on his own sword, and the armourbearer dies with him. Israelites across the valley and beyond the Jordan abandon their towns. Next day the Philistines cut off Saul’s head, send the news through their land, put his armour in the house of Ashtaroth, and fasten his body to the wall of Beth-shan. The men of Jabesh-gilead march all night, take the bodies down, burn them, bury the bones under a tree, and fast seven days.

The chapter is short and stark, and it is not the only account of Saul’s death. In 2 Samuel 1 an Amalekite tells David he finished Saul off at his request, and the book leaves readers to weigh his story against this one.

historicalContext.label: Author
historicalContext.text: Not named in the text. The Talmud credits Samuel, with Gad and Nathan completing it (1 Chronicles 29:29); many scholars see it as part of a larger history compiled in the 7th–6th century BC from older sources.

historicalContext.label: Date written
historicalContext.text: Unknown. Tradition places it soon after the events (11th–10th century BC); many scholars date its final form to the 7th–6th century BC, drawing on older court and prophetic sources.

historicalContext.label: Date of events
historicalContext.text: Saul’s death, traditionally dated about 1010 BC, when David began to reign at thirty (2 Samuel 5:4).

historicalContext.label: Setting (events)
historicalContext.text: Mount Gilboa above the Jezreel valley; Beth-shan at the valley’s eastern end near the Jordan; Jabesh-gilead across the river in Gilead.

historicalContext.label: Parallel accounts
historicalContext.text: 1 Chronicles 10:1–14 retells the chapter; 2 Samuel 1:1–16 gives the Amalekite’s version; 2 Samuel 21:12–14 tells how David later reburied the bones in Benjamin.

31.hermeneutics:
Beth-shan has been dug more thoroughly than almost any other mound in the land. The University of Pennsylvania’s expedition of the 1920s found two temples in the stratum it called Level V, and the excavator Alan Rowe identified the northern one as the “house of Ashtaroth” where Saul’s armour was hung (v. 10) and the southern as the temple of Dagon where, in Chronicles, his head was fastened (1 Chronicles 10:10). The Hebrew University excavations under Amihai Mazar (1989–1996) date those temples to the 11th century BC, Saul’s own century. The names on the buildings remain Rowe’s proposal, but the town did have temples in that age where a victor could hang his trophies.

Displaying a defeated king’s head and body was a known act of triumph. Reliefs from Ashurbanipal’s palace at Nineveh show the head of the Elamite king Teumman, killed at the battle of Til-Tuba about 653 BC, carried off from the field, and in a later scene hanging from a tree in the royal garden while the king and queen dine. David had carried Goliath’s head to Jerusalem (17:54). The Philistines treat Saul the same way, sending word to their temples and their people (v. 9) and fixing the body on a city wall above the road through the valley.

Chronicles tells the story almost word for word but drops the burning, saying only that the men of Jabesh buried the bones under the oak (1 Chronicles 10:12). Burning the dead was not Israel’s custom, and the chapter gives no reason for it here.

notes: **Fell:** *naphal* comes 4 times: Israel’s slain fall (v. 1), Saul falls on his sword (v. 4), the armourbearer falls on his (v. 5), and the Philistines find Saul and his sons fallen (v. 8).
**Armour and armourbearer** share one Hebrew word, *keli*, which comes 6 times (vv. 4 twice, 5, 6, 9, 10). The man who carried Saul’s gear dies with him, and the gear ends in a Philistine temple.
**Sons:** “sons” comes 6 times (vv. 2 twice, 6, 7, 8, 12). They die with their father, as Samuel said they would (28:19), and are buried with him.
**By night:** the men of Jabesh go “all night” (v. 12), as Saul had gone by night to Endor (28:8, 25).

Chapter 31 ends 1 Samuel and the outline’s last section. It fulfils Samuel’s word at Endor, “to morrow shalt thou and thy sons be with me” (28:19), and David’s oath that Saul would “descend into battle” (26:10), the verse the Church’s footnote at v. 5 points to. In the Hebrew Bible there is no break here, and 2 Samuel 1 carries the news to David at Ziklag.
**Back:** Jabesh-gilead repays the rescue that began Saul’s reign (11:1–11). **Forward:** David blesses the men of Jabesh for burying Saul (2 Samuel 2:4–5).

traditions.text: Josephus stops the story to praise Saul as a model of courage. Saul knew from the prophet that he would die, yet he did not flee or betray his people, and he took his sons into the danger, judging it better that they die bravely than live on uncertainly. True courage, Josephus argues, belongs to those who go into battle knowing they will not return.

Josephus joins this chapter to 2 Samuel 1. Saul falls on his sword but cannot drive it through, so he asks a young Amalekite standing by to finish him; the youth does, takes the gold bracelet and the crown, and runs. Only then does the armourbearer kill himself. Josephus says the bodies were hung on crosses at Bethshan, and that the men of Jabesh buried them at a place called Aroura and mourned seven days with their wives and children.

Pseudo-Philo also has Saul fail to die on his sword. The man he calls to finish him is Edab, son of Agag the Amalekite king, and Saul recognizes Samuel’s word that one born of Agag would be his stumbling block. He sends Edab to tell David, “I have slain thine enemy,” and to ask David not to remember Saul’s hatred or his wrongs.

In the midrash Saul tells Abner and Amasa that Samuel promised victory and high office for his sons, and takes his three sons into battle. Reish Lakish says God called the angels to look at this man. People do not take their sons even to a feast, for fear of the evil eye, yet this one goes to war knowing he will die, takes his sons, and rejoices in the judgment that will strike him.

Genesis 9:5 is read as forbidding a man to take his own life, but the midrash finds in its first word, “surely,” a limit, and its first example is Saul. Like Hananiah, Mishael and Azariah, who were ready to die rather than worship an idol, Saul’s case is set apart from the prohibition. The midrash gives no further reason; v. 4 gives Saul’s own, fear that the uncircumcised would abuse him.

Kimhi reconciles this chapter with Chronicles, which says the Philistines fastened Saul’s head in the temple of Dagon (1 Chronicles 10:10). Both happened, he says: they cut off the head (v. 9) and hung it in Dagon’s house, and nailed the body, and his sons’ bodies too, to the wall of Beth-shan. Each book records what the other leaves out. The armour, he adds, was only his clothes and weapons, since the Amalekite had already taken the crown and bracelet.

The Aramaic Targum does not let the men of Jabesh burn the bodies. It renders v. 12 as burning over them, as is done over kings, and Rashi explains, citing the Talmud, that burning a king’s goods at his burial is allowed and is no heathen custom. Kimhi adds other readings: spices were burned, or the flesh had already decayed and was burned so the bones could be buried with honor.

traditions.text: Kimhi holds that Saul did not sin in taking his life, though Genesis 9:5 forbids it. Saul knew from Samuel that he was to die in this battle, and with the archers upon him he could not escape, so it was better to die by his own hand than be abused by the uncircumcised. He reads “Saul was dead” (v. 5) as near death, to fit the Amalekite’s story, and allows that the Amalekite may have lied to please David.

Why did the men of Jabesh fast seven days (v. 13)? Kimhi connects it to the seven days’ respite Nahash the Ammonite had given their city (11:3), the days in which Saul came and saved them. They remembered that rescue, he says, and that is why they took up Saul’s cause.

This midrash makes the men of Jabesh-gilead the model for comforting mourners. They asked whether they were not bound to show kindness to the man who had saved them from the disgrace of the Ammonites (ch. 11), and they marched all night to Beth-shan for the bodies. God, the midrash says, promised to repay them: when Israel is gathered at the end, Manasseh, the tribe of Gilead, will be gathered first, as “Gilead is mine, and Manasseh is mine” (Psalm 60:7).
